LITTLE CHICKS. Baby loves to see the chicks, Chicks in fluffy yellow, Baby loves to hear them chirp "I'm a saucy fellow." Baby loves to watch them peck, Stretching each an eager neck, Twicklety twee, it is such fun, • All in a hurry to see them run. Baby Jim loves all the chicks: All the chicks love baby Jim ! They fancy he's a big big bird, And tell such funny tales to him. Baby hears and answers all As they come running to his call. Twicklety twee! it is such fun, All in a harry to see them run. With a "chicklety chy ! chicklety choo ! Little bird, baby-boy, how do you do!" " Chicklety choo, chicklety chy, Why don't you spread your wings and fly?" .".80-Peep."

TarittitS. --I;ihen-th-e-hitittin comes off the back of a man's shirt his choler begins to rise. CAUSATION.—" What a time you've been about that egg, Mary I" "Yes, marm ; but the new kitchen clock has such large minutes!" An absent-minded woman in Kentucky put a corn plaster on a letter and stuck a postage stamp on her corn. The letter turned up "dead," but the corn is still alive. Tits VENEERING OF SOCIETY.—FIashy, rich merchants, who delight to overpower their guests with the splendour of their furniture, the provisions of their tables, and the jewels of their wives and daughters. A Quaker, giving evidence on a trial, was asked by one of the magistrates, who had been a carpenter, why he should not take off his hat? "It is a privilege we, as Quakers, are allowed." "If I had it in my power," said the angry Jus- tice, "I would have had your hat nailed to your head." "I thought," returned Obadiah, "thou hadst given over the trade of driving nails." Toms Tos was the name assumed in the 17th century by a clique of young blades of the "better" class, who de- lighted in breaking windows, upsetting sedan-chairs, molest- ing quiet citizens, and rudely caressing pretty women in the streets, These brawlers took successively many titular names, as Mans, Hectors, Scourers, afterwards Nickers, later still Hawcabites, and lastly Mohawks or Mohocks. . IMPREsSIONS OF A SALVATION ARMY SERVlCE.—rlardly has his voice died away when the captain's place is taken by the sergeant, a nice modest young girl, in a black jacket and brown straw hat; she never moves but simply stretches out her right hand, in her left she holds a well- worn hymn book. Very clearly and sweetly the young voice ascends in the hymn, "He is knocking, oh, how fair!" and goes on touchingly through all the gentle pleading. "That is Miss—, one of our sergeants," says my faggot- girl; and as I look down and round on women whose faces bear the impress produced upon their souls by the low sur- roundings of their lives, and by the cruel injustice with which they are too often treated, and from which injustice England has as yet no laws to protect them—as I look upon thousands of men who are only just beginning to guess at the Divine sonship to which it is possible for them to rise, 1 do not wonder at the stillness with which the young girl's sung message is received, and to me at least it seems most fitting that this daughter of the people should stand amongst "her am n folk" and sing to them of the love of Jesus. There was not the slightest touch of self-assertion or self-satisfaction about any one who took part in the service. Each of the officers was just absorbed in his or her mission. The vast crowd of hearers was not preached at, but to, and on the other hand the great God was not (as so often disgusts one in prayer meetings) addressed as an usual and told (if we may dare state such a thing) what He is to please to do.—Mrs. Charles Garnett, in Good Words. W. C. BRYANT ON MS MaontaoE.—Dar Mother' —I hasten to send you the melancholy intelligence of what has . happened to me. Early in the evening of the 11th day of the present mosth I was at a neighbouring house in this village. Several people of both sexes were assembled in one of the apartments, and three or four others, with my- self, were in another. At last came in a little elderly gen- tleman, pale, thin, with a solemn countenance, pleuritic voice, hooked nose, and hollow eyes. It was not long be- ,• fore we were summoned to attend in the apartment where he and the rest of the company were gathered. We went in and took our seats. The little elderly gentleman with the hooked nose prayed and we all stood up. When he had finished most of us sat down. The gentleman with the hooked nose then muttered certain cabalistic expressions, which I was too much frightened to remember, but I recol- lect that at the conclusion I was given to understand that I was married to a young lady of the name of Frances Fair- child, whont I perceived standing by my side, and I hope in the course of a few months to have the pleasure of intro- ducing her to you as your daughter-in-law, which is a matter of some interest to the poor girl, who has neither father nor mother in the world. I have not "played the • fool and married an Ethiop for the jewel in her ear." I looked only for goodness of heart, an ingenuous and affec- tionate disposition, a good understanding, Sic., and the character of my wife is too frank and single-hearted to suffer me to fear that I may be disappointed. Ido myself wrong. I did not look for these or any other qualities, but they trapped me before I was aware, and now I am married in spite of myself. Thus the current of destiny carries us all along. None but a madman would swim against the stream, and none but a fool would exert himself to swim with it. The best way is to float quietly with the tide. So mach for philosophy. Now to business. * * Your affectionate son. WILLIAM." - MRS. CARLYLIeS Larresos.—Here is one of the very latest, written nineteen days before her death, while her husband was delivering his rectorial address in Edin- burgh Dearest,—By the time you get this you will be out of your trouble, better or worse' but out of it, please God. And if ever you let yourself be led or driven into such a horrid thing again, I will never forgive you—never! What I have been suffering, vicariously, of late days is not to be told. If you had been to be hanged I don't see that I could have taken it more to heart. This morning, after • about two hours of off-and-on sleep, I awoke, long before daylight, to sleep no more. While drinking a glass of wine and eating a biscuit at five in the morning, it came into my mind, 'What is he doing, I wonder, at this moment?' and then, instead of picturing you sitting smoking up the stranger-chimney, or anything else that was likely to be, I found myself always dropping off into details of a regular execution !—Now they will be telling him it is time! now they will be pinioning his arms and saying last words! Oh, mercy! was I dreaming or waking? was I mad or sane? Upon my word, I hardly know now. Only that I have been having next to no sleep all the week, and that at the best of times I have a too fertile imagination,' like poor David.' When the thing is over I shall be content, however it have gone as to making a good 'appearance' or a bad one. That you have made your 'address,' and are alive, that is what I long to hear, and, please God! shall hear in a few hours. My imagination' has gone the length of representing you getting up to speak before an awful crowd of people, and, what with fuss, and bad air,' and confusion, dropping down dead. Why on earth did you ever get into this galley ? " Here is a characteristic ex- tract from a letter written to a friend who made a special effort to console her soon after the death of her mother : " Only think of my husband, too, having given me a little present he who never attends to such nonsenses as birth- days, and who dislikes nothing in the world so much as going into a shop to buy anything. even his own trousers and coats; so that, to the consternation of cockney tailors, lam obliged to go about them. Well, he actually risked himself in a jeweller's shop, and bought me a very nice smelling-bottle! I cannot tell yon how was his little gift made me, as well as glad; it was the first thing of the kind he ever gave to me in his life. In great matters he is al- ways kind and . considerate; but these little attentions, which we women attach so much importance to, he was never in the habit of rendering to anyone; his up-bringing, and the severe turn of mind he ids from nature, had alike indisposed him towards them. And now the desire to re- place to me the irreplaceable, makes him as good in little things as he need to be in great."—Letters and Memorials of Jane Welsh Carlyle. A DESEIRVED RenuKß.—Nothing is truer than the maxim that great events turn upon small hinges. Look well to , the small things of life, gentle reader, for upon them may depend the greater ones. These wholesome reflec- tions are inspired by an incident of a murder trial at Oroville last week. When the jury retired for consultation the foreman announced that the prisoner had conveyed to him the fact that he had only ten dollars left to "put up." "Ten dollars" exclaimed one of the twelve indignantly, "What does the fellow take us for? We are willing enough to do the fair thing Heaven knows; but ten dol- lars—i call that rubbing it in "If he had only made it' a dollar apiece," snorted another. "I tell you what it is, gentlemen," said the foreman, solemnly, "if this sort of thing keeps on.; they'll be having Chinese jurymen next, so the lawyers will get it all. There's little enough money in our profession now. It's about time we made an example of some one. S'posen we hang this man ?" And, by Jove, Tiotros."—The book is one in they did' —B,dancoFirrEsi.aneteßOPst LA° BALZAeS which the tremendous imagination of Balzae has fullest scope and shows at its ripest and most luxuriant. It is rich in human interest and emotion; in those culminations of reality, those blossomings of life and circumstance, which are the very stuff of romance; in those surprises of nature in the fact which are the essence of art. And it is rich, -too--richer, perhaps, than any modern book—in the matter and spirit of the grotesque. Balzac imagined and made it with a keen relish of the old esprit gaulozs in its rankest and least tolerable expressions, so that it is a work which anybody may be forgiven for declining to peruse, and which to many can only bring disgust and loathing. In form it is a masterpiece of imaginative pedantry; and in substance it is the strangest mixture (and one of the strongest) that ever came from the brain of man. It reminds you of Rabe- leis and of Boccaccio of Bichat and Antoine de la Salle, of La Cousine Bette and La Moyen de Parvenit, of Louis Philippe and Louis Onze, of the France of the Burgundians and Annagnacs and the France of Musset and George Sand. It is full of tragedy and coarse joviality, of moving drama and ribald wit, of brutal fan and violent and terrible ex- perience—so closely interwoven as to be inseparable, Bfl fused and run together as to make disintegration impossible. In this debauch of genius, this full-flooded and full-flavoured expression of romanticism at its strongest and most reck- less, Dore, the last of the romantics, found his happiest and greatest chance.-77te Magazine of Art.

A tradesman in a small town in Devonshire has sent 34,500 bunches of primroses to London during the last fort- night, all of which are gathered by children in the neigh- bourhood, who are paid at the rate of a penny for six bunches. POTATOES as A FIELD CROP.—Messrs. Sutton and Son have issued a small pamphlet describing the varieties of seed potatoes which they offer. Testimonials from various parts of the country, testifying to the excellence and pro- lific nature of the different kinds, are also given. - A meeting of the committee of the Essex Agriciiltural Society was held last week at Colchester, to arrange for the annual show to be held in that town. Mr. Bateman stated that he was constructing some silos at Brighlingsea, and in- vited the members to visit them during the show. Speaking a few days back at Remiremont, France, M. Maine announced that M. Claude, member of the Senate, had offered to the Department, for a period of fifteen years, a domain that belongs to him, for the purpose of founding a school of practical agriculture, and that the Qpuncil-General had voted an annual sum of £l6O towards the expenses. This practical school in the department of the Vosges will bring the total number up to nine. . THE IMPORTATION OF DISEASED CATTLE.—Mr. Duckham, M.P., chairman of the Central and Associated Chambers of Agriculture, has received a communication from Lord Car- lingford, Lord President of he Privy Council, consenting to receive, on the Bth prox., a deputation from the Central Chamber and other, imporea.nt agricultural bodies on the subject of the means of checking or preventing the impor- tation of diseased cattle from foreign countries. In a letter to 'Mr. Duckham the Prime Minister expresses his intention to be also present on the occasion if his other engagements permit. A. series of recommendations has been made by Professor Ciastance to the South Australian Government in reference to the Agricultural College, which establishment will shortly be ready to receive some 25 students. These are to be not less than 14 years of age. Students may enter the College in either of two departments—Department A, practical stu- dents • department B, science students. Practical students I will be required to work regularly on the farm, and to ac- quire a thorough knowledge of the various operations con- ducted on the farm, also of the different meehines and im- plements. A portion of each day will be devoted to instruc- tion in the college. Practically, students will be paid for the work performed by them, so that atvindustrious student will be able to get a good education at a very small expense. The Agricultural Society at Breslau has offered a prize of 1,000 marks to be given to the inventor of the most effectual and useful remedy for the destruction of field mice. Quite contrary to all expebtations, this announcement has already had 82 answers, and the time given for the compe- titors to send in their names is not yet complete. Unfortu- nately not one of them meets the requirements and con- ditions prescribed, for many of the remedies are already well known, some are not at all practicable, and others are not sure remedies. The society has resolved to renew the competition, which will be open till the autumn of this year, when the sum originally offered will be awarded to the best and most practical mouse trap sent to the society. Another prize of 2,000 marks will be given to the discoverer of an infe2tious and fatal disease which can be given to one mouse and ea carried to many. . THE PRICES or SHORTHORNS.—Those interested in the shorthorn ,will be satisfied with the result of the Birming- ham sale.' The 74 cows and heifers of the first class were all sold; highest price £53 us., average £33. The 17 heifers over two and not over three years were also sold; highest price £52 10s., average £3l. The 16 heifers sold out of 17 composing the third class averaged £24; highest price, £33 12s. ,The 14 heifer Calves averaged £lB las. 6d.; highest price, £37 16s. The 34 bulls over 20 months and not over 30 months averaged £39 13s. 6.6., all being sold;. highest price, £B9 ss. The 17 bulls over 30 months old were all sold; highest price £5O Bs.' average £3B 10s. 'All the 58 bulls over 15 and not over 20 months were sold at an aver- age of £37 14s. 6d.; highest price, £73 103. There were 16 bulls over 10 and not over 20 months old, 12 of which were sold at an average price of £65 19s. 6d.; highest price, £2lO. The bulls over 12 and not over 15 months old, 97 in num- ,ber, were all sold; highest price £llO 55., average £3B 10s. Of the 121 bull calves, 115 were sold; highest price £l7B 10s. average £37 3s. DEVELOPMENT OF WHEAT.—The researches made by Pierre some years ago on the growth of wheat and on the changes which take place at different stages in the life of the plant have recently been extended by Deherain and Meyer. They have published tables showing the percentage composition of various parts of the plant, at different dates, and others representing the weight per acre of the substances determined. The tables are far too voluminous to reproduce here, and we can only indicate the several conclusions which the authors derive from their tabulated results, which are the following. In 1881, at Grignon, France, the total dry matter of the wheat increased in weight up to harvest. Only in those plots in which the crop was allowed to re- main beyond harvest was a loss of dry matter observed, but this loss was considerable, and confirms the excellence of the practice of reaping as soon after maturity as possible. The pin in dry weight from June Ist to July 23rd con- sisted of starch and cellulose, the nitrogenous compounds and ash constituents remaining stationary during these last two months of growth, but the authors believe the cessation in the absorption of nitrogen and minerals to have been due to the peculiarities of the season. Bright days favoured the assimilation of carbohydrates (starch sugar, cellulose, &c.), while drought hindered the assimilation of nitrogen and mineral substances through the agency of the roots. THE VETERINARY REPORT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL, published on Tuesday evening, will be referred to with un- usual interest. It shows that the foreign supplies of live animals increased in 1882, notwithstanding the large falling off in the number of cattle from the United States. The deficiency from that country, which was due to the great increase in the price of meat in some of the large towns in the States, was more than compensated by the additional imports from Denmark, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Portugal. The total number of imported animals from out- side the United Kingdom was 1,483,838, against 1,284,711 in 1881. The falling off from the United States was in cat- tle only; there was an increase in sheep, the number being 58,922 in 1882, against 49,223 in 1881. It appears from the inspectors' returns for 1882 that the proportion of cargoes in which disease was detected among the animals was much less than in 1881. The total number of outbreaks of foot- and-mouth disease in 1882 was 1970; in 1881 it was 4,833. The animals attacked in 1882 amounted to 37,950; in 1881 the number was 183,046. The report states that "in com- parison with the number of live stock in the county these are insignificant, but in order to keep the disease within the limits to which it was confined it was necessary to impose restrictions which in some cases were extremely onerous, l' and it was not uncommon during the time to hear the cora- -1 - p atnt that the frequent reimposition of restrictions owing to accession of disease in different parts of the country caused more loss and inconvenience than were occasioned by the disease, while no progress seemed to be made towards its . complete extinction. , A New FERTILISING AGENT.—In England we flatter Ourselves that we know how to "sweeten the soil." In the t north of France they do it literally—with treacle! This statement is certainly startling, and fearing to jeopardise - even for a moment our reputation for sober sincerity, we hasten to shed a little light on this singular employment of sweetness. In the region just specified many of the farmers are also manufacturers. They not only cutivate the beet, but extract from it a sort of sugar, which, if we err not, is the pet abomination of every properly dignified British housewife. The refinement of this sugar leaves a residue of treacle, of molasses, or of what the French term "vinasses." Having arrived at the stuff last named, the force of 'refine- ment can no further go; vinasses are—or rather were for- merly—regarded as a waste product. Not knowing how otherwise to get rid of this liquid, the refining farmers dis- tributed it over their land by means of irrigation. Sweet are the uses of adversity, how ever; and out of this dire necessity arose an unexpected virtue. According to the chemists, this liquid contains all the fertilising agents which are absorbed from the soil by the parent beet. It therefore follows that if the vinasses be returned in sufil-* cient quantity no other manure need be used. Moreover, land thus dressed will for a time yield splendid crops of cereals, including wheat—a fact that oddly suggests the existence of a subtle affinity between the elementary consti- tuents of bread and treacle. Under this treatment, how- ever, cereal crops gradually deteriorate both in quality and quantity, unless the cultivator resort to the liberal use of phosphate of lime in addition to his vinasses.—Live Stock , Journal. A Clemons Tr= STORY.—A respectable inhabitant of Copford, named Joseph Bailey, recently had the misfortune to lose the two horses with which he earned his livelihood. Much commiseration was expressed for him by his neigh- bours, and the matter coming to the ears of the rector, the Rev. B. Ruck-Keene, that gentleman kindly undertook to write an appeal to the villagers in Bailey's behalf, with a view to obtain funds which should purchase him another horse. As an English gentleman and a Christian minister, the rector generously headed the subscription list with a donation of £2 10s., together with 10s. from the offertory fund, and further arranged to see the inhabitants at his end of the village on the subject, the remaining portion being allotted to other persons. The proceeds of the canvass amounted to a total of £9, and the rector called at the resi- dence of the intended recipient presumably Apr the purpose of handing over the amount. div.head: T. HE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 28 1883
div.p: T. HE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 28 1883
COTTAGE GARDENING.

HERBS.—Every well-informed wife knows the value of these for broths, &c. Their presence is indispensable where there is an attempt to serve tasty dishes. We have known cottagers make these more remunerative than anything in the garden by supplying their neighbours who may not have a garden with two or three pennyworth at a time. SAGE, so much esteemed in various stuffings, is apt to die off when the plants are four years old or more, 'According to the nature of the soil. From now until June is a good time to put in slips—that is slip off a branch with two or three small shoots by messing it down, which severs it from the parent plant; insert it in the ground in a shady cover, three inches deep, pressing the soil moderately firm. Any old plants having unduly long shoots should have them shortened back. This will induce them to throw up several young shoots. Autumn is the usual and proper time for cutting this back, as it secures a supply for the winter. We have found that the plants exist longer if only two- thirds of the shoots are taken off at that season and the remainder in spring, just as it starts to grow. THYME.—This may be increased by sowing seeds at the present time in a drill, half an inch deep, covering it over with a fine soil, by passing the ordinary soil of the garden through a half-inch sieve, or rubbing it with the hand. It is unreasonable to expect the plant which will be produced by such puny seeds to heave up heavy lumps of soil. Thyme may also be propagated by dividing the roots at this time, especially the lemon variety. This is highly appreciated by some cooks. Thyme succeeds best on light soil having a dry bottom. CHIVES will thrive in any soil, and is increased by divi- sion of the roots planted Gin, by 12in. MINT, if left alone too long, will from some cause or other die off entirely. When there are symptoms of decay it is advisable to select a fresh piece of ground. Cut out trenches 21n. deep and Sin. apart; in this lay the roots and cover over. The old beds will sometimes be taken posses- sion of by troublesome weeds that are not easily eradicated without partial injury to the mint. This also makes it de- sirable to make a fresh planting, and the old mint bed may be destroyed and the space devoted to a crop that offers greater facilities for cleaning. CAZIOMILE.—This herb is highly appreciated by rustics for its medicinal properties. A decoction of the flowers acts as a tonic; and if taken strong and warm as an emetic, and when applied to the face as t cataplasni in MO of neural- gia and toothache, they have a mollifying and soporific effect. The camomile will grow on any kind of soil, but it is longer lived on dry ones. We would therefore com- mend it to the notice of railway officials, who must be at a loss to know what to plant on some of the dry banks which they so commendably endeavour to cultivate. If the flowers are not required at home, we believe there is always a sale for them.

FRONT GARDEN.---Where there is a paucity of perennials the deficiency should be made up by sowing annuals, and to assist cottagers in their purchase we give a list of the best twelve we are acquainted with and are to be procured in one penny packets, a price certainly not very ruinous. Candytuft crimson, do. white, collensia bicolour, nemophilla insignia gilia tricolour, supinus nanus, mignonette, nastur- tium, Tom Thumb or mixed, marigold, Virginian stock red and white. Another dozen may be added -without ex- hausting the list. The wallflower is a hardy biennial and must be sown now, and another a month hence. This will give a succession of bloom; and whilst one may not stand over the winter so well, the other may. Canterbury bells and Sweet William are hardy biennials and may have a small sowing made, reserving some for June. They are to be procured in one penny packets. In sowing annuals we form a circular drill with the finger or blunt stick. In this the seeds are sown and the finest soil put over them. We write the name of the seed on a wooden label and place it in the centre: Another method is to procure the requisite number of sticks, split them at the top, and insert the empty seed packet in the slit, fixing the sticks in the centre of the patch to indicate that there is something sown, and when they c'ome in flower, if they are not known, it will be interesting to draw the packet out to see the name. We ought to have stated that the circular space which the seeds surround seldom exceeds 12in. diameter, and we sometimes

drop a few seeds in the centre of it. Annuals are usually left. too thick, six plants occupying the space requisite for one. Sweet peas are charming flowers. They have an agreeable perfume; they are of all colours, most suitable for cutting to put in the room or for a bouquet. They should be sown at once. If the soil is not good dig holes if t. deep, mix manure with the soil in the bottom, fill up the hole and add more to the. soil replaced- Two or three such patches adjacent to a wall or fence will be sufficient. THE WlNDOW.—Parrixo.—This is a term applied to the operation of transferring a plant from one pot to another. It is also applicable to the placing of a plant in a pot, though it may mit have been in one previous. To perform the first perplexes the uninstructed so much, that when they attempt to execute it they invariably ruin their plants or temporarily paralyse them. Yet the act is so simple that if we had our readers before us we could instruct them in 30 seconds by giving a practical illustration. The pot that is to receive the plant should be perfectly clean, and, with few exceptions, those from 41n. to flin. diameter will require one inch of drainage at the bottom and for this puipose pieces of broken flower pots are usually used. Select a piece that will partly cover the bottom ;. place it concave side down- wards, and on that one inch of such pieces as would pass through an inch sieve, with a sprinkling of smaller ones on the top, and on the whole a layer of decayed moss or half- decayed leaves, which are usually plentiful in autumn and should then be secured and stored for this and other pur- poses. Their use in this instance is to prevent the soil from filling up the interstices, thus obstructing the free passage of water through the crocks, involving serious consequences, which should be resolutely avoided. THE PRINTER'S DEVIL.-11.
[ST ANGLO-SCOTUS.]

Barbers are credited with having a patron saint in the spirit of Saint Louis, and that is perhaps, the reason they succeeded in executing their devil in the person of Olivier Ledain. Burglars, drunkards, fools, lawyers, thieves, and . even Scotch reformers are also credited with having patron saints; but the poor Printer alone is cursed with a satanic I imp. And this has been the case since the earliest times. In the sixteenth century at least, bell, book, or candle bad , evidently no terrors for the Printer's Devil. One of the most egregious of all literary blunders is that of the edition of the Vulgate, by Sixtus V. According to the elder Disraeli, his holiness carefully superintended every sheet of the work as it passed through the press; and, to the amaze- ment of the world, the work remained without a rival—it swarmed with errata! A multitude of scraps'were printed to paste over the erroneous passages, in order to give the true text. The book made a whimsical appearance with these patches, and the "heretiss" of the time exulted in this ludicrous illustration of so-called papal infallibility. The copies of the book that had been printed were called in, and attempts made to suppress it, but a few copies still remain, and at a sale one of the "Bibles of Sixtus V." fetched close upon a hundred guineas. The book itself, wi,h its blunders, was amusing enough; but the amuse- ment was intensified by the bull of the editorial Pope prefixed to the first volume, whick excommunicated all , printers who in reprinting the work should make any altera- . tion in the text! So we see that the man who took upon I himself to excommunicate kings, and who was bold enough to over-ride the rules made in the 24th session of the Council of Trent by making a Cardinal of his nephew, Alessandro D. Peretti (then only a mere youth of fourteen years of age), could not manage to lay or conquer the Printer's Devil. Let young Caxtonians—and old ones, for that Matter—at all times beware of the insidious advances of the chief satellite of King Carelessness. But Sixtus V. himself, as Pope, may be instanced as a notable example of "the exception that mars the rule." The exceptional instance of a lay Cardinal being admitted to Conclave did certainly occur when Sixtus V. was elected. It is a strange irony on the high-handed actions of Sixtus, that during the sixteen years' reign of Pope Gregory XVI., it befell him to create no less than 75 Cardinals, which are five more than • the Sacred College can count, according to the Bull of Sixtus V., then in force. What varied shapes and forms Nemesis takes! But to get back to mcdern times. Not long ago a gallant and dashing military officer found him- self described En one of the service newspapers by the extraordinary title of" Shovel Field Colonel." The com- positors then employed on the same paper must have certainly believed in the existence of "Horse Marines," seeing that a detachment of the "Jollies " were described as "Mariae Foot Artillery." But more apparently incredi- ble than any of the foregoing mistakes was the illus4ation of "mental fog" shown by a compositor fresh from a wavzgoose dinner, at which he had most probably met with or tasted the flash of pheasant for the first time. In the portion of an article on agrarian outrage in Ireland he had to set up, allusion was made to "peasants shooting their land- lords." He evidently confused the Pbasian bird with the human biped, for he asked the overseer "whether the writer had not made a mistake;" and on being told that the words in the copy were all right, he went back to his frame, remarking "that he knew the Irish were a funny lot of people, lint be could not see how it was possible for even an Irish pheasant to shoot a man!" In the same connection may be mentioned a curious mistake that was lately made iu one of the "society" papers. It occurred in the descrip- tion of the menu of an aristocratic dinner, and "oysters, fried and stewed,' were made to figure under the head of "fruit." I know all about vegetable tripe, and bird-nest soup; but oysters in connection with tree, bush, or runner, I never heard of. The compiler of the menu or the writer of the paragraph muse have been reading Lucian's "A Traveller's Tale," and have fallen asleep over the story of the island of cheese three miles in circuit, on which grew vines the grapes from which yielded milk, and on which stood a temple dedicated to Galatea, daughter of Nereus. The name of the queen of this curious island was said to be Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus. Lucian is kind ezough to explain that "Galatea signifies milk, so does Tyro signify cheese;" but the modern "seciety " metamorphist does not explain why oysters, fried or stewed, are classed under the denomination of "fruit." Possibly it may be that in the present genera- tion there exist direct lineal descendants of Lucian's "ox- headed people."
A child of seven or eight said that when the Bible speaks of "children's children" it must mean dolls.

Too many have no idea of the subjection of their temper to the influence of religion, and yet what is changed if the temper is not? If a man is as passionate, malicious, re- sentful, sullen, moody, or morose after his conversion as before it, what is he converted from or to ?—John Angell James.
THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.
THE PRISONERS AT BOW-STREET.

The examination of the men charged with treason-felony in connection with the recent discovery of explosives in London and Birmingham was resumed on Thursday at Bow- street before Sir James Ingham. The prisoners' names are Albert,deorge Whitehead, Thomas (Dr.) thallagher, Henry Wilson, Bernard Gallagher, Henry Dalton, John Curtin, and William Ausburgh. Mr. Poland, Mr. Pollard, and Mr. Wright appeared for the prosecution. Mr. G wirey, Mr. Preston, Mr. D. Smyth, Mr. Sims, and Mr. Brown were de- fending the prisoners, the two latter gentlemen appearing for the first time as counsel for Dr. Gallagher. Interest in the proceedings increases rather than diminishes, and the whole of the space on the bench was occupied by ladies and gen- tlemen who had succeeded in gaining admission to the court. Two clerks at the American Exchange, Strand, proved that Dr. Gallagher first visited the Exchange in November last. About April 4th he introduced a-man as Daniel Galer, and this young man, to the best of the Wit- nesses' belief, was one of the prisoners. Evidence was given by Birmingham witnesses to the effect that White- head, in February last, purchased large quan- tities of glycerine and nitric and sulphuric acid. John Boyd, police superintendent, of Glasgow, produced a statement made by Bernard Gallagher at the beginning of April, in which he mentioned Curtin, White- head, and his brother Daniel, and gave some account of their movements between Liverpool, Glasgow, London, and other places. A witness from Glasgow gave evidence as to finding employment for Curtin on the recommendation of Thomas Gallagher, and said he last saw Thomas Gallagher in October, 1882, when the prisoner said he had come over for a trip. Curtin left for Blackburn, after working for a few weeks in Glasgow. The witneas had saen Curtin at Gallagher's lodgings. The prisoners ware remanded till Thursday nest, when the depositions will be attested.

Some dynamite has been found on the Chatham fortifica- tions, but with no fuse attached or any indication to show that a serious attempt was intended. On Tuesday a quantity of explosive was found under a hedge in Swansea, and the public analyst, who has ex- amined the material, pronounces it to be dynamite. In consequence of a threatening letter received by the au- thorities at Rumford, two companies of the let Essex Rifles were paraded on Sunday evening, and ths rifles and aminu- OOP Were removed. At a Meeting of the Birmingham Watch Committee -on Tuesday, it was resolved, on the motion of the Mayor, that the question of the award to be given to •Detective-sergeint Price and the other officers engaged in the discovery of nitro-glycerine ba referred to a judicial sub-committee. It-is stated in a Renter's telegram from Washington, dated Wednesday, that at a Cabinet Council a hypothetical question was framed as to the proper policy to be pur- sued by the Government of the United States regarding the dynamite plot, and that the members expressed their views upon it: , In cunstquence of informeion in the possession of the authorities at Portsmouth. policemen in plain clothes have been detailed to watch the local branch of the Bank of Eng- land and the Inland Revenue offices, both of which are situ- ated in high-street. At the same time other precautions have been adopted to ensure the safeo of the buildings.

It is understood that the Post Office authoriaes have in- stituted, through the medium of one of the city detectives, a strict inquiry with a view to ascertain whether any cor- roboration eln be obtained of the extraordinary story told by a Post Office official named Guy of his having been kidnapped by a supposed Fenian. No information, how- ever, can be obtained that is at all likely to throw any light on the matter.

A letter intimating that a design was on foot to blow up the General Post Office in Dublin has been received by the authorities, and the document has been handed over to the police. Some unobtrusive precautions were taken on Sun- day, the police on duty around the building having been furnished with arms, and the utmost vigilance being ex- ercised. So far as it is known, however, nothing occurred to justify the warning. Further progress was made at Cork, on Saturday, in un- ravelling the branch of the dynamite conspiracy that as been discovered there, and with which the men Deasev and Flanagan, who were arrested at Liverpool and St. Helens respectively, are believed to be connected. Evidence was given showing that the two men Featherstone and O'Herlihy, had intercourse with Deasey, and that Deasey was coming to Flanagan, who had been asked to find him employment. Featherstone's real name, it appeara, is Edward O'B. Ken- nedy, and he is believed to be connected with the Birming- ham and other conspirators.

The Curragh Camp correspondent of the Dublin Express says :—" No small surprise was created here on Sunday by the issue of a private memorandum from the Major General commanding, addressed to officers commanding regiments in camp and Newbridge, informing them that the police had discovered the existence of a Fenian plot to make an attack on the Camp within the next few days. Orders have been issued accordingly for a large increase of the centres around the Camp. Civilians are to be excluded from the lines unless provided with passes. A large inlying picket is to remain under arms all night in future, the men composing it carrying 40 rounds each of ball ammunition, while patrols of cavalry and infantry ara to ex- amine-the surrounding country from tattoo to reveille." The quiet Welsh town of Holywell has just been disturbed from its equanimity by the report that an infernal machine had been found on the steps leading into the County Hall, and adjoining the police station. Two men noticed what appeared to be a copper canister on the steps, and immedi- ately gave information to the police, who took possession of the suspicious-looking contrivance, from one end of which projected a partly-burnt fuse. Upon examining the con- tents it was found tkey consisted of a great deal of smithy dust intermixed with a small quantity of gunpowder. The material was evidently quite incombustible. Superintendent Hughes and Sergeant Matthews at once made searching in- quiries, and soon ascertained, that the piece of copper piping had come from a local brewery, and that two foolish young fellows employed there had invented the supposed bomb and placed it where it was found, just for a lark, expecting that it would cause a great public sensation.

Don't remark that there's nothing new under the sun. There are sixty new styles of spring bonnets. "You seem to walk more erect than usual, my friend." "Yes, I have been straightened by circumstances,"

Josh Billings says—" A reputashun once broken may possibly be repaired, but the world will alwus keep their eyes on the spot where the krack was." The editor of the Albany Express says that the only rea- son why his dwelling was not blown away in a late storm was that there was a heavy mortgage on it. At a meeting of the Ambassadors held at the Foreign Office, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Earl Granville, the Danubian Convention was formally signed. The Prince of Wales, at the command of the Queen, held a levee at St. James's Palace, on Monday. Mr. Gladstone, the Lord Chancellor, and other ministers attended. Nothing so helps a newspaper as the imparting of useful information. "How shall I keep ants out of the sugar bowl ?" asks a correspondent. "Fill the sugar bowl with salt."

Lord Castlereagh made so many new words that Canning callcd him the literary coiner. "-He has got a mint in his mind," said he. "Mint in his mind !" rejoined Sheridan, "Would he had sage in his head !" A little boy had his long curls cut off the other day, and was annoyingly reminded of the fact by the remark of all his friends. Going with his family into the country, soon after his arrival he came running into the house in great sorrow crying—" Mamma, mamma, even the hens laugh at the;" they all say," Cut-cut-cut-got-your-hair-cut !"

How many people carry tbeir—tralle marks about with them and never know it. In a certain country township was a shoemaker, and he went to Professor Simon to be sub- jected to his phrenological, physiognomical, and physio- logical criticisms. The innocent cordonnier no sooner reached the platform than the professor said, in his prompt paragraphic style, "Keen, intelligent face, sharp eyes; you would make a good shoemaker, sir." Quoth the subject in astonishment to a friend, "Good gracious, however could he have guessed my trade ?" Replied the friend sarcastically, "Why, you had it sticking out a foot. You went stooping on to the platform with your bands spread out as if you were drawing a couple of waxends through a boot upper." That crushed him.

BANK HOLIDAY AT BETHNAL GREEN.—There yet re- mained unexplored one portion of the Museum, namely, the basement beneath the side galleries. This portion we found to contain a rather limited exhibition of furniture, an ento- mological collection, and, what was infinitely more attrac- tive to a large proportion of visitors, the refreshment coun- ters. With this semi-subterranean portion the attractions of the Museum and our visit came te an eRd. It is difficult to over-estimate the good effects of such an exhibition thus placed. They are mainly of two kinds, intellectual and moral. Such a collection, intelligently examined, is in itself an educational course. To the skilled artisan of certain trades it offers an opportunity of comparing his own handi- work with that of other men in other countries. This im- parts a healthy stimulus to his own efforts, and tends to make him a better workman. It must be confessed also that our working classes are as a body, lamentably igno- rant of the first principles oidomestic economy. When they were at school, education was not dealt out with the liberal hand it now is to their children. Here, however, is an effort to supply that lack by object-lessons on a large scale. The moral results, too, must be equally good. A walk around such a building cannot but give a healthy tone to the mind, and lead it up from the hard struggles of every-day life to an atmosphere of higher and purer things. Bank holiday, moreover, has everywhere its own peculiar temptations, to which the Museum is an excellent antidote. Is the place valued? The record exhibited on its walls replies by a dis- play of figures, "Yes." Equally conclusive is the answer given by the presence there in considerable numbers of men, women, and children of several classes, some even ragged, dirty, and unkempt, but all quiet, decorous, and un- doubtedly interested in their surroundings.—Cassell's Family Magazine.

THE PIRENIX PARK MURDERS.
TIM KELLY'S SECOND TRIAL.

On Monday morning Timothy Kelly was again put on his trial at the Queen-street Commission Court, Dublin, before Mr. Justice O'Brien aud a special jury, charged with the murder of Mr. Thomas Henry Burke, in the Plicenix Park, on the 6th May, 1882. Mr. Justice O'Brien took his seat on the Bench punctually at 11 o'clock, and was quickly fol- lowed by the law officers of the Crown (the Attorney-General, Mr. Murphy, Q.C., and Mr. O'Brien, Q.C.), mad the counsel for the defence (Mr. Dennis, B. Sullivan, and Mr. M'lnerney).—Mr. Murphy, in a deliberate and carefully- worded speech, placed the case for the Crown before the jury. There was no new feature developed ia Mr. Murphy's address. He went over the same ground as of old in the terms that are now familiar to everyone who has perused the reports of the trials of the past three weeks.— The first witness called was the approver James Carey, who, after narrating the attempts on Mr. Forster's life, said that an the 3rd May " 'No. 1' called and told us that this gentleman would not come back to Ireland any more, and that we should go for Mr. Burke and Colonel Hillier." He wanted it done on the 4'h May, but that was "too busy a day," owing to the departure of Earl Cowper. The ap- prover's demeanour under cross-examination was character- istically shameless. He said that what recommended him for appointment as one of the assassination committee was his "hitherto good conduct, which nothine• can blacken." He did not regard the object of the Invincrbles as murder. It was warfare, and all was fair in love and war. Asked was it himself who selected his brother Peter Carey for membership of the Society, he replied, "Yes; and a very good man." Witness supplied Kinkle with knives for the attempt on Mr. Forster on the 3rd March. They were to be used "without any compunction at all " to re- move a tyrant. Witness was true to his associates till he found that there was a conspiracy to murder him. They were all jealous of him. Robert Farrell, Michael Kavanagh, Alottley (the hatter), Joseph Smith, and other witnesses were examined, the most important evidence given being that of Glynn, the master builder, who stated that Kelly was not in the group of men he saw in the park while he was speaking to Carey. The trial of Kelly was reeamel on Tuesday morning. Thomas Huxley, who in May last was a gardener in the employ of Mr. Cecil Guinness, and passed the Phoenix Monument about a quarter to seven o'clock on the evening of the murders in the park, spoke to seeing a group of four or five men near a clump of trees in the locality of the scene of the crime. Ho noticed them particularly, and, said the witness, looking at the prisoner, "I saw that man there." Huxley added that he would know one other of the group if he saw him. There was little fresh in the evi- ' dence of the other witnesses examined for the prosecution. In addressing the Jury for the defence, Mr. Sullivan argued that the case against the prisoner depended entirely on the evidence of the carman Kavanagh, who knew that if he gave the real 'names of the four men who were driven on his car vengeance would follow him to the utter- most ends of the earth; and he appealed to them not to condemn a fellow-being on the testimony of a scoundrel like James Carey. The statement of Mr. Glynn, a Crown wit- ness, who knew Kelly, that he did not see the prisoner among the group of murderers was disproof of the story of the informers. Mr, Sullivan spoke of the positive testimony of the gardener Huxley as being as reckless a piece of evidence as was ever given in a court of justice. The witnesses who were called on Friday last to prove an alibi, repeated their evidence, and, in addition, Charles M`Gowan. a property owner, said he knew the prisoner. On the 6th of May the witness was going past Shannon's public-house when he saw the prisoner approaching. The time was about twenty minutes Oefore seven o'clock. In cross-examination, he said he did not know before the pri- soner was arrested that his name was "Tim," but he found be was the Kelly he knew when he read in the paper that he was connected with Brown's establishment. Other wit- nesses were called to prove the prisoner's whereabouts on the night of the murder. Mrs. Kelly, the prisoner's mother, was the last witness for the defence. Mr. M'lnerney then summed up the evidence for the prisoner, and was followed by the counsel for the prosecution, after which the court adjourned. The trial was brought to a close on Wednesday. Mr. Justice O'Brien, on the assembling of the court, at once pro- ceeded with his summing up, entering most exhaustively into all the details of the case, and occupying three hours and twenty minutes in his address. The jury then retired to consider the verdict, but after about an hour's delibera- tion they returned, unable to agree. They were sent back again, with a similar result, and on presenting themselves a third time, they asked to. have the evidence of the wit- nesses Huxley and M`Gowan read over to them. This was done and they again retired, but still failed to agree, and were ultimately discharged. This second failure to obtain a ver- dict either for or against the prisoner has again aroused keen interest in the proceedings, and public opinion in Dub- lin is much excited as to the eventual result. TRIAL OF MICHAEL FAGAN.

Michael Fagan was next put in the dock, and charged with murdering Mr. Burke. He pleaded not guilty, and, having chosen Mr. M'lnerney to defend him, the Crown appointed Mr. R. Adams and Mr. J. O'Byrne in addition for his defence.—ln stating the case against Fagan, Mr. P. O'Brien, Q C., said that three independent witnesses, two of whom would probably be reluctant witnesses, would be pro- duced to prove the presence of the accused man in the park on the evening of the assassinations. James Carey, as in the previous case, was the first witness called. He deposed that the prisoner was in Phmnix Park when Mr. Burke was murdered, and had been present on several occasions when abortive attempts had been made to " remove " Mr. Forster. Two printers, named Michael Keown and Thomas Wlneeny, were then called, but Keown was very reluctant to be sworn, and Mlneeny absolutely de- clined to take the oath. The judge very sternly commanded him to take the book on peril of being sent to gaol for twelve months, and to emphasise the threat he sent for the governor of Kilmainham. But before that gentleman arrived the witness succumbed and proceeded to give evidence. Both Pe and Keown testified to having seen Fagan in the park and spoken to him, and they had both been acquainted with the prisoner before. Corporal Sandford, who was in company with these two witnesses, gave corroborative evi- dence, but failed to recognise Fagan. When, however, Jos. Hanlon was placed in the dock he identified him as one of the men be saw.

The trial of Fagan was resumed on Thursday morning. Joseph Smith, one of the approvers, said Fagan was at the scene of the assassinations in the park. James Carey was recalled, and said he was positive that Fagan was there, but be contradicted Smith's statement that Edward M`Caffrey was also there. The carman Kavanagh failed to recognise the prisoner. Peter Carey (brother of James Carey) said the prisoner was one of the " Invincibles," was usually in company with Joe Mullett, and was one of the party who lay in wait to murder Mr. Forster. Farrell an- other approver, gave similar evidence. The prisoner's late employer proved that Fagan was not working on the 6th of May, or after breakfast on the sth. Counsel for the defence admitted that Fagan was in the Park on the evening of the 6th May, but his explanation of his presence there was that he had simply been watching a cricket match and was bn his way home when he was seen by the three fresh witnesses at about six o'clock. Witnesses were then called to speak to an alibi with regard to the precise time of the murders. Among them were Mrs. M'Mahon and her daugh- ter, mother-in-law and wife respectively of one Arthur For- rester, who were cross-examined at great leagth as to that person's connection with Fenianism and his present where- abouts. It was elicited that he was at present in London, that he had latterly been in various towns in this country, and that he was at one time arrested in Liverpool for travelling with revolvers. The wife said she had a letter from Forrester last week, which was written from Manches- ter, and said, " I start for London." Mr. Adams then summed up on behalf of the prisoner, and Mr. Murphy re- plied for the Crown.

It is stated that eleven of the jurors engaged in the fruit- less trial of Kelly which closed on Friday were in favour of a conviction, and that the dissentient was a person who had from the first intended not to agree to such a verdict. With regard to the second trial, ten of the jury in Kelly's case were for a conYiction, and two for acquittal, and it is said only on of the two was obstinately for acquitting the prisoner, while the second gentleman might but for his support have been induced to yield. It is the intention of the Crown, though not announced in court, to put Kelly on his ttial a third time after the terminatiota of Fagan's case.

"NUMBER C."—lt is understood that the evidence which has now been accumulated connecting Tynan with the Phenix Park assassinations is of a sufficiently satisfactory nature to justify decisive action on the part of the Govern- ment in asking for his extradition. The evidence has reached the authorities, not only from informers in Dublin, but from other and independent sources, and this evidence in a marked manner confirms Carey's statements.—Tiincs.

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

Sixteen persons have been burnt to death at Warsaw in a fire which originated in a cabinetmaker's workshop. Intelligence received from Cairo states that reports ate current there that the insurgents under the Madhi have captured Khartoum.

The cyclone which occurred in the States lately cut a path 1,000 yards wide throdgh a swamp in Barnwell County, South Carolina, felling the tiraber as if it had been cut to form a highway. ANOTHER DYNAMITE EXPLOSION IN SPAIN.—An explosion occurred on Sundayafternoon, at a dynamite manufactot7 at La Perucca, in the provinc6 of Leon. Seven people are known to have been killed and five injured, but it is feared that the loss of life will ultimately prove greater. The Parliament House in the city of Quebec has been burnt down. It was intended to pull the building down and erect a new Houae. and tbe contract was signed only a few weeks ago. The New York Herald says it is believed that the fire was caused by a Fenian incendiary, but the local reports state that the origin was unknown. The Swedish Anthropological and Geographical Society held a meeting at Stockholm,on Tuesday evening, at which the Vega medal, instituted to commemorate the return of the exploring vessel Vega, was awarded to Mr. Stanley, the African explorer. The American Minister was present, and received the medal on behalf of his compatriot. - DEATH OF SULEIMAN PAsna.—The death is announced, at Bagdad, of Suleiman Pasha, who was well known as the brave but unsuccessful defender of the Shipka Pass against the Russians. At a critical period of the war, Suleiman rapidly transported a large force from Albania and held the Shipka Pass for some time. The principal Russian fort was at one time actually in his hands, but he neither did not know it or was incapable of taking advantage of thej oceasion, and the opportunity never recurred. He died an exile and in disgrace. THE CLAYTON-BULWER TREATY.—The reply of Lord Granville to Mr. Frelingeuyhen's despatch on the Clayton- Bulwer treaty is published—at New York. The foreign Secretary contends that the meaning and effect of the treaty are not open to doubt, and that we have done nothing in Honduras which can be construed as a violation Of its pro- visions.. Should the canal be completed the British Go- vernment will be ready to consider the advisableness of preserving the neutrality of the waterway in time of war, but negotiations on the subject now would be premature. DEsntualvs cYCL9N4.-41 very destructive cyclone passed over a portion of the state of Ai ississippi on Sunday. Its effects were felt not only in Mississippi, but also in Georgia, Alabama, and Tennessee. The loss of life is great'; that of property immense. The small town of Beauregard, in Mississippi, was entirely swept away. Two hundred dwellings were destroyed, and a pine forest was blown from its site. Some of the bodies are mangled beyond recogni- tion. A child was transported a hundred yards unhurt. No sign of the railway station remained. Two brick build- ings were literally scattered over several square miles. The thunder and lightning, torrents of rain, and a deep rumbling sound shaking the windows as though by an earthquake foretold the approach of the storm. SLAVERY IN BRAZIL.—The slave population of the muni- cipality of Rio de Janeiro en September 30, 1882, was 35,855, a decrease of 8,771 in nine years, although 7,083 had been added to the primitive number by the excess of entries over departures. In the nine years the deaths were
8,373, and the emancipations 9,939, only 446 of which were official ones. The value of the slaves thus freed was pro.

bably about £BOO,OOO. In the province of Rio de Janeiro the original 301,352 existing on the register at the end of September, 1873, had been increased 31,597 by surplus of entries over departures; but at the end of last August had decreased to 268,831, by 51,269 deaths, and by 12,849 eman- cipations 1979 of those being official. In Ceara. it is esti- . . .
mated that the 35,000 registered slaves have diminished in about nine and quarter years to .18,000. _ _

THE PonTei FINANCES.—The finances of the Porte are described as being in a more than usually deplorable con- dition. Long arrears of salary are due to the civil officials and functionaries, and the Times correspondent at Constan- tinople reports that many of these persons, "unable to pro- vide for the daily wants of their families and even for their own personal locomotion," are forced to abstain from attend- ing to their duties. The Sultan has ordered a remedy to be found," but the Ministers are helpless, and "hopeless misery is imminent." The correspondent, summing up the state of affairs, says :--" Payments are put off, assignments on provincial revenues are repudiated, garrisons are left for months without pay, officials are driven to beg in the streets, stores and provisions of daily necessity are unpaid for, aid the contractors refuse to provide any more without a pay- ment on account. Although these evils may not for a time produce a stoppage of the daily routine of public govern- ment, yet the moment may not be far distant when they will bring about that natural result." REMARKABLE MURDER. IN BRITTANY.—The Paris corre- spondent of the Times writes :—At the Cotes-du-Nerd Assizes five days have been occupied with a mysterious case of murder, throwing some light on Breton superstitions. One morning last September, in the village of Hengoat, a farmer named Omnes, 25 years of age, was found suspended from the top of a tumbril. He had been thrashing on the previous day, bad slept in the barn, in order to guard the corn from thieves, and bad evidently been strangled in his sleep, and hung up when dead. His mouth was gagged with a hankerchief and his arms extended, as though cruci- fied, by a stick which was placed in the coat sleeves. He was the mainstay of his aged mother, was about to marry, and was popular in the village, except with his sister and her husband, Margueritg and Yves Guillou. They had for three years borne a gf`...4dge against him, because on his father's death, he had s4orn to a debt of 150 f., which they had been obliged to pay. They maintained that they had not left the tavern kept by them all night; but a woman asserted that she saw them coming home from the direction of the scene of the murder at two that morning. Another person declared that Marguerite's shoes were muddy that day. Yves. moreover, despite a policeman's prohibition, washed his trousers, which were soiled at the knees with dung, and the marks of knees were noticed near the corpse. A month previously they bad hired an old woman for sf. to go to a neighbouring village, where there is a chapel containing a statue of St. Yves, which is resorted to by the whole district as a means of obtaining sure vengeance. The old woman was commissioned to invoke vengeance on Omnes for perjury. But she was unable to perform the errand, for the priest, scandalised at the evil passions which made the shrine frequented, had re- moved the statue to his back garden, and, on the wall being scaled to invoke it, had locked it up in his loft. The theory of the prosecution was that, despairing of saintly interven- tion, the couple resolved on avenging themselves, and what clinched the popular suspicion against them was that the candle sent by Guillou to an altar at Guingamp, with an invocation for his brother-in-law's benefit, would not burn. At the trial, however, the witnesses to the facts that the two prisoners were out late at night, and that t',l) woman's shoes were muddy, were less positive than when originally examined; and the prisoners were acquitted, notwithstand- ing evidence that they had made no secret of their wish for the deceased's death.
ANOTHER LEGAL TRIUMPH FOR MR. BRADLAUGFI. IMPORTANI JUDGMENT.

The Lord Chief Justice of England delivered judgment on Monday in the action of "Bradlaugh v. Newdegate," in which the member for Northampton sought to recover damages to the extent of .Z 5,000 from defendant for having maintained Mr. Clarke in his action against tho plaintiff for having sat and voted in the House of Commons without having subscribed the oath. His lordship stated that this action was argued before him on the 9th and 17th of March. There was a spacial jury empanelled, but as the facts were agreed upon it was decided to dismiss the jury and to leave the question to his lordship to decide on the question of law alone. As his lordship learned that his decision, whichever way it went, would be appealed from, he thought it best not only to state kis judgment hut the grounds of it. The plaintiff and defendant were both mem- bers of the House of Commons, and the plaintiff having sat and voted without having subscribed the oath, he rendered himself liable under the pro- visions of the Act of Parliament to a penalty of £5OO. The defendant appeared to have been anxious to sue the plain- tiff. His lordship then narrated the circumstances under which Mr. Clarke was met by Mr. Newdegate, who gave him his bond and encouraged him to bring and pursue an action against Mr. Bradlaugh. By the authorities, main- tenance was held to be a factitious interference in a suit with which the persan so interfering had no personal in- terest, and it could not be denied from the evidence that Mr. Clarke would never have commenced his suit, or have gone on with it, had it not been for the encouragement which he received from Mr. Newdegate, and had it not been fer Mr. Newdegate's bond Mr. Clarke would never have been able to have paid the costa if he had been un- successful. Unless maintenance was struck out of law digests for the future it could not be said that Mr. New- degate was not guilty of it, kr to bind one's self at the commencement of a suit with a person of no means has al- ways been held to be maintenance, and for such mainten- ance an action would lie. It was argued that maintenance to subject the defendant to a penalty, must be against good morals and public policy. His lordship held that the defendant had been legally guilty of bad morals and in- justice by putting Mr. Bradlaugh to great expense through the instrumentality of a man of straw. Having decided that an action lay, his lordship .considered the measure of damages, and held that Mr. Bradlaugh was entitled to an indemnity for everythiag that Mr. Bradlaugh had suffered in costs by Mr. Newdegate's maintenance of Mr. Clarke. If the parties could not agree as to the amount it must go to the official referee, on receiving whose report his lordship would give judgment for the amount.

Trumpeter Williams, of theist Royal Dragoons, shot him- self dead on Thursday in the barracks at Dublin by dis- charging a pistol into his mouth. IN THE WRONG PLAC:E.—A stranger entered the office of an ocean steamer agent, on Griswold-street, yesterday, and asked, "Can a man cline from Ireland by your line ?" "He can, sir."—" Will you bring over my eldest brother ?" "We will that."—" For how much ?" "In first-rate shape for 30 dols."—" I think I'll pay the money," said the stranger, but, as he was pulling out his wallet, the agent asked, "In what part of Ireland is your brother?" "In the Dublin gaol, sir, as a suspect ! .If he were out he would be plenty able to take care of himself, he would."—" But we can't get him out of gaol, you know." "Neither can I, you know, though I've written seven letters to the jailer to do a decent deed, and let Barney go."—Detroit Free Tress.

A Californian adventurer was recently lamenting to an- other his folly in leaving the comforts of home, with a kind wife and two beautiful daughters. The other, after listen- ing in silence, replied, "My case is much worse than yours, for I have a wife and six children at home, and never saw one of them." "How can that be ?" said the first speaker, "were you ever blind ?" "No, sir." . "Then, pray, what do you mean ?" "Why, simply that one of them was born after I left home." The querist considered himself "sold." COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS AND PRIVATE Rooms.—An interesting statement on the rights of commercial travellera in hotels, was made on Saturday at Lancaster by Mr. Higgin, QC. The proprieter of an hotel at Morecambe, was charged with allowing card playing in his house The playing took plc ) in the commercial-room of the hotel, and the "commercials "pleaded that this particular room was always considered "private, " so private indeed that the" commercials" had even the power to turn the landlord out of it. This notion. Mr. Higgin said, was neither sense nor law, and it was monstrous to pretend that a particular room in an hotel, belonged to a particular class of persons. The nonsense about turning the landlord out was "preposterously absurd, " and if the landlord sub- mitted to anything f the kind it was some evidence that he had neglected his duty. The Bench, in dismissing the case, wished Mr. Longmere to understand that card playing in a commercial room, was an illegal act, and that it was his business to make himself acquainted with what was ' going or there.

FITZ:UV:U/7CE stated that the cession of the Portuguese fort at Whydah, on the West Coast of Africa, and of the rights inherent to the sovereignty of it, had formed part of the negotiations between this country and Portugal.

EMIGRATION FROM THE WEST OF IRELAND.—The CHIEF SECRETARY for IRELAND announced that the Government had teen in communication with certain persons in regard to the emigration of a considerable number of selected families from the West of Ireland to Canada, but though the Government sympathised with the movement the details of the sehe Ile had not been considered. The right hon. gentleman also stated that Mr. Hamiltcn, who had tempo- rarily performed the duties of Under Secretary since the death of Mr. Burke, had now consented to hold that office permanently. AGRICULTURAL INTERESTS.—III reply to Mr. Duckham, the PRIME MINISTER Ecommunicated the substance of an arrangement for the special and separate consideration of agricultural interests and affairs. It is proposed to direct that certain members of the Privy Council being members of the Government, be appointed a committee for the con- sideration of all matters relating to agriculture which matters are to be referred to the committee to consider and report thereon. The head of the committee is to be the President of the Council, and in his absence the proceedings of the committee are to be presided over by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. THE AFFIRMATION BILL. The debate on the motion for the second reading of the Affirmation and Oaths Bill was resumed by Sir H. D. WOLFF, who insisted that a great distinction ought to be drawn between the right to be elected and the right of those who were elected to sit in the House. He complained of the conduct of the Lord Chancellor in sitting and giving judgment in a case in which the Government of which he was a member was so much concerned, and of his example being fol- lowed by another judge, not a Minister, who had given political opinions in the midst of a great judgment.—Mr. GLADSTONE protested against the prolongation of the de- bate by the introduction of extraneous matter. He argued that there was nothing in the existing law that could prevent an atheist daly elected from sitting in the House, and said it was only the acci- dental expressions used by Mr. Bradlaugh that had pre— ventedhim taking his seat. It was because the Government thought it rightlthat the controversy should be closed and an end put to the scenes they had witnessed that they had given the bill its present position of precedence over other matters. He believed in the general sense of justice of the English people, although he admitted that on questions of religious prejudice it was more difficult to obtain that full sense of justice than upon any other. The object of the Government had been to keep within the boanis of tholaw and the constitution. The right hon. gentleman shafpky rebuked those who were willing to dispense with Christi- anity so that they could only retain the oath, and he con- tended that the interests of religion as well as of civil liberty were concerned in the passing of the bill. A seat in the House was regarded as a high political prize, and to continue the test which was still applied was practically putting a bribe before particular individuals to tamper with their religious convictions. When the interests of religion were ostensibly associated with injustice it led to a state of things which he regarded as the most inexpressible calamity that could fall either on a man or nation.—The debate was continued by Mr. Stanley Leighton, Mr. Daly, Mr. Court- auld, Lord A. Percy, Mr. Peddie, Viscount Lewisham, Mr. Inderwick, Mr. Gibson, and Mr. 0. Morgan.—On the motion of Lord H. Churchill the debate was adjourned till Monday.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Twenty men, said to be in respectable circumstances, have been arrested at Miltown Malbay (Ireland) on the charge of being members of a secret society the object of which was "to do away with " landlords, agents, and Government officials.

John O'Brien, town councillor, and Richard Hodnet, 'ex-suspect, were on Saturday morning released from custody, having served two months' imprisonment for intimidation at a National League meeting in Bantry. No meeting of the National League has been held in the county since. Mr. Healy, M.P., who is at present a prisoner in Richmond Jail, Dublin, has received an address and a present of a well- chosen law library from the coroners of Ireland in recogni- tion of his successful efforts in carrying through the Irish - Coroners Act. Mr. Healy expressed regret that the severity of the prison rules prevented his personally receiving the i address.

The Land Corporation of Ireland have agreed to take over between 40 and 50 of Lord Cloncurry's farms in the disturbed districts of Limerick from which the tenants have been evicted. The annual value of the farms is about £1,150, and the Land Corporation have taken them at the rents which the evicted tenants refused to pay.._. -

tHE WORKING OF THE LAND Act —A Blue-book issued on Monday sbows that durinc, the month of December, 1882,-there was a total of 1,638' cases in which judicial rents had been fixed; 696 of these were in Ulster, involving an acreage of 15,472; the tenement valuation of this was £11,402, the former rent £14,023, and the judicial rent £10,922; in Leinster the cases were 316, acreage 9,663, tenement valuation £5,140, former rent £7,636, and judicial rent £6,047 ; in Connaught the eases were 240, acreage 5,475, tenement valuation £2,402, former rent £3,304, and judicial rent £2,703; in Munster the cases were 386, acre- age 16,558, tenement valuation £8,826, former rent £13,718, and judicial rent £11,131.
