CONSERVATIVE LECTURE AT NEWTON

div.head: TOWN HALL,
div.p: TOWN HALL,

In cmnection with the Newton Polling District Conserva- tive Club, Earle-street, Earlestown, a public lecture on "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform" was given by Mr. H. Byron Reed, of Darlington, in the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday evening last. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. H. B. Westhead, of Newton. Amongst those present were the Rev. W. F. Lovell, curate of Newton, Mr. R. Brierley, Mr. Woolacott (Golborne), Jrc. The Cuentmax thought at the critical juncture at which this country had arrived that Mr. Reed was well able to instruct them, and he hoped they would extend to him not only a silent and patient hearing, but a contemplative hearing and a sympathetic attention. He (the chairman) had previously appeared before them in that capacity, but it was at a meeting in support of Mr. Gladstone when he was seeking the suffrages of the electors of the county. When Mr. Gladstone came to Newton in 18'05 he (the speaker) had occasion to tell him, though he had been the chairman of one of the meetings to promote his interest in getting him elected, to tell him that as far as he was able to discern he thought the measure he was then advocating —the discs- tablishment of the Irish Church—was one frought with so much danger that he felt convinced if the measure was carried that it would only be a stepping atone for demands made by the sister province of Ireland of such a nature that he himself would never be able to concede. He hoped he would not be as true if he were to say that night that the passing of the Affirmation Bill for abrogating the oath of allegiance, which had been one of the great bulwarks of this nation, would be the first great fracture in the constitution of this realm. (Ap- plause.)

Mr. H. B. REED Was then called upon to nice his address, and was very heartily received. He remarked that the chairman had informed them that not very many years ago he was a supporter of Mr. Gladstone, and he (the lecturer) wanted to know why it was that he now occupied a position as chairman on a Conservative platform. Was it that he and others like him had changed their political opinions? No, it was that Mr. Gladstone and his party had changed theirs, and it was that the old-fashioned, progressive, ad- vancing Liberalism of 15 years age had become the FeTro- grading Radicalism of the present day. Liberalism they all believed in. Liberalism promoted reform, Liberalism adopted. old institutions to the altered necessities of altered times; Liberalism believed in Free Trade and fairness with free- dom; Liberalism believed in the privileges of the people's representatives in the Commons House of Parliament; Liberalism believed in the main- tenance of the constitutional relations between the Queen, Lords, and the Commons; Liberalism believed in the maintenance of the religious systems and institutions of the country, while Radicalism, on the other band, be- lieved in a spurious sy§tem of Free Trade, free and fair for the foreigner, but unfair to this country; Radicalism made pinchbeck promises at Birmingham, and falsified them when in power; Radicalism endeavoured to bring about conflicts between the Queen and the Lords, and the Lords and the Commons, Radicalism put a gag and a " bit" into the mouths of the free representatives; and Radicalism at that very moment was endeavouring to blot out the silent his- tory of 1800 years of Christianity and place on the statute book of the realm that there is no God so far as the Parlia- ment of this country was concerned. (Applause.) Remark- ing that the present Government had laid themselves open to criticism during the past three years, he proceeded to give a rapid and cursory reference to the various political topics which have come before the country during that period. He maintained that the Government had made their way into office by promises of peace, retrenchment, and reform, and said that they were all good things in their way but it did not follow that the men who talked the , loudest of peace were the most peaceful of men, or that those who called out retrenchment " spent the I least money, while as to reform, the Radicals were the most retrogressive political beings that it was possible to con- ceive. If they had not fulfilled their promises they ought to be denounced as men who unworthily obtained office upon false pretences, and at the firstopportunity ought to be sent to durance vile and suffer exclusion from office for a long term—at least until the expiration of the present century. He said that the Tory party were in power for six years, and made two wars, while the Gladstone Govern- ment, who had only been in office for three years, had also had two wars, and if it was wrong, wicked, base, vile, and blood-thirsty for Lord Beaconsfield to make two wars in six years, what could be said of the present Government , who made two wars in exactly half the time? Lord IBeaconsfield's wars had the merit of being successful, bat Mr. Gladstone's war against the Boers was a very dishon- ourable and disasttous transaction. In alluding to the in- come tax he stated that he had recently been looking over a return, and found that since it was established it had been the highest when a Liberal Government was in power, when it was 19d. in the X, while it bad been the lowest by 2d. in the £ when the Tories were in office. If they took the whole of the years, and got the average amount during the years the respective parties were in office, it was found that when Liberals held office it was 7d. in the X on an average, and it was sd. in the £ with the Tories. (Ap- plause.) He maintained that the men who now com- plained of obstruction were the very men who set obstruc- tion going,'and such was the inconsistency of Mr. Glad- stone that when out of office he actually wrote an article in the Nineteenth Century defending obstruction. Obstruction, Mr. Gladstone said, was not an offence nor even an indis- cretion—it was the only legitimate means by which a small minority could make itself heard, and he hoped the rights and liberties of the House would never be abridged. (Laughter ard applause.) Since then the same Mr. Glad- stone had put a gag, the cloture, and the " shut-up "on the mouths of the people's representatives. When they were out of power the Radicals preached peace. but when in office they made war. When they were out of office they denounced the income tax, hut when in power increased it, and when out of office " spouted " about reforms, but when in power they wrapped reforms in brown paper, tied them up with a string, and put them in pigeoa holes until they were wanted again. (Applause.) When in opposition they had obstructed and used all the forms of the House to do se, but if anyone for five minutes ventured to obstruct them they howled for a week. With the spurious Liberalism of to-day it was party first, principle second; Glad- stone first, country afterwards; and they schemed and sacrificed anything for the expediency of temporary partisanship, banishing all principle and sending it to the four winds of heaven, so long as Mr. Gladstone and his party could by intriguing remain in power for a few months longer. Those who said the Tories had been guilty of obstruction spoke falsely, and it (lily remained for the people of this country to send the Government into the cold shade of opposition as soon and for as long as they could, The present time was for action, anl the masses of the country should be educated and shown the way in which they had been deceived and hoodwinked by the men in power at the present time, and what a hollow sham the cry of peace, retrenchment, and reform had been. Whilst they were good things in their way, they had simply been used as stepping stones to place and power, and the people had been deceived by ministers who were now laughing in their sleeves at the deception they had practised. On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. WOOLACOTT (Golborne), a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment having been accorded to the chairman, the proceedings terminated.
PRESENTATION AT WARRINGTON.

Mr. Joseph Bissell, who has been superintendent of the i Primitive Methodist Sunday school, Legh-street, Warring- ton, for the last ten years, was on Saturday the recipient of a handsome illuminated address, from the teachers and scholars in recognition of his services. The presentation was prefaced by a tea, to which about 300 persons sat down in the schoolroom. Mr. William Crampton, junr., presided at the meeting, and be was supported on the plattorm by the Rev. J. Morton Messrs. J. Bissell, W. Miller, A. Cook, J. Titchett, and J. Swales.—The CHAIRMAN said it was a pleasure to witness such an occasion as that, and he believed it was the first time anything of the kind had taken place in connection with their Sunday school. They were met together to do honour to a man who by his impartiality, punctuality, and Christian zeal had won the respect and regard of the whole of their school—be alluded to Mr. Bissell, their superintendent. (Applause.) It was in the middle of February that a presentation was first mooted, but it was not until the beginning of March that it was de- cided the testimonial should take the form of an address as a small token of the esteem in which they held Mr. Bissell, and of their appreciation of the valuable services he had rendered to the school during the ten years he had been superintendent. If at any time—which he trusted would not be the case—circumstances compelled Mr. Bissell to leave them, he hoped the address would remind him of the happy days ha had spent in that Sunday school, and that it would be the constant source of satisfaction to him that he had done his duty. (Applause )—The Rev. J. MOUTON ex- pressed his perfect sympathy with the object of the meeting. He had known Mr. Bissell for two years, and he had the good impressions, the entire sym- pathy of all parties connected with the school , and the society. In connection with his duties las superintendent, Mr. Bissell was punctual, persevering, I and impartial, and he hoped when Mr. Bissell had fulfilled his mission he would have the grand testimonial from the great Master : '• Well and faithfully done." (Applause.) —Mr Job SWALES described how Mr. Bissell came to succeed him as superintendent, and remarked that Mr. Bissell was I not only a Christian, but a man who commanded respect wherever he went. (Applause).—Mr. W. MILLER testified 1 to the worth of Mr. Bissell's services as superintendent, and I said that be bad always found him consistent in all his dealings, and that the success of the school was attributable in a great measure to Mr. Bissell's assiduous efforts. (Ap- , plause.)—Mr. J. Terciture fully endorsed all that had been i said respecting Mr. Bissell. He remembered ten years ago ; they were only a few collected together in one corner of the !chapel, but they worked hard together and were soon able 'to build a school. Since that time they had grown from ! good to better, and they had now about 260 scholars and 30 ! teachers, and would soon have to appeal to the authorities of the school for more room. (Applause) He might say that , ever since Mr. Bissell took the reins of government into his I hands the school had prospered hoth temporally and spiritu- ally, and he could say that he had found Mr. Bissell to be a \ Christian, straightforward and upright in all his dealings. 1 (Applause.)—Mr. A. COOK, in making the presentation, said 1 that during the six years he had been secretary he had al- ways found it a pleasure to meet Mr. Bissell, who he be- lieved was the right man in the right place, and that they were doing honour to one to whom honour was do, tAp-
plause.) He then presented to Mr. Bissell the address, which was ag follows :

To Mr. Joseph Bissell —Dear Sir,—We, the teachers and scholars of the Primitive Methodist t'unday School, Legh- street, W,trrington. present this address to you in r..cognitiln of your services as superintendent for the last ten years. Dur- ing this time the school has made eneeureging progress, which has been not a little attributable to the efficient manner in which you have performed the duties of your office. Your uniform kindness a•tcl courtesy, combined with other qualifi- cations which so eminently fit you for the office of superinten- dent, have secured for you the confidence and respect of both teachers and scholars, and we trust that this expression of Gur esteem for your character and work will afford you some encouragement as an evd!ence of our appreciation of your labours. We shall ever cherish grateful memories of your association with our school, and of the useful work you have performed amongst us, and we trust when you cease to serve tne Church of Christ on earth, the reward of the faithful will. he yours. Siened, on behalf of the school. W. Miller A. Cook, J. Titchet,. J. Swales, J Podmore, C. Littlewood, W. Cramp- ton.—Warrington, April, 1883.

—Mr. BISSELL, in acknowledq,irr the presentation, said he was greatly surprised when he beard that such a presenta- tion was going to be made, and he thought they were over estimating his services. However, he accepted the address with the greatest pleasure, and wculd ever remember the kindness of which it was a token, and he hoped it would stimulate him to greater endeavours fo7 the welfare of the Sunday school. (Applause.)—The audience were during the rest of the evening entertained with selections of music, &c., and the meeting elosEd in the usual way.

div.head: SALVATION A I Y AT _ WAHL\ UrTON.
div.p: THE SALVATION A I Y AT _ WAHL\ UrTON.

The Salvationist attack upon Warrington commenced at an early boor on Sunday morning last. Soon after six o'clock a brass band from Widnes marched through the town to the barracks in Academy-street, and with lively airs proclaimed the advent of the any, At seven o'clock there was "knee drill " for the soldiers, and at half-past nine they again assembled at the barracks prior to the com- mencement of hostilities. Large placards had been posted throughent the town, announcing that the army would "mount guns" at ten o'clock near the fair ground, but on Saturday the Deputy Town Clerk intimated to the secretary and treasurer of the Warrington Committee that instructions had been issued by the Mayor that the army would not be permitted to assemble on the fair ground or upon any other public land. An intimation was also conveyed to the officials of the army that the Mayor considered their placards ridiculous and improper ones, and they were ordered to cover the placards within two hours, otherwise it would be done for them. In coosequence of this order, the bill- stickers were busily engaged on Saturday evening in cover- ing the "blood and fire" placards with announcements of auction sales and public entertainments, and on the fell° v- ing morning the result of their labours was viewed with considerable surprise by many of the townspeople. Shortly before ten o'clock the " warriors," accom- panied by brass bands from Widnes and Run- corn, and preceded by a red flag, on which was inscribed the motto " Blood and fire," left headquarters for the fair ground near which place an immense crowd had gathered. On the edge of the fair ground Inspector Berry , and six or eight constables had taken up positions, and when the army arrived the inspector headed them for Golborne- street, along which they proceeded, followed by several thousands of persons.. The Salvationists paraded the principal streets, the bands playing popular tunes, to which the processionists sang, and then Marched to the barracks. The building had been visited during the week by the Borough Surveyor, who served upon one of the officials the following notice:—" Dear Sir,—My attention has been called to the fact that you are proposing to hold meetings of the Salvation Army in a building off Academy-street, formerly used as a malt kiln. Upon examination of the floor. , of the building, I do not consider it safe for the assemblage of a large number of peoph,, and would therefore impress upon you the necessity of having the same thoroughly examined and strengthened b2fore any number of people are admitted into the building. A copy of this letter I have sent to Major Taylor, Ardwick-green, Man- chester.—Yours truly, T. LONGDIN, pro. F. W. W." This notice resulted in a number of supports being plaeed under the floor to prevent the possibility of any catastrophe. There was a terrible rush for seats, and in a few minutes the building was packed. The doors were then closed and guarded, but until the close of the exercises demands for admission were made by the outsiders, who had congregated in numberS sufficient to fill to overflowing the Public Hall. The platform was occupied by the Salvationists, and the "inside firing" was conducted by Captain Brain and two young ladies (Captain Reed and her lieutenant), the two latter "warriors" being in command of the station. Capt. Brain appeared to he about 22 years of age, and the ladies about two years younger. The congregation were at times inclined to be rough, but the Captain was able to produce silence by uttering the words " steady there," or by blowing a whistle.

Captain BRAIN, in addressing the assembly, said: Some of you have heard what strange people we are. We are birds with strange tails. Some have been disgusted before we came, and others have said it would be well if we were dead and buried. Some have sat as a jury and given their verdict before we came, but we understand you all already, because it is not the first place we have been to. Wherever we go we can always draw a crowd. Wherever the Salva- tion Army goes there is not much fear of them having small congregations. We come here to do the work of God, as the children of God; to tell to a dying world that Jesus has died to save. At the commencement let me say we don't come here to rob any church. We don't want to take anybody from any other place of worship. God forbid. We don't say a word against any denomina- tion. God forbid. We lift them up in prayer, and pray for everybody who love Jesse. Our object is to reach those who go nowhere; our object is to speak to those men and women who never think of eternity, or how they may get salvation. Thousands and thousands of drunkards have been rescued and washed in Jesu's blood through the efforts of the army in various parts of the world; and in the town of Warrinq,ton before this day week you will see plenty of drunkards will come to the feet of Jesus. A weak point of the members of the Salvation Army is that they shout "Amen," and you must excuse them. You will no doubt get used to it in time, and perhaps be quite as anxious to shout "Amen" as we are. I only wish the place were six times as large as it is ; if it were we could fill it. It ap- pears that some eople have been doing us harm before we got here. Only during last night some one took a pane of glass out of the window, and took the door-step away and tried to do us a great deal of injury. But Jesus is love, and we love everybody. There is not a man or woman in War- rington whom I cannot love in the name of God. You people know the Mayor. God bless him. (Cries, of "Amen.") He had our bills covered up, though we had not said or done anything to offend him. When I got into the town yesterday I saw the bills covered up, but I never saw that done before in any town I have visited. But I dcn't think they have done us much harm. (Cries of "No, it has done us good.") Some people asked "how long are you go- ing to stop?" Well, we are going to stop until the Judg- ment Day. There have been a tot of imitations of the army up and down the country. Men bad gone in the name of the Salvation Army to places where they have stayed a few weeks, and people have been prejudiced as they had left in an improper manner. However, don't make any mistake in regard to us. It is easier to get us into a town than it is to get us out of it. We have commenced in a malt kiln, but in the town we are going to stop as long as the place can hold us, and until we can get a larger one. We shall have meetings to day and every night in the week. The. captain and lieutenant will take charge of the place. Oils of them gets 15s. and the other gets 12s. a week—that is if they can get it. Every fathing that is received in this piece will pass through the hands of the secretary and treasurer who will be selected from your townsmen. They will pay the rent, gas, &c., before these officers receive a penny of their wages.

In the afternoon the army again missioned the streets,head- ed by their bands and followed by large numbers of persons. Their arrival at the barracks was awaited by an immense concourse of spectators, who thronged Buttermarket-street from Scotland-road to Orford-street, and the greater portion of Academy-street. In the crowds—morning as well as afternoon—were ex-mayors, aldermen, and councillors, and indeed, persons of all classes of society, who watched the movements of the soldiers with the greatest interest. At the service in the afternoon there was also a crowded attend- ance, and a similar state of things prevailed in the evening, when the rush for seats wee so great that one of the Salva- tionists. named Millington, a painter, of Runcorn, who had charge of the door, had his arm badly crushed. The crowd remained in the streets until a late hour, but through the ad. mirable police arrangements, under the superintendence of Inspector Berry, everything passed off quietly. At a meeting of the Corporation Watch Committee, held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, the following memorial from ratepayers living in Academy-street, in whieh the " barracks " of the army are situated, was read : Vire, the undersigned ratepayers residing in Academy- eirtreet, respectfully desire to bring to your notice that we are suffering very materially in our comforts, businesses, and professions through the unseemly and riotous behaviour of crowds of people called together daily by a few indi- viduals who style themselves "The Silvation Army," and we humbly request that you will use your authority to protect us from such an annoyance and injury, and your petitioners. ac in duty bound, will ever pray." The petition was presented by Dr. Cannel]. No processions have taken place during the week, though services have been held each evening, and large numbers of persons have congregated in and about Academy-street, and at times caused slight disturbances.

A curious question arose on Thursday morning at the Wigan Quarter Sessions during the hearing of a case in which a blacksmith was indicted for stealing a duck out of the Corporation park, the Recorder said he doubted whether the jury, being burgesses, could try a man for stealing their own property, the mayor, alderman, and burgesses of the borough being the °synth's of the park. He decided, however, to hear the case, and the difficulty was settled by the jury acquitting the prisoner. At the Law Courts, on Thursday, in the Freethi,iker case, it was arranged that the the trial of Messrs. Foote and Ram- say should not be renewed certainly until Tuesday next, and that in the meantime the prosecution should decide whether the charges would be proceeded with. In the course of a short discussion between Lord Coleridge and Sir Hardinge Giffard, his lordship said he had it on the autho- ritv of the governor of Holloway gaol that Foote's health had suffered consid.erably in consequence oi prirA)n dii- ciple.

CROSS'S question f'llher:st,,be, answered by putting to him an- "rhy should he and his friends dis- el i„'!cts se„ a constituency because _ it its representative a gentle- rrl othe legally disqualified ; and ar °E PI, of constituencies followed tlie ex- Northampton, would he and his

[friends disfranchise these constituencies also? Sir RICHARD and his followers by their action rouse the spirit of bigotry and intolerance of a former time which it is not wise and it is not just to countenance. It is to us surprising that any member of the Jewish or Roman Catholic persuasion should oppose this Bill; yet we are told all the Par nellite and Roman Catholic members will vote against it, and Baron DE WORMS, in the bigotted remarks which he delivered on Monday, announced his intention of voting against it also We should have thought that after the rights acquired for them, mainly through the in- strumentality of the Liberal party, they would have been only to() glad to avail themseves of any opportunity to remove a condition pre- cedent to taking his seat obnoxious to any duly elected member; -their gratitude, how- ever, we now find, ends when their own sel- fish objects have been attained. BARoN DE WORMS was somewhat exultant when he re- produced a passage from a speech of the PRIME MINISTER'S in 1854 on the Oaths Bill, in which he expressed himself most un- equivocally as in favour of the oath being ad- ministered to members before proceeding to the discharge of their duty. ]he PRIME MINISTER may be of the same opinion still, and yet be acting perfectly in accord with his former declaration, for even then exceptions were made in the case of certain members, and that exception it is only proposed to ex- tend. But we commend to the notice of Baron DE WORMS the following facts taken from a leaflet issued by the National Liberal ' Federation which may have escaped his at- tention in his researches in HANSARD :—" On the 1 rth May rBB (Earl DERBY being the Prime Minister, with Mr. DISRAELI as his Chancellor of the Exchequer) a select Com- mittee was appointed to draw up reasons for not ag eeing to the Lords' amendments to the Oaths Bill. On the r3th of May, that com- mittee (of which Mr. DISRAELI was a mem- ber) presented their report, which assigned nine reasons for disagreeing from the Lords, and the said reasons were agreed to seriatim. (HANSARD, 3rd series, vol. 150, p. 520.) 2. • Because the exclusion of British subjects from seats in Parliament and offices in the State on the ground of their religious opinions, is contrary to the general maxim of freedom of Conscience.' 7. • Because the rights of the electors of the United Kingdom have been peculiarly effected by a law which has been construed to prevent the admission to the House of Commons of persons who have been lawfully returned as members of that House." With these reasons in view the Liberal Government may be said to be only now legalising the principles held by the Conservative party, and advocated by their own leader (Mr. DISRAELI) twenty-five years ago. It will be interesting to observe how Sir S. NORTHCOTE will reconcile the attitude he now assumes with his very recent declara- tion that he would be happy to co-operate with the Government in any way he possibly could to conduct the settlement of the oath difficulty to a satisfactory conclusion. Now is his opportunity to prove his sincerity. He has already, as well as the whole Conserva- tive party, in fact, voted for the principle contained in this Bill in the form of a resolu- tion, and we fail to discover their consistency in refusing to support the same principle now. If they are successful in their opposition they must accept the responsibility of per- petuating that profanity which they condemn. After all it is to be regretted that a Bill of this nature was not introduced by the Government when the difficulty first arose, for we have been compelled to come to it at last. The opponents of it may do their very worst— they may prove, as we believe they will, false to their principles and false to their party— still the Bill will pass, for the justice of it will surmount all obstacles. KEEPING A DOG WITILOrT LICENCE AT RUNC0121,7.--,tt Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Peter Phillips, clothier, Church-street, was summoned on a charge of hav- ing, on the 23rd February, kept a dog without licence.— Mr. Heal, supervisor of Inland Revenue, prosecuted.—Mr. Bingham, an officer for the Inland Revenue, stated that on the day named he saw a dog at the lodgings of the defend- ant, who admitted it was his, but be was under the impres- sion that a licence was available for 12 months. Witness informed him that all licences expired on the 31st Decem- ber, and that unless he took out a licence he would be pro- secuted. He refused to do so, but after the lapse of some weeks he shot the dog, and then took out a licence.—The Bench fined the defendant is and costs, 95 6d.

MARRIAGE OF MISS WALKER AT M•LPAS.—On Thursday morning week the quaint little town of Malpas was quite alive in consequence of the marriage of Miss Walker to Mr. Thomas Foulkes. The wedding was fixed to take place at 10-30, but long before that time a great number of old and young people, well-wishers and friends of the bride, bad as- sembled in the church and churchyard anxiously awaiting the arrival of the bridal party. The marriage ceremony was performed by the Rev. C. W. Cox, rector. After the service was over Mr. Edwardes, organist, played Mendels- sohn's Wedding March, and the bells sent forth joyful peals. The happy pair left Malpas station at three o'clock en route for Wales to spend their honeymoon. The wedding presents were numerous and costly, both bride and bridegroom being widely respected.

A WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.—Yesterday (Fridayi, at the Liverpool Assizes—before Mr. Jnstice Day—Thomas Quinn, 30, labourer, Was indicted for maliciously and feloniously wounding John Clarke, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, at Widnes, on the 12th February. Mr. Shand prosecuted. Prisoner was undefended. The prisoner and prosecutor lodged together at St. Helens-street, Widnes, and on the night of the 12th of February they were having supper together in aledroom when they quar- relled about some butter, and the Misoner seized an earthen- ware vessel that was in the room and struck prosecutor on the head, the force of the blow breaking the vessel to pieces. Proseecutor was knocked through the window, and would have fallen into the street if he had not saved him- self by holding on to the window sill. He sustained a severe injury to the head, and was for some time an inmate of the Whiston Workhouse. Evidence was given that prosecutor, owing to the effect of the injuries, was unable at the present time to resume his employment. The jury found the prisoner guilty of wounding with intent, and he was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment.

THEATRICAL LICENSE FOR RUNCORN PUBLIC HALL.— 'lt a special session on Monday, the Runcorn magistrates renewed the license for the performance of stage plays in Runcorn Public Hall, on the application of Mr. Arthur Salkelcl, the secretary. The magistrates on the bench were Messrs. C. Reynolds, S. B. Chadwick, A. Thomas. and W. Bankes. Mr. A. Salheld's sureties were Mr. W. Whittaker and Mr. W. F. Salkeld. THE UNITED METIIODIST FREE CHURCH BAZAAR AT RIP.4ICORN realised upwards of £lOO. Numerous articles remain unsold, and later in the season will probably be utilized for a sale of work. During the alterations to the church, services will be conducted in the schoolroom in Sutherland-street. Mr. Simpson, who performed the opening ceremony, generously gave a donation of £lOO, ly‘lides aid- ing the project by numerous purchases. WIDNES RECREATION FOOTBALL CLUB has just concluded a most successful season. Out of the 16 matches played, 13 were won, two drawn and one lost; the club scoring four goals, 27 tries, and 73 minor points, to their opponents one goal, three tries, and 25 minor points. The officers for next season are : Captain. Mr. G. Jamezon ; sub-captain, Mr. R. Grundy ; treasurer, Mr. H. R. Hewitt; secretary, Mr. J. Passey ; assistant secretary and umpire, Mr. A. Critchlev. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—Mr, G. H. Danb.7,-, clerk to Widnes School Board, prosecuted the following per- sons, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, for breaches of the Education Act :—Albert Dearden, Patrick Calland, Peter McCarthy,Luke Kelly,James Hughes, Esther Mitchell, Maria Wright, James Branwood, Pat :McFarland, James Handy, Nicholas Farrell, Ann Feeley, Martin Flanaglian, Martin Dunne, John Shandley Richard Edgerley, Thomas Painter, Richard Glassey, John Knockton, Martin Leonard, Thomas Frain, James Cummins, Edward Taylor, Michael McDermott, and Mathew Connor. The usual line of ss. was imposed in each case. SINGING BEE AT RUNCORN.—There was a good atten- dance of members at the weekly session of the Hope of Runcorn Lodge 1.0. G. r., on Friday evening last week, when upon the conclusion of the ordinary business a sing- ing bee was held. Five competitors entered, viz., Bros. Hughes, Linden, Fox, Pears, and Bushell. The first prize, a book, entitled "The throne of David," and presented by Bro. John Faulkner, was awarded to Bro. Ernest Hughes for his rendering of "The village blacksmith." The second prize, presented by Bro. Machin, and entitled "The pillar of fire," was awarded to Bro. Jos. Bushell for his rendering of " Just arrived from France."

TEETOTALISM AT WESTON POlNT.—Under the auspices of the Weston Sons of Temperance a meeting. was held in the Wesleyan Sunday School, Weston Point, on Friday last week. Mr, Richard Clark presided, and there was a large attlienee, Mr. J, Faulkner and Mr. J. Parker delivered addresses on temperann topics, especially bearing npon the work of the Sons of Temperance. At the conclusion, Mr. Clark intimated his intention of becoming an honorary member of the order, and he strongly advised the people of Weston point to join, so that they might be prepared to meet sickness RIVI death when the time came. The usual votes of thanks were passed. A YOUTH SERIOUSLY INJURED AT Ey SCO aw.—Tho al 16 Humphreys, a youth, living in Pool-lane, Runcorn, and employed at the yard of Messrs. Blundrit and Co. as a ship's carpenter, was seriously injured on Monday afternoon. At the entrance to the yard is a large gate, and this was being closed when it fell from its position upon Humphreys, who was standing near, crushing him beneath its ponderous weight. The unfortunate youth was picked up in an un- conscious state and conveyed in a cab to the surgery of Dr. Robinson, where he was attended to by Mr. Hefferman, surgeon. His skull was torn partially off and the skull seriously fractured. After having his wounds dressed Hum- phreys was taken home, where he lies in a precarious condi- tion.

HEAVY SENTENCE ON A DRUNKEN DRIVER. - Henry Grace, carter for a contrac`or named Percy, was brought up at Widnes Petty &ssions, on Wednesday, charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and harry. About four o'clock, on Monday afternoon, P.S. MacGregor saw the prisoner " hanging to the shafts" of a lorry he ought to have been driving. The officer stopped the horse, and then discovered that the prisoner was unable to stand. He drove the lorry to the police office, sent a man with it to its destina- tion, and took the prisoner into custody.—Supt. Barker re- marked that the prisoner had been frequently convicted of similar offences, and hit liiaster was before the Bench on a similar charge a fortnight ago.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour without the option of a fine. YOUTIIFUL ROBBER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- shans, on Wednesday, John Dean, 13 years of age, was charged with stealing 141bs. of resin, worth 9d., from the Widnes resin works of Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. —Thomas Anderson Reade, manager of the works, who lives at 10, Deacon-road, Appleton, stated that he believed the resin belonged to his employers.—P.C. Savory deposed that on Sunday afternoon', the 15th inst., he saw the prisoner along with some other boys, coming from the Old Marsh. He stopped the prisoner, who threw some resin to the ground and ran away. When he, after a chase, captured the prisoner, he found that he had 141bs. of resin concealed in an apron under his coat. The prisoner alleged that the other boys had given him the resin; but there were traces of resin on the footpath to the prosecutor's works.—The Bench sen- tenced the boy to receive six strokes with the birch rod. MEET FROM A DrrroN FAum —Martin McHugh, a hale looking fellow, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with stealing two horse cloths and four b igs, value 21s, the property of William Swain, farmer, Ditton. The evidence showed that up to three weeks ago the prisoner was in the employ of Mr. Swain, and consequenly well acquainted with every portion of the farm buildings. Mr. Swain bad a "peculiar way" of fastening the stable door, and on Monday night everything was duly made safe. Next morning, however, it was discovered that the stable had been entered, and the articles mentioned stolen. About three o'clock on the afternoon of Tuesday, P.C. Palmer and P.S. Coutts went into the straw shed of Cottage Farm, Dit- ton, and found the cloths and bags concealed in the straw. They were allowed to remain there, and at half-past eleven the same night P.C. Palmer again visited the place. He saw the prisoner sitting on the cloths in the act of undressing himself, and at once took him into custody. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour. ATTACK ON A WIDNES POLICEMAN. - Before Mr. 11. S. Hall and Mr. F. H. Gossage at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Patrick Harvey, an elderly man, was charged with assaulting and resisting P.C. Pitt in the execution of his duty. Shortly after midnight on Tuesday, P.C. Pitt observed the prisoner loitering in the neighbourhood of Moss Bank in a rather suspicious manlier. He therefore walked up to him and asked what he was doing there at that that time of night, when the prisoner replied, " You can go to and find it out. I will not tell you anything about me." The officer told him that unless he gave a satisfactory account of himself he would be arrested, but the prisoner instead of giving the required information, struck the officer a blow on the mouth with his fist, and he was at once arrested. He then behaved very violently, and savagely kicked his custodian on the legs and body.—The prisoner declined to make any defence, but, in answer to the magistrates, he said he did not live in Widnes, an.l got his living in the best way he could. He was fined 103. and costs.

IiE9,RTLESS ROBBERY AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Ann Smith, a middle-aged woman, was charged with stealing 5s from Ellen White widow, of 9, Thorpe-street, Widnes. Abotat eight o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner entered Mrs. White's house, and the latter asked her to have a drink. Prisoner consenting, Mrs. White took a shilling from a cup in the cupboard, which also con- tained four shillings more. She placed the shilling on the table and went into the, kitchen. When she returned the prisoner was still in the room, but the shilling had disappeared from the table and the 'cup was empty. Next day the pri- soner acknowledged she had the shilling, but refused to give It up, and threatened to strike Mrs. White, who is an old woman. Elizabeth Murray, married woman, of 12,, Thorne- street, stated that on Saturday night she looked through the window of Mrs. White's house, and she saw the prisoner there close to the cupboard. Mr. White appeared to be under the influence of drink, and the prisoner was feeling about her pockets. P.C. Altnond deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who Inspector Barnett said was a bad char- acter, and the Bench sentenced her to a month's hard labour.

FARNWORTII AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY AND ITS PRISES. —At the St. Helens County Court on Wednesday last, Job Rawnsley, Bingley, Yorkshire, sued the secretary of the Farnworth Agricultural Society for £l5 15s, accumu- lated balances in respect of the 'prizes for exhibition of poultry at the Farnworth cattle show.—Mr. Riley appeared hs ell said, l d uhlasdsobieleenan exhibited exhibitorpo ul poultry f poultryfor the pal ta iangt ri ff,wl t uh roe' l at the Farnworth show, and was awarded prizes amounting to £l4. Ha was paid £lO, which left a balance of £4 to be, carried forward. in 1831 he again exhibited and won prizes amounting to £lB 10s, and this amount, with the £4, made £22 owing to him, but he was only paid £Bs 10s, which left a balance of £l4. In 1882 he again exhibited and prizes to the total amount of £7 lOs were awarded to him, making the total amount due to him to be £22 10s. prom this, however, there was to be £5 15s deducted for entrance fees, which reduced that amount to £l5 15s, which was now claimed. Defendant had never repudiated the liability, and he (Mr. Riley) was therefore at a loss what defence was going to be made.—Plaintiff's son said he had seen the c ads showing the prizes awardel to his father, but he had not kept thOse cards.—Mr. Husband, of Widnes, appeared on be- half of defendant, and contended that the court was entitled to have the cards referred to by last witness produced.—His Honour advised that an amicable arrangement should be come to between the parties; bat after some consultation between them it was found they could not agree, and con- sequently the case again cams before the court. After a further hearing, in which it was cantended that the defen- dant, as secretary, was not the person liable, his Honour agreed with this contention, holding that the society as a whole was liable, and non-suited plaintiff with leave, each aide to pay its own crlsts.

POOR RATES FOR ASTON..—At Rancorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. the magistrates sanctioned a poor rate of is in the £ for Aston Grange, and is id in the £ for Acton-by- Sutton. Mr. Robinson, the assistant overseer, made the applications._

- ALLEDED WATCH ROBBERY AT ,WIDNES.-7-Yesterday at the Widnes Follea Court, Thomas Dasmond and Letitia Desmond were brought upon remand charged with stealitig a gold watch, the property of Charles Etches, Waterloo-road, Widnes.- On Wednesday, the prisoners, along with several others were helping the prosecutor to remove his furniture from Waterloo•road to another house. In a bax were a number of watches, which Etches had received in order that he might repair them, and whilst they were being trans- ferred, a gold watch was missed. The prisoners were ac- cused of the robbery, but they stoutly denied any knowledge of the article. Subsequently they were searched, and the watch was found upon the female prisoner.—The prisoners were remanded until Friday next. BOY DROWNED AT RUNCORN.— Mr. Ridgway, the coroner held an inquest at the Cemetety Offices on Thursday, on the body of George Jones, a boy 14 years of age, who was drowned in the Iron Ore Arm basin, Bottom Locks, Run- corn, on Tuesday afternoon. Evidence was given by Mary Nash, who stated the deceased was the son of a woman now in gaol, and by Mary Howard, wife of Thomas Howard, a waterman living in Greenwell-street, Stanley-road, Liverpool. It seemed that on Tuesday afternoon the deceased was play- ing on a raft which was floating in the Iron Ore Arm basin, when he fell into the water. Mrs. Howard, who was watch- ing him, made a fruitless attempt to reach him, and then told her husband of the occurrence. He vcovered the boy from the water with a I_ oat-hook, and every effort was made to restore animation, without effect. A verdict of " Acci- dentally drowned" was returned. OPER AIR CONCERTS FOR RUNCORN—During last summer The Examiner advocated the establishment of open air c,mceits in Runcorn, and endeavoured to prevail upon the brass bands, of which the town may be proud, to perform gratuitously. Some interest was created at the time, and we are pleased to find that our efforts were not altogether in vain. Mr. C. Dutton, the market superintendent, took the ptoj,ct in hand, and he has succeeded in organising a series of concerts for the summer months. The Volun- teer, Mill Brow, Parish Church, and Camden brass bands have kindly promised their services, and we have no doubt their performances will be a source of enjoyment to the public. The series will commence on Tuesday next— May Day—when the Mill Brow brass band will go through an excellent programme on the plot of ground above the Market Hall. Mr. Dutton, whose efforts deserve all praise, will provide a number of seats for the ladies who may attend. The bands unfortunately are without stands, and Mr. Dutton solicits subscriptions to defray the small cost that will be incurred in obtaining them. The public, it is hoped, will generously respond._

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL—We understand that a deputation from the Ship Canal Committee of the Run- corn Board of Commissioners had an interview with the directors of the Ship Canal project, on Tuesd ty. The gentlemen forming the deputation were—Mr. Ughtburn (chairman of the committee), Dr. Steele, Mr. W. Fisher, Mr. W. H. Linaker, and Mr. W. Barker; and they were re- ceived in a very friendly and conciliatory spirit. The various clauses of the petition adopted by the Commis- sioners came under review, and their reasonableness was to a great extent conceded. The directors expressed them- selves willing to secure the rights of Runcorn as a port, and to fully provide for the drainage and sewerage of the town, while It was understood that the apprehended danger from silting up through the diversion of the " scour " of the river would be guarded against. In the event of the company purchasing the Bridgewater Canal, the directors were not opposed to the retention of the present scale of tolls and charges. No doubt a clause embodying these matters will be drawn up in due course, submitted to the Commissioners, and included in the Bill. TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT FARNWORTH.—Under the auspices of Farnworth Temperance and Total Abstinence Society, the Rev. T. J. Madden, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture in the Girls' school-room, Farnworth, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. G. Bond presided.. The lecturer alluded to the prevalence of drunkenness among women, remarking that men had become sober by joining the Temperance So- ciety and the Blue Ribbon Army, but be was afraid they had forgotten the women. Fortunately, the Church of England Temperance Society had risen to the occasion, and had formed a Woman's Temperance Pillion. He believed that if the women were enrolled, they would be a great power in the temperance movement, for how much depended upon the mothers. If men had not good mghers,,, might God have mercy upon the nation! If woman was not sober and God-fearing, the children would contract habits of intem- perance and of ungodliness and would become non-church goers and outcasts from God. He asked those present for the sake of their husbands, and for the sake of their children, to out this curse from their firesides, and God would help and bless them. During the evening a programme of songs and recitations wag gone through, and the usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

THE WIFE WITH TIIE BAD TONGl7E."—Frederick Evans was brought up in custody at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife Mary Jaae Evans.—The prosecutrix, who gave her evidence with great reluctance, stated that on Saturday night her husband broke the lamp, whereupon she struck him, and he struck her in return. The occurrence arose through her own tem- per.—By the Clerk: Her husband struck her on the head.— Inspector l3arnett : Did you not say last Saturday that the prisoner made a violent assault upon you? I don't know what I said in my temper.—Did you not say he struck you on the bead with a chair leg? I don't know.—Were you not bleeding from the head when you came to the police station? Yes, sir; bat lam very sorry.—Did you not say that you were afraid 'le would murder you? In my temper I did not really kna,v what I did say.—Were you not in Shrewsbury Hospital for five days through your husband's violence? Yes; but I aggravated him to do it. It was all through my temper. I have a very bad tongue when I am aggravated.—ln answer to her husband, witness said she was very passionate, but she would try to curb her temper in the future.—The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO, and two sureties in £65 each; or in default, a month's imprisonment. A WIDNES APPEAL CASE. At the Liverpool County Sessions, yesterday week, an important appeal affecting friendly societies came on for hearing, before Mr. E. Gibbon. The United Kingdom Assurance Corporation (Limited) ap- pealed against the decision of the magistrates sitting in patty sessions at Widnes, on the 14th ult., whereby the society was ordered to pay £lO 10s to Mary Urquhart upon a policy of insurance on the life of a woman named Mary M‘Namara, deceased. Mr. Swift appeared for the applicant and Mr. Segar for the respondents.—The deceased woman Mliamara was a pauper in receipt of 2s a week, besides which she had an allowance of lOs a month from Messrs. Goulding, of Widnes, in whose employ her late husband had been. Her daughter, Mrs. M‘Dermot, who also lived at Widnes, had insured her life in the appellant company for ten guineas, and she paid the weekly premiums. The old woman died in November last, and Mrs. Urquhart, who had been appointed executrix, applied to the company for the amount insured. This the company declined to do, on the ground that they bad been deceived as to the deceased's age, and that information that they had insured her in other societies had been withheld from them. The petty sessional court had, however, made an order for the payment of the money. The appellants contended that the respondent had no pecuniary interest in the death of Mrs. MBNamara, as she was not mentioned in the policy as an interested party, and that the policy was void under the Act 14 George M. cap. 48. The court reversed the decision of the court belt without costs. '

RUNCORN BRIDGE FARES: A PROSECUTION.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. F. H. Gossage, Ralph Peacock, vraterman, Nelson- street, Runcorn. was charged on remand with having on the 19th inst., whilst crossing the railway foot bridge across the Mersef at Runcorn refused to ply his fare, or give his address, to Collector Macklin. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors department, Lime-street, appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company. The prisoner was further charged with being drunk on the same day; and he pleaded guilty to both charges. Mr. Ferrand observed that the case was a very bad one, and pointed out that the prisoner had rendered himself liable to s penalty not exceeding forty shillings for refusing to pay his fele, and of five pounds for obstructing the collector. The prisoner, however, had not been charged with the second offence. From the evidence of Samuel Macklin, the collector, and P.C. 1193, it seemed that the de- fendant on Thursday afternoon, passed over the bridge from Runcorn to Widnes. When asked for his ticket, he stated he had a contract, but finding that he was required to pro- duce that, he alleged that he had left it at home. Thereupon Macklin demanded the usual fare, when the prisoner, who was drunk, threatened to throw him over the bridge if he did not allow him to proceed. He became very violent, but was nevertheless detained until the arrival of a constable, who took him into custody. For some time he would not tell his name, but at last said he was" Sir Humphrey Gud- geee."—The Bench fined the prisoner 5s and costs 6s ed for being driink, and 103 and costs is 63 for the other offence, or in default 14 days' hard labour. ROBBERY FROM RUNCORN COCOA COMPANY'S /tomes: MAGISTERIAL STRICTURE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, On Monday, Samuel Cox was charged on remand with stealing a florin, the money of Wm. Moores.—Frovn the evidence of James Moores, son of the prosecutor, who is manager of the Runcorn Cocoa Company, it appeared that about seven o'clock on Friday morning the prisoner entered one of the company's rooms in High-street. He had a stick with some "blue stuff" at one end, probably of an adhesive nature, and whilst the prisoner was alone in the room money was heard to jingle. When he hail gone 2s. was misaed from the bar behind the counter. Witness explained that money was kept on this bar, which was about five feet behind the counter.—Mr. Reynolds remarked strongly upon that way of exposing money. It was a direct inducement to steal, and witness was little better than the prisoner.—P.C. Morris deposed that on Friday night the prisoner was brought to the police station by his brother, who gave him is. 2,14., all that remained of the florin. The prisoner admitted that he had stolen the money.—The brother of the prisoner informed the Bench that the latter, who was 23 years of age, was not always in full possession of his faculties, and was unable to get work in consequence. He never knew him to steal anything before.--. Superintendent Williamson con- firmed this statement.—Mr. Reynolds said the Bench would take a lenient view of this case, not on account of the pri- soner's intellect, but because of the careless manner in which the money was left about. He considered the prose- cutor very much to blame. The prisoner had quite enough intellect to form a plan to steal, aid he would be fined is and cote, 1s; or, in der 14 d tyC nAri.-1 lt-rar.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,
The monthly meeting was held at the offices of the Board, on Thursday. Mr. T. S. Timtnis presided, and there were present—Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, Hartland, R. H. Davies, and G. H. Danby (clerk.)

div.head: SCHOOL EXTENSIONS RESOLVED UPON.
div.p: SCHOOL EXTENSIONS RESOLVED UPON.

The CHAIRMAN said he was sorry to sae so few members present, because the important question of increasing the school accommodation was to be discussed. The subject was adjourned from the last meeting for the reason that there was only just a quorum of the members present, but he thought they would have to deal with it now because the question was pressing. As it would want pretty full discussion, he proposed that the Board resolve itself into committee.—Mr. BRADSHAW seconded the motion, which was carried.—The CHAIRMAN said the first business was the recommendation of the District Education Committee, which read as follows :—" That, sub- ject to the approval of the Education Department, the senior boys' department at Simm's Cross school be increased, so as to accommodate 200 boys; and that the infants' be increased, so as to accommodate 350 children; that the infants' de- partment at the West Bank school be increased, so as to accommodate 350 children." The Chairman thought it would be well to first settle whether it was worth while to provide more accommodation and decide how it was to be done afterwards, because if the Board resolved that it was not necess try to do the former they need not discuss the latter at all.—The minutes contained st ttistics showing the certified accommodation and average attendance in the Board's schools. In the senior boys' depart- ment at Simm's Cross school the certified accom- modation was 136, but the average attendance had risen from 89 in 1879 to 170 in 1882, while the estimate foe 1883 was 185. The senior girls department possessed the same accommodation, but the average attendance, which in 1879 was 90, was in 1882 12C, the estimate for 1883 being 135. The junior boys and junior girl departments had each accommodation for 170 scholars, and the average atteniance had risen from 73 and. 75 respectively in 1879, to 153 and 148 in 1882. The estimated attendance for 1883 was 165 and 180 respectively. The infant department had accommo- dation for 200 scholars, while in 1879 the number in average attendance was 153, in 1882, 197, and in 1883 (estimated) 200. At West Bank the average attendance in all depart- ments, with the exception of the infants, was less than the certified accommodation. The accommodation of the infants' department was 200, and in 1882 the number in average attendance was 204, and the estimate for 1883 was 230. —Mr. DEACON said the committee had thought that the Board might defer extending the schools until they were warned by the Government Inspector that unless they pro- vided the accommodation he should reduce the grant. The Inspector always gave warning, but he had not warned the Board yet, and they might wait until he did so at the next examination. But he (Mr. Deacon) thought that was a poor way of doing business, when the Board knew that the schools were overcrowded. At one time the committee thought it was possible to send the senior boys from Simm's Cross to Warrington-road school, but the result would be to leave Simm's Cross without head master, and would have the effect, probably, of reducing the average at- tendance. That argument would apply still more strongly against the removal of the senior girls to Warrington-road, and there was again the fear of a falling off in the aver- age attendance.—The CHAIRMAN said the points to consider were what the cost to the ratepayers would be if it were decided to increase the accommodation at Simm's Cross, and also what would be the expenditure if they reduced the fees at Warrington-road school.—Mr. DEACON: It would not pay to reduce the fees. We should get more children on the rolls, but the average attendance would decrease very much. —The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Holmes, architect, estimated the increased accommodation required at Simm's Cross could be given at a cost of £2.000, which at the Board's rate of in- terest would be £B5 5s per annum. Then Mr. Dauby estimated the extra establishment costs at £l7O, making the costs altogether about £250 ss. Against this there were the extra fees, which would amount to about £156 13s 4d, leaving £9B 7s 8d as the annual cost. Taking the alternative scheme of utilising Warrington-road and reducing the fees of the seniors to 3d and juniors to 2d, the result would be that they would only get £l4 from the fees. Against this there were the establishintnt expenses, so that the cost to the ratepayers would be £164, while in the other case it would only be £9B. He had altered his opinion since the last meeting. He was then under the belief that if they reduced the fees they would get the school full at a less cost to the ratepayers.—A few remarks were made with regard to the railway crossings which impeded the way to Warrington- road School, and the CHAIRMAN said the railway com- pany had been asked to place a bridge over the Bradley footpath, but they wished the question post- polled for a time. He had come to the conclusion that if the Board did anything at all it must be at Simm's Cross.—After some further dis- cussion, the resolutions were adopted in this altered form "That subject to the approval of the Education Depart- ment the boys' department at Simm's Cross be increased by 160 places, and the infant's department by 150 places." Also " That the infant's department at the West Bank School be Increased by 150 plac

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reeOramended fees to be paid in 65 out of 84 cases. There were 233 persons ap- peared before the Committee for c3ntravention of the Edu- cation Act during the month of March, and 52 were prose- cuted before the magistrates. Fifty-one were conricted.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT- COMMITTEE,
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT- COMMITTEE,

This committee recommended that the following teachers be appointed to the positions, and at the salaries specified below, rising according to the scale of the Board, viz.:— Miss M. L. Duncan, assistant mistress, senior girls, Simmrs Cross, £5O per annum; Miss Morgan, assistant mistress, infants, Simm's Cross, £35 per annum; Miss A. D. Dods- worth, assistant mistress, senior girls, West Bank, £5O per annum ; Miss Ball, assistant mistress, infants, West Bank, £35 per annum.—Recommendation, that Esther Ann Pownall be engaged as a pupil teacher in the Simm's Cross Schools, at a salary according to the scale of the Board, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to her indentures.—The committee reported that they had let two rooms in the Simm's Cross School to the vicar of Widnes, one room in the Warrington-road School to Mr. R. Mercer, and one room in the West Bank School to Mr. Hartland, for the purposes of Sunday schools, from April Ist to Sept. 30th, for the sum of one shilling and twopence each room per Sunday, all in ac- cordance with the scale of hire laid down by the Board. That Miss Gowing had been appointed reacher of the his- tory class for the instruction of female pupil teachers, in the place of Mrs. Morgan resigned. That Mr. R. Holden Davis having expressed his willingness to give prizes to those pupil teachers who had distinguished themselves in the annual scriptural examination, they beg to recommend that the best thanks of the Board be given to Mr. R. Davis, and that his offer be accepted.—ln moving the adoption of the mirutes, with the exception of the report, Mr. DAVIS said the committee had not yet prepared their report with regard to the teaching of cookery in the Board's schools, and they wished that subject to be adjourned.—Mr. DEACON moved the adoption of the report; and the minutes were agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that the members were very much obliged to Mr. Davis for his generosity in giving these prizes, which would no doubt be productive of great good.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £604 193.7 d. Duringthe month the committee bad paid into bank £132 28., which included school fees from Simms Cross schools £54 4s. 7d. ; West B tnk, £4B Us. 6d.; Warrington-road, £22 lls. 11.d.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. BRADSHAW, and the Board rose.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Committee of Selection have appointed Tuesday next for the consideration of this bill by a Select Commit- tee of the House of Commons. The Committee will con- sist of Sir Robert Loyd-Lindsay (chairman), member for Berke; Mr. A. P. Vivian, West Cornwall; Mr. Reginald Yorke, East Gloucester; and Mr. Stuart Bendel, Mont- gomeryshire. There is an antagonism (writes a correspondent) between navigation and drainage which never can be reconciled. It must not be forgotten that the proposed canal will not only be a navigation, but also the main drain for the sewage and rainfall of the of the whole of the watershed of the county. The river Thames above Teddington weir passes through a level country, but notwithstanding this, the currents just above the weir during floods run at a great velocity, and are an insuperable obstruction to navigation. It appears that the upland floods at Trafford Bridge, Salford, sometimes rise to a height of 75 feet 5 inches above the level of the ordnance datum, or 14 feet 6 inches above the ordinary water level, and that the intended low-water level below the proposed locks at Latchford, a distance of 161- miles from Trafford Bridge, is to be 13 feet below the same datum, making a total fall of 88 feet 5 inches, or an average of 5 feet 4 inches per mile. This excessive velocity of the current must inevitably put a stop to the use of tbe canal for navigation purposes, for there would be no steerage way for vessels passing downwards; nor could they stem the strength of such a current in passing upwards. In ordinary circumstances, the rate of travelling on the proposed narrow canal must not exceed two miles per hour, exclusive of the time it will take to pass through the locks; and even then the abrasion to the banks will be very destructive. It is said that the pound of the canal between Latchford and Irlam would be semi-tidal. This is a misrepresentation. Only just the top water of a spring tide of a rise of 24 feet at the Latchford locks, as sown on the Parliamentary section, could reach Irlam. It is impossible that this portion of the canal, with any degree of truth, can be called semi-tidal. It may be mentioned that Mr. Hamilton Fulton's amended proposal consists of a direct tidal channel from the sea to Barton Aqueduct. From Barton Aqueduct to the site of the intended docks at Salford it is proposed to construct a short canal, of a length of 1-&-- mile, with two locks of 20 feet lift each, so as to have the dock quays on the same level as the natural surface of the ground, and so avoid any extra amount of cutting—in- deed, it is only placing the entrance to the Manchester docks a short distance further down the river than is sug- gested by the parliamentary scheme. It may be here men- mentioned that the engineers of the proposed Panama Canal are prepared to encounter a depth of cutting of 312 feet rather than the canal should be encumbered with one lock. The present bed of the river between Barton ar.d Trafford Bridge would also be be straightened, which would admit of the uninterrupted discharge of the 071 and floods into the tidal portion of Mr. Fulton's navigation at Barton, and so on to sea without the obstruction, of any lock or sluice.
LATEST NEWS.
THE PIICENIX PARK MURDERS. THE SENTENCE OF FAGAN.
The trial of Fagan was resumed and concluded at Dublin yesterday. The judge having summed up, the prisoner was found guilty, and he was sentenced to death in the usual manner.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT IN THE MERSEY TUNNEL. TWO MEN KILLED AND TWO INJURED. . Shortly before three o'clock, yesterday morning, a shock- ing accident occurred at the Mersey Tunnel excavation works at Liverpool. About the time mentioned, four labourers, named William Dixon, George Jones, Charles Thomas, and Henry Vickersey, were descending No 1 shaft, which is about 180 ft. in depth, in an iron cage, and had got down about 50ft., when the naphtha lamp which one of the men was carrying seems to have been upset or flared up, and Vickersey and Thomas either fell, or in • their fright leaped from the cage to the bottom of the shaft, and were killed on the spot. The other two were burnt severely by the naptha. Agonising cries were heard from below, and in a short time The unfortunates were brought to the surface. The bodies of the deceased men were removed to the Prince's Deadhouse. Both were married, Vickersey leaving behind him one child, and Thomas five children to mourn his loss. The injured were promptly removed to the Northern Hos- pital, where their injuries were attended to. One was able N !ewe in 3 short time, the other still remains an inmate of the institution.

div.head: DISCOVERY OF A NITRO-GLYCERINE
div.p: DISCOVERY OF A NITRO-GLYCERINE
MANUFACTORY.

The Northampton correspondent of the Central News telegraphs that a discovery was made at noon yesterday which it is believed will show that a nitro-glycerine manu- factory on an extensive scale has been in operation in that town for some time past. It appears that in consequence of information received by the police as to the suspicions movements and demeanour of the tenant of No. 1, Aberdeen- terrace, St. James's End, Northamptonl the premises were entered yesterday. Oils and various compounds were found spilt about the floor, and there were other indications that the place had been used for the illicit manufacture of explosives. The letting of the house is in the bands of Messrs. Barker and Son, house agents, and it was hired last Easter by a man described as of Yankee appearance. No furniture has since been taken into the house, and the winlows front and back were painted so that no prying eyes could see what was going on within. Outside an announcement was posted to the effect that photographs were taken; but no photographic business ap- pears to have been transacted. A few days ago a rail- way van arrived with a box, and it was then observed that the American looking tenant appeared to be busily at work in the kitchen where a fire was burning. Subsequently a man called and took away two heavy boxes. When the house was entered about noon yesterday no one was found inside, and as no arrests have yet been made it is supposed the mysterious tenant has managed to get clear away. The report of the discovery attracted crowdeto the house, and the public excitement is intense in consequence of recent anonymous threats to blow up public buildings in the town.

div.head: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER.
div.p: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER.

At Taunton Assizes, yesterday, before Baron Huddlestone, George White, labourer, pleaded guilty to murdering his wife at Henstridge, Somerset, last month, and was sentenced to death. The prisoner, who had been separated from the deceased, stabbed her twice, and then kicked her to death.
FALL OF A HOUSE AT.ILIVERPOOL : TWO MEN KILLED AND THREE INJURED.

While a number of workmen were engaged yesterday morning demolishing some houses at Bootle, acquired for the extension of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, the gable end of a house fell without warning a few minutes after the men commenced work, burying five of them in the cellar:A gang of labourers:speedily set to work to:remove the (11,bris, when it was discovered that two men were dead and three others severely crushed. There was a storm of wind at the time of the accident. THE LIVERPOOL DYNAMITE SEIZURE.

Daniel O'Herlihy and Timothy Featherstone, alias Ken- nedy, who were arrected in Cork in connection with the dynamite seizure at Liverpool and St. Helens, arrived in Liverpool, via Holyhead, at nine o'clock yesterday morn- ing, and were soon afterwards taken before the stipendiary charged with being unlawfully in possession of explosives with felonious intent and conspiracy iQ commit felonies. The prosecuting solicitor said he would be able to prove the connection of the prisoners with Deasy and Flannagan, already committed, and would ask for a remand. Evidence was then given of the finding of the letter on Featherstone signed by O'llerliby, but in Featherstone's writing, and in the same handwriting as documents found on Deasy with reference to the supply of nitric and sulphuric acids from Montgomery and Co., chemists, Glasgow. Letters from the same firm were delivered at O'Herlihy's house. The pri- soners wete remanded for a week.
Colonel Burnaby makes .siow progress towards recovery. John Grady, process server, has been severely beaten at Clare Island.
Cardinal Manning has written to the Pope, postponing his visit to Rome until the autumn because of ill-health.

An imperial ukase is issued ordering the formation of a department of the senate at 3.loscow during the coronation, for giving effect to the Czir's decrees. A dead body was found, on Thursday evening, in the lake near Claremorris, and is believed to be of a man who has been missing for two months. A man is in custody on suspicion. Early yesterday morning, the Albert Mill, Blackburn, occupied by Messrs. Green and Son, was found to be on fl-e, and before the flames could be subdued, the premises were gutted. The damage, estinnted at £7,000, is covered by insurance. The origin of the outbreak is unknown. The principal member of the firm is the ex-Mayor of Darvren. Yesterday mornine. at Burnley, a weaver from Bacup. named Levata Chaffer, was committed to the sessions for trial for breaking a window and doing damage to the amount of £2O. On Thursday evening the prisoner threw a large stone through a jeweller's shop window in St. James-street, smashing three glass shelves, a largo number of gold and silver earrings, bracelets, alberts, (te.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS. The report of the amendment on the Contempt of Courts Bill was brought up and agreed to. The Medical Act Amendment Bill was read a third time, and the House adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
ILLNESS or TIM SPEARER.—Owing to the illness of the Speaker, the chair was takcia by the Deputy-Speaker, Sir A. Otway. _

REMOVAL OF CATTLE IN IRELAND. Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Mr. Harrington, said the restrictions the Privy Council had placed on the sale and removal of cattle in Ireland had been imposed to prevent the spread of disease. They would be removed as soon as possible. TRE MAILS.—Mr. FAWCETT said that in any contract for accelerating the night mails, care would be taken that the arrangement should apply to Scotch mails. LOCAL TAXATION. Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Mr. R. Yorke. said it certainly was the intention of the Govern- ment to introduce a-Bill on local taxation, but be could not state the time in the present condition of public business. Locett, OPTION.—On the motion for going into Commit- tee of Supply, Sir WILFRID LAwsore called attention to the urgency of the demand for legblation for giving effect to the Local Option resolution already passed by that House. He moved a resolution stating that the best interests of the nation urgently required some efficient measure of legisla- tion by which, in accordance with the resolution already passed, the licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors might b 3 placed in the hands of persons most deeply in- terested and affected, namely, the inhabitants themselves. He asserted his resolutions asked for nothing unreasonable. The bon. baronet impressed on the House the necessity that existed for giving the inhabitants of localities the power of preventing the opening of houses for the sale of intoxica- ting liquors in their midst and in defiance of their wishes. Every judge and magistrate in the country bad spoken of the ruin to which drink was bringing the people, anti, in the face of such (pinion, was it too much to ask that the people should have the power of protecting themselves? He thought it nothing but right that the people should have a veto on the subject. What would be the effect of a propo- sal to open a public-house near the park gate of the rich man ? Why he would crill on the magistrates who be- longed to that class to prevent that being done, and his call would be attended to. Why, he asked, should not the poor man have the same privilege of preventing the opening of a drinking shop near his boos:. `11;; experiment had been

tried of prohibiting the opening of public-houses on the- Shaftesbury estate, and the result had been eminently sus-! cessful. He asked that the experiment might ba tried on a large scale, and he called upon the Government to intro- duce a bill for that purpose, as no private member stood the slightest chance of passing a bill on the subject. I was not his duty to draw up a bill. He was only an agitator —(laughter)—not a legislator, but if the Government would only adopt his advice, and the Home Secretary was to introduce a bill giving popular instead of personal veto, they would be taking a practical step in favour of improving the condition of the working class, both morally and men- tally, and also the surest way of securing their future hap- piness and prosperity.—Mr. CAINE seconded the resolution. He believed the Government were in favour of local option,. and if they would but speak out and say that they were only waitimr" until the feeling of the country was more pronounced before they introduced the bill, they should have what they required in a very short time.—Mr. TAT,- um. did not believe local option would carry out the design of Sir W. Lawson. He objected to the resolution, but would support any satisfactory measure introduced by the Government with the object of checking the evil of intent- perance.—Sir W. HARCOURT said practically there was not much difference of opinion amongst them, as they were all agreed that the subject was one that ought to be considered without delay. He pointed out that they already had local control and restrictive powers in the licensing magistrates, but although they might be good judges in some things, he thought they were not the best authority for knowing the wants of the people, as they already had re- striciions. The next question that arose was— who were the best parties to administer it? In his opinion those restrictive powers ought to be carried out by a body of elected reprventatives of the local senti- ment on the subject (Cheers.) The Government would, therefore, vote for giving that power into the hands of the persons who were interested in it, reserving to themselves the right of determining how the opinion of the locality was to be ascertained. (Loud cheers.)—Sir J. KENNAWAY opposed, and Mr. FRY supported the resolution.—Mr. DALT opposed the resolution, and thought if money spent in blue ribbon businet:s had been held out in healthy literature more would have been done fer temperance. ii.EFT SITTING.] ,

div.head: SAD SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT RUNuORN. '
div.p: SAD SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT RUNuORN. '

Ellesmere-s!reet Chapel, Runcorn, is at present under- going extensive alterations and improvements; and for the purpose of whitewashing the ceiling,, scaffolding has been erected by Mr. Statham, the contractor. About half.past ten o'clock yesterday morning, Mr. Frodsham, painter, &c., with several of his men were working upon this erection, when the part upon which Mr. Frodsham was standing gave way, and he fell to the floor beneath, a distance of about 16 feet. The portion of the scaffolding adjoining also came down upon the rostrum with a crash, Magill..° with it the three men who were standing upon it. Mr. Frodsham, in falling alighted upon an iron pipe with his forehead, and became insensible, but the other men who descended upon the platform of the rostrum, and consequently did not fall so far, maned with a sligbt shaking. Dr. MacDougall and Mr. Hefferman' surgeon. assistant to Dr. Robinson, were sent for; and Mr. Frodsham was conveyed home in a cab. He was attended by Dr. MacDougall, who found that he was suffering severely from concussion of the brain. His neck was also much injured, but fortunately no bones were broken. Everything that medical skill could suggest was done for the injured man, who lies in a critical condition.
