THE TOWN CLOCK.

Sir,—As a native, and for many years an inhabitant of your good old town, I remark with interest the latest instance of your worthy Mayor's genercsity—namely his determination to provide the public, at his own sole expense, with a thoroughly reliable clock. In these days of cheap watches, which are within the means of almost everyone, public clocks are not so absolutely necessary as they were in former times, nevertheless, where they do exist, there is nothing much more annoying than to find them always wrong. The present Trinity clock has, during nearly the whole of its existence been a great sinner. At one time, in common with a good many others, I blamed Mr. Welsby for not looking after it better. One day, however, that much maligned gentleman was good enough to take me up into the Trinity Church tower and give me a practical demon- stration of the utter impossibility of keeping such a clock right for many days together, especially in windy weather. From that day I ceased to blame him; in fact I felt sorry for him, for he still had to bear the complaints of countless grumblers to whom he could not give the explanation he gave me. In the paragraph in last Saturday's Examiner on the subject of this clock, I notice that von say "a sugges- tion has been made that the clock now in Trinity Church tower should be placed in the tower of St. James's, Latchford, and there is no doubt if the suggestion were carried out it would be of great benefit to the residents in that part of the town, in which there is no large clock of any description." Now, if this clock has been so utterly unreliable in Sankey- street, what on earth is the use of putting it up anywhere else, to carry on the same old game, and simply to mislead and annoy another section of the Inhabi- tants? I hope this idea will not be for a moment entertained unless the clock is so reorganised as to make it do what it. has seldom done yet—tell the truth. Whether the clock is worth the reorganisation necessary, is doubtful; I have always understood that it was not worth spending money on at all. If an instance of the folly of removing a poor clock from one place to another is wanted, you need go no further than St. Paul's. Could anything be more lamentable than the state of this clock ever since it was put up there? This, I believe, was the original " town clock." Let us benefit by experience, and when the present Trinity clock is removed, let it be destroyed, that a too confiding public, whether hailing from Latchford or any other quarter, may no longer be cajoled into missing appointments, losing trains —and tempers—&c., ate., through the vagaries of a dis- reputable old servant, whose long and intimate connection with the " church " has had so little salutary influence upon its adamantine conscience, and who ought therefore to submit quietly to removal off the face of the earth.—Yours truly, CORRECT TIME OR NONE. P.S.—With respect to that miserable clock at St. Paul's, there used to he current some very curious stories relating; to its removal and refixture, more especially as to the financial arrangements. Whether that so demoralized the clock that it felt it was hopeless even to try and be respec- table and truthful, I cannot say. The events I allude to, however, took place long before the incumbency of the pre- sent worthy vicar, who, as everyone knows, is the very soul of all that is honourable and straightforward.

div.head: WHAT IS THAT FIVEPENCE FOR?
div.p: WHAT IS THAT FIVEPENCE FOR?
Sir,—Last year our Runcorn Improvement Rate was is 10d in the £. This year it is 23 3d. Why this increase, and where is the Ratepayers' Association ?—Yours truly, Runcorn, April 25, 1883. REDTAIL.

THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS AT RUNCORN. Sir,—After penning my last letter, I ventured the opinion that when ccnfronted with so direct a contradiction, Mr. Handley's allegiance to the Ratepayers' Association would become secondary to his determination to extricate himself, if possible, from his unpleasant situation, and his reply de- monstrates how accurately I estimated the character of my opponent. Passing unnoticed Mr. Handley's modest pre- tentious to superior information of ancient acquirements, I hasten to remove the false impression ho seeks to create when he refers me to "those who attended the meeting," for, as he knows, I myself was present and heard his state- ment, and I assure him that it contained neither the words, nor conveyed the sense, of the garbled sentence he bedecks with quotation maths, which are wrsqly omitted in a subse- quent letter to your contemporary. The question was raised by Mr. Whinyates, a prominent member of the association, and I have his authority for stating that Mr. Handley's reply clearly satisfied him that the Union and not the town- ship would be burdened with the cost; and I can furnish Mr. Handley with the names of many other gentlemen who are unanimous in their opinion that this is the only inter- pretation which his remarks would bear. In further sub- stantiation of my charge, I quote verbatim the following extract from a circular, issued by the association of which my opponent is so energetic a member :—" You must bear in mind that the cost will not fall on the township alone, but on the entire Union." With these facts before him, I leave Mr. Handley to ruminate on his lack of lucidity, which, as he 13 so well informed and had no disposition to mislead, must be the extent of his fault ; and I conclude by hoping that this correspondence will result in making our local leaders more careful in their oftieial utterances, and the .Ratepayers' Association more certain of its authorities before it again publishes statements which are misleading. —Yours truly, F. J. N. RuncornrApril, 1380.

DefenJant took the bucket and threw the contents over the c3mplainant at the , same time using course langusge.—Defendant's husband was '• ordered to be bound over for her vocl behaviour. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES—Thomas Oottrill, teamsman, Whitley Superior, was summoned for neglecting to send his child, Mary -Alice, to school. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs, 3s 6d, and to send the child to school —John Owen, bricksetter. Whitley Superior, was summoned for not sending his son, Samuel, regularly to school. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs, and to send th 3 boy to school. The cases were proved by Mr. William Worrall, attendance officer of the Whitley United District Schr.ol Board.
ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gaskell.

GUINEk OAT.—Thrze youths, James Aehtim, Richard McQuire, and James Wright, were each fined is and costs for playing at guinea cat in the street. FIRED CHIMNEY.—Charles Rowe, of Travis-street, Parr, was fined Is and costs for haying allowrd his chimney to be on fire. _ _

BRE4CIT OF THE PEACE —Joseph Adamson was bound over to keep the peace for three months for having been fighting in Albion-street on the 14th inst. A CARELESS CARTER.—A man named Charles Morrin was fined 28 6d and costs for having allowed his cart to stand in the street at Button, on 13th mat, longer than was necessary for the purpose of loading or unloading. MONDAY.—Before Mr. W. l'ilkington and Mr.J. C. Gamble. STEALING COAL.—A girl named Margaret Jane Wreck, whose parents live at 74. Bo_d-street, was charged with stealing a ciaantity of cal. worth Id fr,m Shornley Colliery premises. Fined ICts inedluding coAs. ASSAULT.—Anne Griffilig. a married woman, was charged with having assaulted Lucy Yat:As, a coloured woman, on the 18th lust, and was bound over to keep the peace for thee months.

div.head: ST. HELENS COUNTY POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS COUNTY POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. W. Pilkington and Mr. J. C. Gamble. A CARLESS CARTER.—RaIth Smith, farmer, was charged with having allowed his cart to stand an unreasonable time on the highway at City-rod, Wirdle, on the 13th March, and was fined 2s 63 and costs.
PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. T. Pilkington, W. L. Evans, and F W. Earle.
DitumursicEss.—Joh-n-Whit'eb.ou-re(iiuytnn). George Hunter (P.oby), and Henry Quinn (Rah hill) were each fuel is. 6d. and costs; and John Burke (Prescot) 10s. and costs.

The will of the late Archbishop Tait has been proved. The personal estate was sworn under .E 35,000. At the Diocesan Synod, Salisbury, on Thursday, Mr. R. M. Wilson, who had just spoken on temperance, fell down dead. The deceased was a county coroner and a magistrate. The second floor of a warehouse in Dean-street, Liverpool, collapsed on Thursday morning, carrying with it five men and two hundred sacks of grain. Four of the men were buried under the sacks and debris, and when recovered two were dead, the others being seriously injured. The fifth man escaped unhurt. The injured were taken to the hospital. Two Greenock labourers, named Mullen and Scott, were on Thursday convicted, at the Glasgow Circuit Court, of the murder of two gamekeepers on Devol Farm, near Port Glasgow, in February last. The prisoners, who were poachers, wtre detected by the keepers and fired at them with a fatal result in each case. They were sentenced to be hanged on the 17th May.

MI. BRIGHT ON DISESTABLISHMHNT IN SCOTLAND.—In a letter recently received by the secretary of Hawick Dises- tablishment Association from Mr. Bright, declining an invi- tation to visit that town owing to other engagements at the time, the right honourable gentleman wrote :—" Your great question will grow of itself, and will, I trust, not be difficult to carry through Parliament, though it will not be disposed of before another general election." Important proceedings respecting joint stock companies are pending in Oldham. The Somerset House authorities have ascertained that sTme of the Olaham companies have accepted loans for and upwards without using a Govern- ment stamp. Ibis is held to be illegal, and proceedings are threatened unless the companies give a satisfactory reason why they have acted in this way. A number of companies are directly implicated. At Burnley, on Thursday, David Chackleton was reman- ded on a charge of stealing .6'13 belonging to Thomas Curl, The prisoner and prosecutor are members of a betting club known as the Astlev Club, and last Friday evening Curl left the sum named in his private desk at the rooms. The desk was ransacked during the night, and the prisoner was seen leaving the place at midnight, some time after the club had been closed.

On Thursday night the body of William Leach, loom jobber, of Hehnshore, was found in a dried water lodge at Higher Hills, Shuttleworth. He had been missing from let February, on which day ho left home to seek work at Red Lumb Mill. Leach was last seen at a public-house at Ash- worth Moor, and nothing more heard of him, although search was made among the hills and several lodges drained. The body was much decomposed. Thomas Mayo s and Eliza, his wife, were indicted at Stafford and Salop assizes, on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Stephen, for the murder of Mary Elizabeth Mayes, daughter of the male prisoner by his first wife. The parties lived at Kynnersley, and the head of the deceased was found in Appley Pool. It was alleged that the stepmother had syste- matically ill-treated the child, and both prisoners had made statements admitting participation in the crime, but contradicting each other in some respects. William Mayo, son of the male prisoner, stated that be was at home on February 1, and so also was I'olly, the murdered girl. His mother sent him out, and when he returned both Polly and his mother bad gone upstairs. He never saw the girl again, his mother saying she had gone to Shrewsbury. Other witnesses saw the woman carrying a basket having rennething heavy in it towards Wellington. Deceased's head was afterwards found in Appley Pool, and other portions of the remains in the river Severn. The jury found the female guilty of manslaughter, and the tnale acceesory after the fact.—The judge sentenced the woman to 20 years' penal servitude, and the man to 18 months' hard labour. THE ROYAL COLLEGE OF MUSIO.—The Royal College of Music has at last (says the Times) become a reality. The Royal charter will in a few days be signed by her Majesty, and the English National Conservatoire will henceforth have,a legal status. That this official recognition of art is in every sense the reflex of putelic opinion is amply provided by the general interest which has been shown in the eyel- fare of the new college. Whether Government aid will ul- timately be required to supplement private liberality is a question which the future must decide. In the meantime English musicians and lovers of music owe a deep debt of gratitude to the Prince of Wales and other members of the Royal family for their unceasing efforts in the cause of national art. The Royal charter in itself is a document the importance of which must not be undervalued. It confers powers and privileges of of no mean osder on the governing body of the new school. The Prince of Wales will be the first president,and there is every reason to believe that he will not look upon his office in a merely ornamental light. The Lord Mayor, also. will be an ex officio member of the council and the active support of the City of London sthatever its future boundaries may be, is the,, we may hope, secured. y, the Duke of West- Other distinguished members, such as the Duke of Edin- mbuinrgahte,r,thseirAr Richardhb l sb o svp oa fl Wallace, t e andrbur many more, will give social repute to a body which also includes some of the leading members of the musical profession.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 28, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 28, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.

ALTRINCIIAM. ACTION AGAINST THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY.—This was an action heard at Man- chester Assizes, on Monday, in which the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company were sued by John Plant and Mary Jane Plant, his wife, for compensation for injuries re- ceived by the latter on the 2nl January, 1831, while travel- ling orf the defendant's railway. For some time before the accident the male plaintiff carried on business at Altrin- chain as an argted water manufacturer. But some specu- lations in which he engaged landed him in pecuniary em- barrassment, and he found it necessary to take a situation with Messrs Boddington and Co., into whose service his wife also entered as the manageress of a public-house known as "The Three Horse Shoes." On Sunday, 2nd January, 1881, the female plaintiff visited her mother at Manchester, and in company with her relative she journeyed by an early train to Farnworth, returning to Manchester again in the evening, and from Manchester back to AI trineham. When the train came up to the platform there was a great rush for seats. There were not seats enough for all the passengers, and the female plaintiff wanted to be put into a first-class carriage, and was willing to pay the difference in the fare. The guard pushed her into the luggage van, and in the hurry of enterinc, she was tripped by one of the ridges in the floor, and tumbled against an iron milkpail. In the fall she sus- tained severe bodily injuries, which so affected and still continue to affect her general health as to render her inca- pable of attending to business or household duties. After haring the evidence, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiffs—damages £BOO, being £450 for the wife and £350 for the husband—and they expressed the opinion that the wife's compensation ought to be settled upon herself...

CALDWELL v. ALTRINCIIAII LOCAL BOARD-At the Manchester Assizes, on Monday an action was brought by Alfred Caldwell, landscape gardener, residing at Range Road, Whalley Range, Manchester, against the Altrincham Local Board of Health.—Mr. Russell, Q.C. with. Mr. Taylor and Mr. Evans, were for the plaintiff; and Mr. Bingham for the defendants.-In opening the case, Mr. Russell explained that his client claimed in respect of services extending over a considerable time, which he rendered as a landscape gardener to the defendants, in advising them, making reports to them, and attending during the hearing of a very long arbitration case. The entire claim of the plaintiff was for £716 25., but before the action was brought the defendants paid £125, which brought the amount down to .f'..591. 23. Apparently the defendants afterwards thought better of the position they originally took up, because since the action was taken they had paid into court the further sum of £350. The sum now in dispute had been thus brought down to £241 23. The question was was the plaintiff entitled to that sum, and, if not, to what less sum was he entitled? After the evidence had been beard Mr. Bingham addressed the jury. The claim made by Caldwell, he held, was most extravagant, and be pointed out that the effect of a verdict for the plaintiff would be to give that man more than £lOO in excess of the claim made by Shaw, as Caldwell's brother, who was in partnership with him bad received £3OO from the Board. He contended that the plaintiff hal been paid quite enough for his services. Mr.'Bingham was proceeding with his ad- dress when the jury intimated that they were agreed in favour of the defendants.—Mr. Taylor thereupon addressed the Court on behalf of his clients, and at the close of his re- marks the jury returned a verdict for the defendants. ASHTON. At the Liverpool County Sessions, last week, Robert Eccles (27), pleaded guilty to unlawfully assaulting George Southworth on the 30th December last, at Ashton-in-Maker- field, and, as be had borne an irreproachable character, the Bench fined him £5, or, in default, three months' hard labour. The money was paid to the prosecutor as damages.

. . ODDFELLOWS MEETING AT ASIITON.—The members of the Triumphant Lodge (Ashton-in-Makerfield) of the In- dependent Older of Oddfellows, M.U. Friendly Society held their annual monthly meeting on Saturday evening last, at the Gerrard's Arms Hotel, Ashton. There was a good at- tendance of members. The business was of a routine char- acter. The secretary's statement showed that during the month the receipts had been £3O fis SI, and expenses £43 Is 91-d. DEATHS or ASHTON l'unucitres.—A publican named Jonathan Cunliffe, landlord of the Collier's Arms, Senelev Green, Ashton, died vety suddenly on Wednesday morning. About eight o'clock on the morning of the day, named his wife left him in bed, when he appeared about as usual, but when she entered his room two hours later. lit was quite dead.---On Tuesday afternoon, Robert Simm, landlord of the Park-lane Hotel, Ashton, an old and respected' resi- dent, expired after along illness.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT DFA COLLIERY.—Between seven and eight o'clock on Thursday morning, John Langhan, a young man employed as a collier at the Mesnes Colliery, Ashton, met with an accident by which he received somewhat serious injury. It seems that he was riding on the first of ten loaded waggons, descending a "brow," when by some means be fell off and became entangled in the chain by which empty waggons were returned. His head was very badly injured in several places, his shoulder was dislocated, and by being drawn some distance his body was bruised in two or three places. The poor fellow was removed to his home in Chapel-street, with all possible speed, and Dr. Hannah has since attended him. THE GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT AT ASHTON.— In connection with the Gospel Temperance Mission which has been conducted in Ashton for a few months past, an en- tertainment was given in the Congregational Sunday School, en Saturday evening last. The selections were given by the Earlestown string band, under the conductorship of Mr. Tripp, and a number of friends of the temperance cause from Earlestown. There was a pretty fair attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. H. Wilson. After the meet- ing had been opened with singing, Ste., the band gave "Praise ye the Lord," and Miss M. J. Boughton sang "Children's evening hymn." A violin trio was given by members of the band; Miss E. Houghton and Miss R. J. Appleton followed with the dialogue "Uncle True," and Mr. Holdsworth gave the song "He wipes the tear from every eye." The band nicely rendered the selection "Hark from the upper spheres," after which Miss E. Houghton sine-" "Beautiful Eden," and Master Parr effec- tively recited a "Temperance speech," for which be received a recall. Seven members of the Earlestown Wesleyan Band of Hope gave the dialogue "How a great man's eyes were opened ;' Miss Harriman sang "Beacon light," Mr. and Master Tripp gave a violin duet, Mr. Holds. worth sang "No night there," and the dialogue, "This Sunday school lesson," was given by Miss E. Houghton and Miss M. Appleton. Mr. E. J. Weaver effectively sang "The Permissive Bill," which was encored ; a violin trio was given by members of the band, and the band gave a selection "I was glad." The Rev. H. Wilson then proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the friends from Eirlestown for the entertainment they had hiroured them with. He spoke of the necessity of a cordial relationship between the differ- ent temperance organisations, and concluded by thanking the Earlestown friends. Mr. Samuel Hope s,conded the motion, which was carried with acclamation. Mr. E. J. Weaver briefly acknowledged the compliment, and the meet- ing was brought to a close. CROFT. RETURNING FROM WARRINGTON MARKET.—Jo Sph Howard, farmer' Croft, was summoned to Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, for being drunk in charge of a horse and trap, opposite the Police Station, on the previous Wednesday.—P.C. Chantler, who proved the case, said when in Manchester-lane defendant (who did not appear). ran into a cart in which were Mrs. Cottatn and her daughter-in-law, Mrs. James Cottam, of Uulcheth. The force of the collision threw all the occupants out of the carts, but defendant hearing the constable was near scrambled into his cart and drove off. When he (witness) served the sum- mons defendant, who was badly injured, and would not be able to appear for a fortnight, expressed his willingnese to pay any fine that mieht be imposed.—The Bench tined de- fendant 101 and costs.

GOLBORNE. CROWNING or TILE MAY QUEEN.—Comiderable interest is being taken by the Golborne people—especially the younger portion—in the forthcoming ceremony of "Crown- ing the May Queen," an event which takes place next Saturday afternoon. The arrangements in cennection therewith have been almost completed. The procession of children will leave the May Queen field at two o'clock, and headed by the band of the 9th L.R.V., will parade the prin- cipal streets of the town. OR returning to the field, the •‘ coronation" will be performed by Mrs. Mope!, after which the usual festivities will be indulged in. HIGHWAY ROBBERY.—At the Occasional Court, Winyvick- I street, on Monday, James Charles and John Riley, youths, were charged with robbing John William Walker, an appren- tice of Messrs. Brewis and Co, Golborne, of half-a-crown, and using violence towards him, on the highway, at Gol- borne, on the 21st April. The prisoners met the prosecutor, and wanted him ta pay for beer for them, but he declined, as he had no change less than half-a-crown, which be ulti- mately showed them. They knocked him down, and one of them picked up the money, with which they repaired to a beerhouse kept by Thomas Duddle, for the purpose of spend- ing it. They had not been there many minutes when P.C. Whiting made his app.zarance and apprehended them.— They were committed for trial at Liverpool Assizes. HAYDOCK. CATHOI IC SERMONS AT HAYDOCK.—The annual sermons in aid of the school funds, were preached in the Catholic Mission Chapel, Hayclock, on Sunday last. Both morning and evening there was a crowded attendance, and the elo- quent addresses of the Rev. Father O'Callaghan of Liver- pool, were listened to with great interest and attention. A sum amonting to nearly £3O was realised. Scdoor. EXAMINATION.—The scholars attending the day- school taught by Miss Marnall in the Catholic Mission school, Haydock, were examined in the usual elementary subjects on Wednesday morning by Mr. Glover, H.M. inspector of elementary schools for this district. There is every reason to believe that the scholars give evidence of be- ing efficiently taught, and at the close of the examination they were dismissed for the day.

HIIY TON. NEW RATE FOR HIIITTON.—At Preicot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. Makin, assistant overseer, obtained the signatures of the magistrates to a new rate of is 81 in the X for the township of Iluyton-with-Roby. The arrears of the old rate amount to £4 2s sd.

THE QUEEN'S HIGHWAY.-At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Robart Forster was fined 5s and costs for being found asleep in his cart on the highway in Liverpool-road, Huy ton.—lienry Savage was fined 58 and costs for usurping the footpath in Tarbock-road, linyton, with his bicycle; and David Davies, a carter, was fined a similar sum for riling in his cart, on the highway, at Huyton, without , reins.

POACHING AT HITYTON.—James William Thompson, Smith, and John Scotson appeared before the Prescot ma- gistrates, on Tuesday, on a charge of trespassing in pursuit ' of game on the land of Mr. Joseph Evans, Hirst's House, Huyton. The case was proved by a man of the name of Sanders, in the employment of Mr. Levintoti, who having been sent to watch saw the defendants kill a rabbit.—Scot- son And Thompson were each fined 103 and costs, and Smith 20i and costs.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE AT HUYTON.—At Present, on . Tuesday, Isabelia Pattlm was charged with a breach .of the peace at Horn Smithy, -Huyton, by cursing and swearing, and otherwise making a disturbance. She submitted that she had made all the bother on her own door step, and therefore had acted within her legal rights. The magistrates took a different view, and required her to enter into recog- nisanees for her future good behaviour.—Thomas Radley was also charged with disturbing the peace of Huyton by fighting with William Kenyon, and was held to bail. ASSAULTING AN OLD MAN AT HUYTON.—Thomas Taylor appeared in answer to a summons, at Present, on Tuesday, charging him with assaulting Petter Pendleton. Mr. McKenzie prosecuted.—lt appeared that on the evening of the Bth instant, complainant was walking with his father and mother towards Huyton. On the way they overtook the defendant and some other men, and the defendant made an offensive remark to complainant's father. Of this no notice was taken, but as complainant and his parents were opening the gate of complainant's house, opposite the Huy- ton cricket ground, defendant rushed across the road and attempted to strike the old man. Complainant prevented the assault, whereupon defendant struck complainant and a struggle ensued, in the course of which complainant's thumb was very severely bieten.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 403 and coats.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

BEGGING.—John Ryan and John Lynch, tramps, were charged, the former on Saturday and the latter on Thurs- day, at the Occasional Court, Lymm, before Mr. T. P Norris, with begging at High Leigh, and each was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.______

div.head: R AINFORD.
div.p: R AINFORD.

A RAINFORD BEEMIOUSE CASE—On Monday, at the St. Helens Comity Petty Sessions, Thomas Davis, of Rain- ford, was charged with having been drank on the licensed premises of James Frodsham, landlord of the Foresters' Arms, at Rainford, on the 12th inst.—Sergeant Lawless said that on the evening of the day named, about 20 minutes to seven, he saw the defendant Davis go staggering past his station. Witness went to the door in order to see where Davis was going to, and saw him go into Frodsham's beer. house. He (witness) followed down, and on going into the beerhouse saw defendant sitting there with a glass filled with beer, apparently newly drawn, before him. Defendant took the glass up and drunk about three-parts of it, and then laid it down. Witness spoke to the landlord about allowing the defendant to have beer whilst in an intoxicated condition, but the landlord denied that Davis was drunk, and also said that he was only drinking beer which he had or- dered bafore he went out to get a bundle of straw at a Mr. Green's. Sergeant Lawless then took Davis down to the house at which P.C. Parker lcdged, and Parker there saw the defendant, and also bis landlady, Mrs. Penketh.—Mrs. Penketh and P.C. Parker were called, and corroborated the statement of Sergeant Lawless with respect to Davis haying been drunk.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared on behalf of the defendant, and called several witnesses to show that he was not drunk.—The Chairman (Mr. W. Pilkington) said the Bench were of opinion that the defendant had not been sober, but that he had not been so drunk as to justify a conviction. The case was therefore dismissed.—A further charge which it was intended to prefer against Frodsham for supplying drink to a drunken person was withdrawn. RAINHILL.

HOLT CHAPEL, RAINHILL.—The anniversary services in connection with the mission of the Congregational Union at Holt, Rainhill, began on Sunday. In the afternoon Mr. R. J. Clements, of St. Helens, gave an interesting address to the scholars, and in the evening the Rev. James Johnston, pastor of the Congregational Church at Prescot, preached upon the subject of the "Pleasure and profit of religion." The collection amounted to £3. On Wednesday evening a tea meeting was held, at which a goodly number assembled, and a public meeting followed under the chairmanship of Mr. W. Evans. •In the course of the evening Mr. Evans made a tel)mg speech on "Christian consecration," and was followed by Mr. Welch, of S. Helens, and the Rev. J. Johnston, the latter of whom dealt with the relation of "Privilege and responsibility" in an able and exhaustive manner. Glees, songs, recitations, and readings were after- wards given by members of the congregation, and a most enjoyable and successful evening was spent. WHISTON.

THRFT OF COAT, AT WinsTos —At Prescot on Tuesday. Helen Leadbetter was charged with stealing 841 b of coal from .the Carr's Colliery of the Wigan and Whiston Colliery Company. The defendant was seen removing the coal by P.C. Lay, who had been watching the premises.— She was fined 40s, or in default one month's imprisonment.

div.head: VVINSFORD.
div.p: VVINSFORD.

RELIGIOUS FERVOUR.—There is still prevailing in our midst an amount of feeling in connection with the army of the Salvationists, Blue Ribbon Gospel movement, and the United Free Methodists, as well as the Primitive Metho- dists. The missioning of the streets by the two first con- tinues regularly in different parts of the town, but with considerably diminished numbers. There have been changes of." captains" and "lieutenants" in the expectation of im- proving the meetings, and still further developing the sys- tems. The Sundays' gatherings are not amiss, but the week-days' thin and meagre. The Free Methodist Church hashed Miss McLatchy for weeks now, but with the excep- tion of Sundays her congregations partake of the flagging in like manner. The Gravel Free Methodist Church was nearly full on Tuesday to hear her, but the High-street Chapel far from that the other nights._ _ _

THE NEW WESLEYAII CHAPEL.—The funds for a new Wesleyan Chapel, Winsford Hill, were promoted by a bazaar on Wednesday last, which was held in the school-room, High-street. It was opened at two p.m. by Mr. Edmund Leigh, who expressed the great pleasure it gave him to be present on such an interesting occasion, and to see such an array of work, which indicated an amount of self-denying labour and kindly sympathy oaths pert of many ladies, and no doubt several gentlemen also. He was sure every- thing looked very well, and he trusted everything would speedily disappear by successful sale, for which he said several ladies and gentlemen were ready, so be would pro- nounce the hazier open. The chief promoters are Mesdames Reader, Royle, Hoofs, Twiss, S. Brookes, and Devenport, and the Misses C. Latham, Chesters, Royle, Hoole, &e. These at once took charge of their respective tables. The stalls presented a neat and attractive appearance. The Rev. C. Reader and Mr. E. Hoole exercised their musical abilities on the American organ to the great enjoyment of many onlookers. Toward four p.m. the refreshment table, under Mrs. Hoole and Miss Cheaters, began to be busier, after which there was a lull until the evening gathering lessened the array of goods, enlarged the funds, and gladdened the ladies for their many hours of previous labour. ITEHS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

CATTLE DISEASE IN CIIESITIRE.—The weekly returns compiled by Lieutenant-Colonel flamersley, chief constable of Cheshire, show the following result at the end of last week: Remaining under treatment from the previous week, 75 ; attacked during the week, 46 ; died, 3 ; recovered, 45; under treatment, 73. Sheep scab existed on eight firms, 21 sheep being, under tteatment. The county was still free from pleuro-pneumonia.

ALLEGED FRAUDS BY A CHESHIRE GROCER. Mr. Hughes, Q.O Judge of the Cheshire County Courts, has granted an order for the prosecution of William Heath, grocer, Moulton, Cheshire, for fraudulent bankruptcy. It is alleged that Heath fraudulently disposed of his stock before his bankruptcy, and that he has filed five different petitions during the last seven years, and carried on business at thir- teen different places within the same period. Mr. Cooke, solibitor, Winsford, wilt prosecute Heath. LOCAL CArrLE ORDERS.—The London Gazette contains orders in council declaring areas at Haughton, Lancashire, at Church Lawton, Cheshire, and at Prestbury, Cheshire, to be infected with foot-and-mouth disease from the 22nd, 23rd, and 25th inst. respectively. Further orders notify that areas at Sealand, in Hawarden, and at Menden, Prestatyn, and Gronant, Flintshire. which were declared infected with foot-and-mouth disease, are now free from such infection. . .

NEW BAPTIST CHAPEL AT CREwE.—The memorial stones of a new chapel for General Baptists at Crewe were laid on Tuesday afternoon by the Rev. W. P. Grant, of Perth ; Rev. Z. I'. Dowen, of Macclesfield (on behalf of Mrs. Bury) ; Mrs. R. Pedley, of Winterley House; and the Rev. W. Lees, Walsall, the pastor elect. The building is .estimated to cost about £4,000. The Rev. T. Goadby, president of Chelwell College, Nottingham, gave an address to a large gathering on the site of the proposed building, in which he reviewed the history of the General Baptist Connexion. Afterwards a meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, un- der the presidency of the Mayor of Crewe (Alderman Ains- worth, Jr.) A CHESHIRE Jun ir CENSURED BY THE CORONER.—Dr. Churton, the coroner for West-Cheshire, held an adjourned it.quest, on Monday, at Little Barrow, near Chester, upon the hedy of John Thomas Smith, 11 years of age, whose death was caused by a horse and cart posing over him, on th 6th inst. The horse would seem to have shied and run against a bank, upsetting the deceased, who was in the cart, am passing over him. The evidence went to show that the 9 were no reins attached to the horse, and that the carter was seated at the back of the cart. The coroner, in sum- mine up, dwelt upon these facts, and said the driver was clearly responsible for the death of the deceased. The jury, taking a different view, returned a verdict of "Accidental death," whereupon Dr. Churton said the verdict was not only opposed to law, but also to common sense. THE STABBING AFFRAY AT A WAKES.—At Crewe Sessions, on Tuesday, Henry Brassington, a niggler, of Betley, was charged on remand with stabbing and wounding Peter Williams, at Wybunbnry wakes, on the 4th of March. Mr. C. S. Brooke prosecuted on behalf of the police; Mr. James Newcastle. defended. Further evidence was taken to the effect that the prisoner was at the wakes, and that he was seen to stab tha complainant in the side. Williams fell in the road, and was afterwards taken to the Boar's Head. The doctor said he had lost three pints of blood, and for three weeks his condition was so critical- that little hope was entettained of his recovery. One of the witnesses called by the prosecution stated that the prisoner was knocked down and jumped upon by Williams and several of his mates. Mr. James said his defence would be that the prisoner used the knife in self-defence.—The Bench committed the prisoner for trial.
f n the House of Commons on Monday, Colonel J. Black- burne presented a petition, in favour of Sunday Closing from the Prescot Board of G nardians.

div.head: I THE ARCHDEACONRY OF WAR-
div.p: I THE ARCHDEACONRY OF WAR-
RINGTON. ARCHDEACON BARDSLEY ON THE DIOCESAN i SOCIETIES. 0

, In Wednesday morning Archdeacon Bardsley held his , annual visitatien at St. Elphin's Church, Warrington. There was a good attendance of clergy, wardens, sidesmen, clz.c. Amongst the clergy were the Revs. F. W. Cory, A. M. Mitchell, S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's), T. R. Matthews (Earlestown). After prayers, Archdeacon BARDSLEY delivered his charge. He said: We meet this day for the purpose of admitting you, my ' brethren, the wardens and sidesmen of this archdeaconry of Warrington, to the several offices to which you have been chosen by your respective Easter vestries. The arch- deaconry, since the last visitation, has had its deaneries increased from three to five by the addition of the deaneries of Childwall and Toxteth. May this enlarged organisation result, by God's blessing, in increased spiritual activities, and thus justify and reward the bishop for the care and at- tention which he has bestowed upon this portion of his diocese. Whilst I offer a cordial welcome to those who for the first time represent their parishes under the new titles of Childwall and Toxteth, I desire to express my sincere regret that the archdeaconry loses the services as rural dean of one who for nearly 20 years has presided over the deanery of Winevick. During the 43 years which Canon Hopwood has ministered in the diocese of Chester, many changes have taken place, and many among us know well how his ripe experience and gentle wisdom have contributed in no small degree to that development of church extension which has so honourably distinguished of late years the hundred of West Derby. In the uniform kindness which I have always received at his hands, I ten- der him my tribute of respectful thanks; and, whilst I assure him of our affectionate regard, pray that he may be spared for many years to enjoy the Sabbath of an extended life in preparation for that Sabbath which remains for the people of God. I rejoice, my brethren, that we meet to-day in God's house of prayer in such numbers, representing as we de many parishes. The system of our church is not congregational. although in many large towns there is a danger of isolation and divided interests. To-day, however, we gather together , in holy fellowship and in loyal obedience to the require- ' merits of our common mother. I observe that the bill which bears the name of Sir Gabriel Goldney and Mr. Monk, and which seeks to enable churchwardens after appointment to make their declaration before the rural dean or the incuni- . bent of the parish, stands for second reading on the 30th of this month. I earnestly trust that it may be thrown out, ' not only because it is open to grave objections in itself so far as regards the admission of wardens by their own incum- bent, but because it tends to destroy that manifestation of union and demonstration of fellowship which our present mode of admission strikingly affords. It is my own earnest , desire to recognise as publicly as I can the immense oblige- I tions under Which our church is laid by' the readiness of so , many devoted laymen to accept the office of warden and ' sidesmen, and by the ability and attention with which the performance of the various duties pertaining to these offices are discharged. It is as the bishop's representative that I am privileged to admit you to the office, and as the bishop's representative therefore, I may express his gratitude to those who this day are ready once more to declare that they will truly and faithfully, and to the best of their skill and knowledge, disch irge the solemn responsi- bilities to which they are called. It is likewise my earnest desire to make the office of admission as light as possible; and it would give me pleasure, if spared, to hold on future I occasions a court in each deanery, if such a plan would tend to the general convenience. As it is, I shall make the time during which I claim your attention as brief as possible, by ;dividing my charge and delivering in each centre scme portion only of that which I feel called upon to say. Let me thil morning direct your attention to the Permanent Diocesan Finance Association which is now being estab- lished at the request of our diocesan conference. At the time of the sub-division of the diocese of Chester, a committee was appointed provisionally, and it is matter for some congratulation that during this transitional period of two years funds have been contributed to such an extent as to justify the change from a provisional commit- tee to a permanent finance association, of which Sir Richard Assheton Cross and Laurence R. Baily, Esq., are the joint honorary treasurers. This finance association, it may be desirable to explain, has been established not only to strengthen the five diocesan societies, of whose work I will shortly speak, but being incorporated tinder the Board of Trade it will consist of a permanent body of trustees, cap- able of holding and investing moneys, not only for the diocesan societies, but for any church purpose, such as the building of a cathedral, church repairs, and endow- ment funds. The association already possesses central offices in Commerce - court, Lord - street, Liverpool, where moneys for the church societies can be received, and where information will gladly be given concerning them or any church work which is being pro- moted in the diocese. The association has been sufficiently fortunate to secure the services of the Rev. J. F. Hector. M.A., for some years the incumbent of an important parish , in Adelaide, as their secretary, and I rejoice to add that in , him the association possesses not only an eloquent advocate I whom I can warmly recommend to the clergy as a preacher, I but also an energetic man of large experience and of busi- ness habits, who will at all times be glad to co-operate with I I our lay friends by accompanying them when willing to cm- vase I for additional subscriptions in their respective neigh- bourhoods, and who will further most cheerfully, with the permission of the incumbents, establish in any parish a parochial branch for the promotion of the various , diocesan associetions. My brethren present here to-day will not consider that I dwell unduly on this Diocesan Finance Association when I re- mark that its prosperity means the successful maintenance I of those five societies which provide official machinery for I making our church (so far as the diocese of Liverpool is concerned) in reality what she is already in name, the I church of the people. Those five societies were launched two years ago in the Town Hall of Liverpool, at a great diocesan meeting. Their hearty support was commended to the diocese at large by the bishop in a pastoral, in which I he expressed his own satisfaction with this scheme of organisation, and in which he besought on their behalf most liberal help. The societies thus inaugurated are—first, the Church Building Society, which yet only aids in the erec- tion, the enlargement, and increased accommodation of churches, but also in the acquisition of suitable sites and in the erection or hiring of mission rooms. The second society is the B enefices Augmentation, which promotes the improvements of poor livings by augmenting the endowments, and by the provision of parsonages. The third society is the Church Aid Society, which is admirably suited to promote that great work of aggressive evangelisation which the Bishop has so much at heart, by employing missionary clergymen in poor and populous parishes, and by defraying wholly or in part the necessary expenses incidental to divine worship in poor parishes and districts. The fourth society is the Board of Education and School Society, which seeks . to maintain the two training colleges connected with our dio- cese in the highest state of ° efficiency; to maintain such a I system of inspection of our schools as will secure that sound religious education shall be imparted in them ; to maintain the efficiency of our poorer ' schools by making grants of money upon Certain con- ditions ; and which, further, also, according to its means, contributes to the building and enlargement of schools. Let it be widely known that chiefly in conse- quence of its fostering aid no school belonging to our Church has been abandoned during the past year, notwith- standing the competition of the numerous neighbouring board schools. The fifth society is the one which includes the benevolent institutions especially associated with the place in which we are assembled, and which are keown as the Warrington institutions, one granting pensions to the widows and orphans of the diocesan clergy and the other supplying, on generous terms, an excellent education to the daughters of the ill-paid clergy. Brethren of the laity, I appeal with confidence, and inquire whether it would be possible to devise machinery more complete in its aims and more effective in its results if only adequately maintained? During the past year, I regret to learn, 68 churches in the dioceae have done nothing to aid any one of these diocesan societies, notwith- standing the Bishop's urgent appeal for funds. I am thankful to know that some of these parishes have not neglectecrthe claims of foreign missions during the year, but I may be forgiven if I venture to think that the ability to keep the one is the proof that power is not wanting to sup- port the other, and that as charity begins at home we ought all, whilst doing the oae duty, not to leave the other un- done. The entire amount received for all the five societies in every way during the past year has been £4,7oo—viz., £1,733 from offertories, £2,270 from subscriptions, and £643 from donations. The two great missionary societies —the S.P.G. and C M.S.—received from the diocese of Liverpool during the year, I rejoice to know, for the Gospel in foreign lands, no less than £7,000. I refuse to believe that £4,700 is the measure of our responsibility to the wants of the Church at home. The miserable grants which our Church Building Seciety, to take one example, is enabled at present to make, owing to the scanty income it receives, are rather signs of sympathy than expressions of adequate support for the erection of churches in our poor parishes. An income of £lO,OOO a year for our five diocesan societies would be fairly sufficient to supply all our wants Ttiat income can readily be fur- nished if only our necessaries are known, and if we but in- dividually realise how much we owe to the Giver of every good gift. The remedy is practically in the hands of my lay brethern, for they justly possess great influence in their respective neighbourhoods; and I fully believe that by their hearty co-operation, doing what they can in their respective parishes —be it little or much the income will be found, and God's work will no longer languish in this populous ani wealthy diocese. Our Church, brethren, has enjoyed a great history in the past, and never had she a more glorious opportunity than the one which confronts her in the present. As we all disperse to our respective parishes, let us resolve that, so far as in us lies, we will do what we can to make her an active and effective instrument for the great work it is given her to do. Thus resolving and thus fulfilling our vows, we shall not only promote God's glory in the maintenance and extension of the truth, but we shall establish our Church afresh in the affections of a thankful people. The wardens and sidesmen then made the usual declare- ' tion, and were admitted to office.

ASHTON CHURCII ASSOCIATION.
LEcnyRE ON RITUALISM BY THE REV. DR.
POTTER.

I The last of the series of lectures for the season in con- nection with the Cave-Browne Protestant Insteute Heath. lane, Ashton, was given in that building on Monday even- ing last, when the Rev. G. S. Potter, D.D., of Sheffield, delivered a stirring address On "Ritualism as a conspiracy, a heresy, and an immorality." There was a large and entheesiastio attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Hodgkinson' who was supported on the platform by the Rev. Dr. Potter; Mr. Marsh, president of the Ashton branch of the Church Association ; Mr. Thomas Egan, of Earlestown ; ' Mr. Bryan Hodgkinson, Mr. Gibson, Mr. G. J. Byrom, and Mr. Jameson (late organist of the Parish Church). The meeting was opened with the singing of a hymn, after which the Rev. Dr. Potter offered up. prayer. The Cuenrwede said he need scarcely say how great a pleasure it was to occupy the position he did that night, more especially as they again had the proud privilege of welcoming their esteemed and reyerend friend, Dr. Potter— (applause)—a noble champion of Protestant truth—to their Cave-Browne Protestant Institute.:As-they would no doubt be aware he had to speak to them on a very important sub- ject—a subject no less than "Ritualism as a conspiracy, a heresy, and an immorality." Ritualists as a rule claimed to be the bone fide members of the Church of England; they claimed to be the loyal members of the Church of England, and they regarded those who were opposed to them in any way as being the conspir- ing party, as the disloyal party—that party who in truth were ignerant of the principles they professed. But he (the chairman) ventured to say that that night the tables would be entirely turned, and it would be shown that the Ritual- ists themselves were the conspirators, and that the loyal and true members of the Church were those found in con- nection with such branches as that of the Ashton-in-Maker- field branch of the Church Association. (Applause.) Any man, woman, or child, in the present crisis in the history of the Church, who valued the privileges won for them by the blood of their martyr forefathers, would not hesitate for a single moment to ally themselves with the work of the Church Association. (Hear, hear.) They must never be ashamed of that association, no matter what their opponents might say or do in attempting to ridicule them. They had truth on their side; the Bible and the Articles of the Church of England were for them and not against them, and all loyal members of the Church of England were un- doubtedly on their side. They might say that as their principles were loyal to the Bible, the Articles, and the Prayer Book, they consequently did not savour a heresy; while on the contrary Ritualism, as they all knew, was simply borrowed from Romanism—it was only Romanism under another name, and therefore it was a heresy. (Ap- plause.) He had the greatest pleasure in calling upon the Rev. Dr. Potter to deliver his lecture. The Rev. Dr. POTTER was very warmly received. He commenced by remarking that they had arrived at a great crisis in the history of their church and country, but it was not the first crisis of its kind in the history of the Church of God. Under a former dispensation there was a conspiracy which the prophets denounced, and against which they threatened the anger of God. "Associate yourselves to- gether and ye shall be broken in pieces," said the prophets; and so he (the Rev. Dr. Potter) would say to the conspira- tors of to-day against the English Church, against Protestant truth, and against English liberty, "Conspire together and ye shall be broken in pieces, for Jesus is our head, Jesus is our captain, and Jesus is on our side." He proceeded to quote several passages of scripture, and maintained that it had been predicted that the Church should be afflicted, and in the history of the Church they had only seen it on too many occasions. Not only was it predicted, but in the Epistles to the Thessalonians- and to Timothy the Apostle Paul distinctly foretold the characteristics of it, so that there should be no doubt or mistake about it when it came, and Protestants had no excuse for bearing with apathy the abominable corruption, the odious and hideous apostasy, which was working such a pestiferous evil as a leprosy amongst the people of this country. So plainly was it written that it appeared as it were a beam of light, which the whole world might see, and yet men would not see it because they had not the anointing of the eyes by the Holy Spirit, whereby men's souls and minds could be made to see. It created a paralysis of the moral nature—it affected the whole com- pound nature of man and woman, leaving them pestiferous in the eyes of the people. If he did not prove that he would only say he would be guilty of tall-talk without proof. The first thing he had to prove was that it was a conspiracy. Dr. Pusey, the man who was the originator of the whole of the abominable conspiracy against liberty, light, truth, and free- dom, had told them in a paper called "Plan of the Cam- paign" the aims and objects that were to be attained by his followers, who were to follow the example of the "dishonest baker." Lot them fancy any Christian man, theologian, or moral philosopher recommending youth and age to follow the action of a dishonest baker, who by a little bit of ashift, then by a little shunt, was able to transmogrify and trans- mute a little piece of mutton into a big lump! Dr. Pusey,' the head conspirator, told them to begin with a little thing at first, and then get a bit bigger until by 'a trick, Jesuistry and dishonesty they would be able to get the whole thing. ("Shame.") That meant the worship of the Virgin Mary, the seven sacraments of the Church of Rome, belief in the saints and angels, transubstantiation and all the great abominations of the great apostasy in wor- ship and in faith. If that was not a conspiracy, and a con- spiracy of a very dishonourable kind he did not know what to call it. He could agree with an association that sought by honest means to accomplish even undesirable ends in his opinion, but this conspiracy was a system of evasion, it was a system of subtlety, Jesuistry, and dishonesty, and no true Englishman liked that because it was a moral deterioration of the character, and it was not the character of the English people. (Applause.) He was not contented with merely affirming or demonstrat- ing in his own way that the men were a band of conspira- tors, but they confessed themselves conspirators. In some of the earlier tracts of the Tractarian body, which he had in his possession, they said "We openly confess that we are conspirators and banded together for the purpose of eliminating and rooting out Protestantism in the English Church." (" Shame.") It was a conspiracy against the doctrine, discipline, and practice of the English Church, and therefore it was no heated enthusiastic partisan who dubbed them conspirators and their society a conspiracy. The illustrious late Lord Beaconsfield ha e said, "I mean by Ritualism the practice by a certain portion of the clergy of ceremonies which they themselves con fe: sod are symbolical of doctrines which they are pledged by every solemn compact which can bind men to their sovereign and country to denounce and repudiate," and if that was not a conspiracy he did not know what was. (Applause.) He did not find fault with those men for finding fault with the faith and discipline of the English Church. The system of toleration was estab- lished by William 111., of pious, glorious, and immortal memory—whom he revered more than any monarch who ever held the sceptre of Great Britain, and since then they had affirmed the principle that every man had a right to think upon every subject as he pleased, only he was not to carry his thoughts into overt action—injurious to the community or the civil and Sovereign state. He found fault with the men for the mental evasiveness and subtelty by which they endeavoured to impose untruth for truth on the people, and for trying to persuade men, women, and children that they were honest men whenethey were rogues. What business or right had a man who held office under the Queen and Constitution to write and spread abroad a noxious anti-monarchial republicanism? (" None what- ever.") He had none whatever, and in the same wery what right had a wan, who had a preference for Ritualism, Roman- ism, and everything of the kind to remain in the Protestant Church, allied with the Protestaut Constitution? So inter- woven and intertwisted was the Protestantism of the Church with the Constitution of the country that if they destroyed the one they would break up the other, and what right had a man who sought to do that to remain in the Protestant Church, sapping and mining, and by a system of mental evasiveness, subtlety, ab'ed Jesuitry, trying to persuade them that black was white? He thought they might follow the advice which had been given, that they should educate public opinion and bring it up to the heat of William the Third's days when the corresponding thing was driven out of the country. It was a very dangerous conspiracy, a very un-English conspiracy, and let him emphasize its character by saying that it was a conspiracy against liberty, life, freedom, light, truth, and there was offered to them in the alternative, if they accept it, darkness, bondage, and death. It was not only a conspiracy, but it was a heresy— a heresy being a corruption of the faith. It had been an affliction of the church that there were heretics from the very first day the church was established up- to the present hour. The history of the church showed that as they some- times sung in the hymn, it had been—
By schisms rent asunder,

By heredes distressed. Heresies and schisms were not created by Protestants, but by the Ritualists of the Church, and that was shown by the standard of truth they believed in, the 30 Articles of the Church of England and the Prayer Book. Many of the conspirators taught the doctrines which were there declared to be dangerous doctrines and blasphemous deceits, to be ab- horred by all Christian men, although they had sworn upon their solemn oath before God that they would teach them to be dangerous and blasphemous. He (the speaker) did not know anytning of the vicar of that parish, but had anyone ever heard him since his appointment preach against those errors, and heard him warn his people against them? If he had he was a true Protestant character— (Voices : "He never has ")—and if he bad not, he was simply after the loaves and fishes, and the dirty, ISlthy lucre, destroying 'hie own reputation and character as a true Christian man. (Applause.) He wished, had as it was, that those men could be only thought to be after the loaves and fishes. Many of them not only stuck to the loaves and fishes, but held on to an establishment in which they were pouring doses of the vilest religious po:aon. He would say to every person that if they allowed it they were net worthy the name of father, mother, husband, brother, or guardian of youth, and they were not doing their duty to their country, to their God, and to themselves. (Applause.) He proceeded to allude to the doctrines of purgatory, tran- substantiation, and the mass, and said such abominable superatition ought to be 'spat out, banished, and rep.adiated from the land. It should not be tolerated in a free country. Let those who held them go to the deserts and caves in the remote corners of the earth, away from tha general community, and where they could no 'longer infect, putrify, and corrupt others, and where they could believe that the moon was made of green cheese, a thing egnplly ridiculous. A REAL BONA-FIDE AND SPECIAL OFFER TO THE READERS OF THIS PAPER.

THE REAL TEST OF MERIT PROVED. THOUSANDS require a Good Watch, but few in comparison know where to obtain such. The Prices charged by Dealers are exorbi- tant, and half the Wat• bee Bold of an Unreliable Character. The Finest English Levers in the World are made in Liverpool at STEWART DAWSON ard Co.'s Manufactory, and people living at a dis- tance who Buy at Wach Shops can only obtain the Ordinary Common Made Coventry Watches, or Worthless Foreign Productions for wh!ch Dealers charge Exorbitant Prices, a necessity on account of their Small Sales. THIS IS A POSITIVE FACT _ .

which you shall prove to yourself. If you wish to purchase a Watch, examine in every available source all the Watches you can find for Sale, or that may have been purchased at from £5 to £6, then send to us for one of OUR DIAGNIFIOENT ENGLISH LEVERS, which we will supply you with for £3, and com- pare it with any at those prices. Our Terms to ptove the above are these—We will forward you a Watch on a full week's free trial, and if you are unacquainted with us, you may make your P.O. Order payable Ten Days after Date, so that we cannot possibly keep your . money until you have proved the above. Re- member WE WANT YOU TO PROVE IT,

in order that we may continue to obtain the credit we de.erve. and if you don't find the Watch that we send you to be better in every way than any you can buy in a shop at £5 to £6, or if it does not otherwise meet with your approval, just return it t, us, and your money will be returned in full. It Is no trouble to us in the least to send you one to look at. We live in an age of suspicion, and we live in an age of deception. Suspicions and doubts are fostered by deception, but where truths are proved by actual deeds there can be.no deception. Truth travels with a mighty voice, and zrumbles to dust and ashei those who try to build on lies, hol- low shams, and shallow pretensions, and by truths tens of thousands in every part of the kingdom have proved to themselves the genuineness of this announcement, and no person whatever teed buy a common Watch or one with three or four pounds' profit put on it. when we offer you such advan- tageous and legitimate terms, to enable you to buy - direct from the actual Makers, one of the very best

--- English Lever Watches that can be made. When e. we say English Lever, we mean such, a Watch made entirely In our own Manufactory, of the very highest class. with full plate and full capped Lever Movement, very finest quality and union through- out. containing original and exclusive improve- ments, with very close-fitting extra heavy Sterling Silver Hall Marked Cases, handsomely finished, with Shield and Garter on back, white Enamel Bunk Seconds Dial, and Gold Hands, altogether Matchless in either Style, Finish. Qu*lity, or as Timekeepers. Each guaranteed for Three Years. It's impossible to obtain better than the best; then why throw three or four pounds away to a shop- keeper in profit when you can save this amount to yourself, and likewise have the pleasure of wearing a better article. Therefore, don't fail to send for one of these magnificent English Levers (Ladies' or Gent.'s) if only to look at, and prove to you what capital, modern enterprise, unflinching in- tegrity, and progression can accomplish.
