div.head: – THE SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT
div.p: - THE SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT

WIDNES. ADJOURNED INQUEST. On Thursday, at the Central Hotel, Widnes, the adjourned inquiry into the circumstances of the death of James Jones, 15 years of age, who was killed at Messrs. Carlile's saw mills, Warringten-road, on the 16th mat, was resumed be- fore Mr. T. W. Barker, the coroner. Mr. H. S. Richmond, her Majesty's Inspector of Factories for the district, was present; and Mr. C. H. Lewin watched the proceedings on behalf oi Mr. Carlile, who also occupied a seat in the TOM. The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, explained that the inquest read been adjourned in order to give Mr. Richmond an opportunity of examining the works. He had made that examination, and the jury would have the benefit of his assistance. Tne facts of the accident were very short, and he dare say they would be well acquainted with them. About ten o'cloci,: on the morning of the accident the unfortunate boy made preparations for making some "plaster laths," and was seen on a stack of timber, throwing wood down for that purpose. In about ten minutes afterwards soroe work- , men heard the machinery making a peculiar noise, and on going into the shed they saw the deceased suspended by one leg to the strap, and his brains dashed over all the build- ing. lie was quite dead. It was a most frightful accident, and it would be for the jury to say, when they had heard the evidence, whether tney thought any blame could be attached to anyone, or that they considered the accident as the result of an act of indiscretion on the part of the unfor- tunate youth. If they thought there was 'lame they would have to express their opinion upon it either pnerally or by presentment. It was for the jury to say whether this dan- gerous kind of machinery was properly fenced, and, if not, that it should be so fenced. Evidence was then celled.

Joseph Capper, engine-driver at the saw mills, said he had worked there for three years and a half. The deceased hi been employed at the same place for about two years, a was a very careful, steady boy. On the morning of the accident the deceased had been assisting the sawyer to saw timber. About five minutes before the accident he (witness) alio the deceased getting some deals off the timber stack, and told him to wait there until his return, but when he did return, however, the deceased had gone. He did not know what the deceased had to do in the saw mill. He had not told him to do anything in the saw mill, nor did he know that anybody else had done so. He heard a peculiar noise in the mill a few minutes afterwards, and the sawyer called to him to stop the engine. He did so, and on going into the shed he saw the deceased hanging Lo the strap by tha feet. The deceased must have been caught with a pulley near the bench and carried up to the abaft, which was 10 feet high. He was hanging head down- wards, and was quite dead. He had evidently been killed instantly as the crown of his head was cut off, and the sight was altogether a shocking one. The body was re- leased and taken home. So far as witness was aware de- Ceased was not allowed to cut timber, and he never saw him doing so. Two persons were required to saw wood. Wit- ness thought the deceased had been attempting to push the belt off the pulley with his foot in order to atop the saw, and he had been caught and carried round. There was a piece of wood for the purpose of pushing the strap, and deceased must have known its use and could have used it.— In answer to Mr. Richmond, witness said the wood he men- tioned was a loose piece, and he did not see it after the acci- dent. He had never seen the deceased cutting laths himself, but he knew that he had done so frequently.—By Mr. Lewin The deceased had no right to go into the engine. TOOM until he had finished helping witness. He did not consider that anyone was to blame for the accident except the deceased. He thought it , was a complete accident. The Coroner: Are there any rules :about boys not working this saw except under the supervision of an elderly person? I don't know. —A juryman: Did the deceased get an order to cut laths at! the saw? I don't know.—The juryman: He would never have stopped the saw unless he had had some instructions. %—Witness said the piece of wood was generally leaning against the table. George Matthews said he was the "machine hand" and sawyer at the saw mills, and had worked there for six years. The deceased was the general help in the yard. He last saw the deceased alive at half-past nine. On the morning of the accident he was working at a saw bench, when about 10 o'clock he heard a "thudding" noise in the adjoining shed, and he ran to the engine driver and told him to stop the Before doing so, however, he had looked into the shed, and sAW the deceased being swung round the shaft at a rapid speed. The deceased had gone into the shed to cut plaster laths.—The Coroner: How do you know that? Mr. Cariile told me so.—Had anyone told the deceased to cut ' laths? I don't know.—Have you ever known deceased cut laths before ? Yes.—ls he competent to do that himself? yes; he could do it easily.—By Mr. Richmond : He did not know that deceased had been sawing that morning. He was used to working the small saw. . Mr. Richmond observed that this was the only saw bench that was without a permanent fork with which to put the belt on.

The Coroner (to witness): Why has not this one? I can- I not say. We can put the belt on easily with a stick with- out a fork.—lf it is necessary to have a fork for the others, it it not necessary to have one for this? This one is not much used.—Has it been the practice to put this belt on and off wtth the foot? Yes, I have often done so myself.—Mr. Richmond: Wby did you do that instead of using the stick? Because the stick was not there handy.—The Coroner: There ought to be something fixed there.—Witness remarked that he worked the saw a week before the accident, and started it then with a stick.—ltv Mr. Lewin: He did Sot know what deceased had been doing on the morning of the accident. In answer to other questions witness said he had never been cautioned against moving the strap with his foot, but he had never let anyone see him do so: He could put the belt on with his hand, and had done so.—Mr. Lewin: You would not have put it on with your foot if your master had been looking; would von? No sir. Thomas Astles, joiner, said he had worked at the saw mills over 14 years. The deceased, whom he had known ' for two years, was a very careful boy. The witness corro- borated the statements of the other witnesses with regard to I the position of the deceased when found, and said he assisted I to cut him down from the strap. Besides his skull being fractured, the legs and arms of the deceased were broken. His brains had been dashed to the ceiling. Witness did not I know how the accident had occurred, but he had cautioned the deceased and the other boys about putting the belt on I the pulleys with their feet, and told them to be careful with - the saws.—By Mr. Richmond: He did not hear the saw started that morning.—By a Juryman: He did not know why deceased went into the shed that morning.—By the Coroner: He did not know that there was a piece of wood specially provided for pushing the belt off the pulley.—The Coroner asked if there was any way by which the belt and pulley could be fenced off, but witness said he did not know whether they could work with it.—By Mr. Lewis: There was no more danger in working the saw in question than any other. Mr. Richmond was then sworn, and said on Tuesday last he visited Mr. Carlile's works, and on entering the machine room he found that one of the beams which supported the shaft had been torn out of its socket, and the :shaft was vary much bent, The boy seemed to have been killed by his head dashing against the wall. He came to the conclu- sion that he must have been moving the belt with his foot on to the loose pulley. It was a dangerous thing to do be- cause the surface was so smooth he could hardly help slip- ping forward. The Coroner: Is there anything to flnd fault with at all?

Mr. Richmond said he thought the belt being so close to a door and to the ground eught to be fenced, and he had directed this to be done; and also a permanent fork to move the belt from one pulley to another.

The Coroner: That will be done? r Mr. It'chmond : Of course, it will be required to be done. If a proper fence is put round it the men cannot put their feet near the belt at all. He did not know that there was any actual blame attaching to Mr. Carlile, for although the belt was a dangerous one, it was not directed by Act of Par- liament that it should be fenced. The pulleys are scarcely a foot from the ground, and he thought all pulleys so low were dangerous.

Mr. Le-Win: But you don't think there is blame attaching to anyone? Mr. Richmond: No; I think there is no blame. There would have been had you been told to put a guard there, and you had not done so. Personally, I have not been at the works for some years, but Major Lowe has been there, and he directed certain guards to be erected. What they • were I cannot say, and he has left the district. The Coroner : Mr. Carlile, it says in the police report that you ordered the boy to cut some laths. Mr. Carlile said he never spoke to the boy that morning. The deceased had general orders that when he had nothing eise to do he could cut laths with the saw in question. _ _ _

Mr. Richmond said he did not think a Loy of fifteen ought to use a circular saw. Mr. Carlife said he regretted the accident as much as any- one. The deceased was a very good boy, and he never had a ward of complaint about him from any person in the es- tablishment. The coroner then summed up. It was perfectly de tr that the boy was accidentally killed, and it seemed to him that there could be no blame attaching to anyone. The de- ceased, it appeared, had been cautioned not to move the belt on to the pulleys with his feet but he (the coroner) con- sidered it undesirable that boy; of such tender age—only 15 —ehould be allowed to work a circular saw alone. The de- ceased was a finely made boy, was careful and steady, and it was a question for the jury whether they thought there was any blame attaching to the management, for their course of procedure. If they found no one .o blame they would return a verdict of accidental death, and as Her vi --eiestv's Inspec- tor had already given orders for a guard t to be fixed they need make no presentment on that pom. . It was an ex- tremely sad accident as the poor bey's mother had only recently been left a widow, and he was her main support. Mr. Lewin: I may inform you, Mr. Coroner: that Mr. Carlile has already done something for the widow, and intends to do something more. The Coroner said he was very glad to hear that. A verdict of "Accidental death was recorded.

PEDESTRIANISM AT ST. HELENS.—The sudden change of temperature produced a marked effect on the attendance at the Recreation Grbunds on Saturday, where two races were decided. The first was between G. Wilcock and G. Green, of Warrington, over N yards for a stake of £3O. Wilcock, who ,RS the favourite at 6to 4, won very easily. The re- arming event was between J. Greenell and T. Ashby, the latter of whom received a yard start in 120. As Ashby fell .abortly alter starting, Grecian was an easy winner.

div.head: 'WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: 'WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual general meeting of this club was held at the Central Hotel on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. E. M. Davies. There was a good attendance of mem- bers, amongst those present being Messrs. W. Ireland, J. Burgess, J. P. Kershaw, E. M. Harrison. S. H. Kenrick, T. Hingley, H. W. Cookson, F. Lea, H. Yates, W. Patten, W. Smith, jun., J. Smith, itc. The CHAIRMAN explained the ohle:t of the meeting, and c tiled upon The SECRETARY, who read the annual report of the com- mittee as follows :—Having arrived at the end of the season 1882-3, we now submit to you our annual report. 'I he first team have been very successful in their engagements, having played 19 matches, of which they have won 15, lost two, and drawn twc, the scores being—Widnes 15 goals, 21 tries, and 93 minor points; against 2 goals, 10 tries, and 46 minor points. (Applause.) With regard to the second team, they have played 20 matches, of which they have won 15, lost 3, and drawn 2, the scores being—Widnes 26 goals, 48 tries, and 106 minor points; against 3 goals, 5 tries, and 31 minor points. (Applause.) Nine matches have been cancelled owing to our opponents' inability to raise a team and frost intervening. The results are par- ticularly satisfactory, especially when we consider that one of the first team games (Litherland) was lost through the insufficiency of our team, 11 men only playing. In addition to the ordinary club fixtures, on March 29th a match was played between the club and a strong team from Manchester, kindly brought down by Mr. T. R. Sutton (Athletic News), in which Widnes secured the verdict. Two other extra matches have been played, one on behalf of the Widnes Cricket Club funds, and the other in- aid of the Widnes Accident Hospital. The proceeds of the match between Widnes True Blues and our second team were handed over to the Star of Temperance Brass Band as a small remuneration of their services. The treasurer reports a great increase in the ordinary gate receipts, being double the amount of last season. The playing members have had the benefit of this, half fares being paid all through the season. The ordinary subscription list remains about the same. A rather large item appeared in the balance sheet for teas. This is mainly owing to the teams who took part in Mr. Sutton's match being entertained out of the proceeds of the gate. In closing this repart we beg to thank our presidents, members, and supporters for their kiad assistance in enabling us to bring the season to a satisfactory conclusion. The report also gave a quantity of interesting particulars with reference to the season's play. The president's prize in the kicking contest was awarded to Mr. S. Morris, and the club's prize to Mr. R. Johnson. The following mem- bers were also successful in winning prizes at athletic club sports during 1882 :—S. Morris, £2l 15s. 61. ; M. Doming, £l3 ss; M. Patten and J. H. Smith, £1 55.; E. M. Harrison, £7 55.; D. Connelly, £5 155.; J. McCririe, £3; E. Farrell, 17s. 6d.; the total amount won being CO 15s. 6d. Tries were obtained as follows :—First team: E. Farrell 7, J. H. Smith 7, H. Mason 3, and E. M. Harrison, P. Corns, W. Ireland, S. Morris, J. Moss, W. Longton, and T. Ridyard 2 each, while C. Burgess, W. Patten, D. Connolly, J. Purvin, and A. Brown obtained 1 try each. S. Morris placed 14 goals out of 22 attempts, and S. H. Kenrick 1 out of 4. In the second team J. McCririe obtained 14 tries, W. Patten 10, F. Sampson 8, J. Sampson 6, J. Goulden 4, J. Davies 4, T. Ridyard 3, W. Tipping 3, S. Morris 3, W. Meagher 2, and the following 1 each :—W. Smith, J. Hardman F. Plump- ton, T. Fogg, F. Smith, J. Brown, G. Baguley, T. Wright, J. Parkinson, H.. Yates, T. Hugiaes. S. _Morris placed 10

, . goals and dropped 1, F. Sampsn 9 and dropped 2, J. Samp- son and W. Smith placed 1 each, and J. Brown and W. Patten dropped 1 each. Mr. BURGESS took advantage of this opportunity to say that he was compelled to resign the secretaryship, and to thank the members of the Committee for their kind as- sistance to him daring the past season. (Applause.) Mr. J. P. KERSHAW presented the balance sheet, which showed that the gate receipts at the matches of the first team amounted to £27 Hs 111 d, and those of ths second team to £l5 16s 111 d. The receipts at the contestlwith Mr. Sutton's team were £7 5s 9d, and the match for the benefit of Widnes Accident Hospital realized £4 15s Od. The total Income for the season was £l2l. After paying all expenses including the loss of the annual dinner on Thursday, there was a balance of £25 to the credit of the Club. (Applause.) For the railway fares of the first team there had been paid £l2 17s 51d, and for the second team £l3 3s 41d. Mr. BURGESS moved and Mr. LATHAM seconded a motion that the deficit of the annual dinner be carried over to next year's account, and it was carried without dieent, Mr. COOKSON proposed that the report and balance sheet as read be adopted. He had audited the accounts and found them quite correct. Mr. IRELAND seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. On the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. BURGESS, Mr. H. W. Deacon was unanimously re-elected the president of the club. The following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents : The Revs. George Bond, S. A. Spooner, W. H. Duggan; Dr. J. B. Booth, Dr. McDonnell; Messrs. C. E. Barlow, J. R. A. Gordon, T. T. Matthieson, D. Forster, and J. Morrison. The election of captain was the next business; and Mr. IRELAND, the late captain, said he should like to take advantage of the opportunity to thank the members of the club for the hearty co-operation and assistance he had re- ceived from them during the time he had been captain, and he might say during the time he had held every office in the club. It was with feelings of regret that he deemed it necessary to retire from active participation in the game, but although doing so, he did not intend to retire from the club. (Applause.) He should still continue to take an I active interest in its doings, and be hoped yet to have the I pleasure of seeing the club occupying an honoured place in ' the front rank of Rugby Unionists. (Applause.) It had always been his ambition since the club was formed to attain that position, and for it he had worked as far as he could, with the assistance of the other members. He thought the club had now arrived at a critical point in its career. Next season, in all probability, they would have to play in higher company than they had ever yet done, and it be- hoved the members to be as careful as they possibly could in choosing the management of the club for that period. Some people seemed to think that anyone was fit to be captain provided he was a good player. The idea was false. He had himself seen matches within the last year or two where it was difficult to tell who was captain. If a dispute had arisen during the game, it had been taken up by the mem- bers of the two teams, and they had argued until they were exhausted, and then they had mutually given in. (Laughter.) In the matches the Widnes club hoped to play they must have a captain who had a thorough knowledge of the game and the command of his team. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They would meet teams, he anticipated, Who were so site- ated, and if they could not conduct their team in the same way they might depend upon it they would not live long in good company. He appealed to them to be very careful in their selection of officers for next season. Mr. A. Brown and Mr. S. H. Kenrick were nominated for the captaincy of the first team. On a ballot Mr. Brown re- ceived 17 votes, and Mr. Kenrick 14. The former was de- clared elected. Mr. Kenrick was unanimously appointed sub-captain. Mr. F. Sampson was elected captz.in of the second team, and Mr. J. McCirie sub-captain. The CHAIRMAN in suitable terms proposed that Mr. J. P. Kershaw be the treasurer, and Mr. F. LEA. seconded the motion, which was adopted. Mr. H. Cookson was nnani- mously appointed financial secretary. Mr. BURGESS moved, and Mr. IRELAND seconded that Mr. J. H. Smith, of 6, Frederick-street, be secretary; and Mr. F. Smith, assistant secretary. Mr. LATHAM proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Ireland for his valuable services as captain, to Mr. Burgess for his untiring labours as secretary, and to Mr. Cookson for his thorough examination of the accounts. Mr. HARRISON seconded, and the motion was carried with acclamation.

The gentlemen having suitably responded, the appoint!. meat of the committee was proceeded with. The ballot resulted as follows :—W. Ireland 31 votes J. Burgess 30, E. M. Davies 28, T. Hingley 27, J. J. ; ' Latham 21, W. Smith 21,8. M. Harrison 18, J. Williams 18, W. H. Long- ton 16, Paton 14, Farrell 12, Ridevate 12, Carlile 11, Yates 7. The first nine were declared elected.
A vote of thanks to the chlirman for presiding tet minated the proceedings.

div.head: RETIREMENT OF RUNCORN STATIONMASTER.
div.p: RETIREMENT OF RUNCORN STATIONMASTER.

Passengers to and from Runcorn railway station after Monday next will miss the hoary head and genial face of Mr. James Leach, the stationmaster. Under the rules of the London and North-Western Railway Company's Super- annuation Fund, all officers are requested to retire from the service at the age of 60 years. Mr. Leach has attained that age and accordingly retires. He entered the company's employ in the year 1854, and for the seven succeeding years was in the police service at Crewe. His exemplary conduct and acknowledged ability, caused his promotion at the end of that period to the inspectorship of the extensive district that lies between Stafford and Warrington. It was during the 11 years he held that onerous position, that the terrible accident occurred at Walton Junction, near Warrington, whereby seven persons lost their lives, and many others were injured. He consequently took a prominent part in the inquiries which followed, and was complimented upon the efficiency with which he had discharged his duties. IR 1872, about three years after Runcorn Bridge was opened, Mr. Leach was appointed stationmaster to Run- corn Since that time the line to Chester has been made, and the traffic at Runcorn has more than doubled, but OB every occasion Mr. Leach has shown himself willing to bear the responsibilities of his position, and able to cope with its difficulties. Very few accidents have occurred during his term office, and those have been of a very slight and casual character. Thus, while giving every satisfaction to his superiors by his steady adherence to duty, his never failing courtesy and urbanity have won for him the respect and goodwill of the townspeople, who, we feet sure, will receive With regret the news of his retirement. Mr. Leach will be succeeded by Mr. Appleton, of Tyldesley, near Bolton, a gentleman who has formerly occupied a responsible posi• tion at Runcorn.

1 A CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH AT ST. HELENS.—An in- quest was held by Mr. Barker, county coroner, at the Star Inn, Liverpool-road, St. Helens, on Saturday last, respecting the death of a child, aged two years, named Hugh Rogers. The deceased was the on of a glass work's labourer, who lives at 11, Liverpool-street, and it appeared that on the Wednesday previous at upset a basin containing boiling water, andwas so severely scalded as to cauee its death on Friday morning.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was re-1 tamed.

THOUGHT READING AT RUN- CORN.

In aid of the Free Library Lectures Fund and Camden Sanday School Band of Hope, a lecture on the subject of "Thought reading was delivered in Runcorn Public Hall, on Thursday evening, by the Rev. E. H Sugden, BA., B.Sc., Wesleyac minister, of Bradford. Although the sub- ject was one which has exteusively agitated the public mind during the past few months, it only drew together a some- what scanty audience, and the hall was not more than half full. Mr. F. A. Lake occupied the chair, and on the platform were the Revs. G. Hack, S. Mees T. M. Armson, and D. Llewellyn; Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, J. R. Frith, and F. Joule. In a short and appropriate speech, Mr. Lake observed that as far back as history and even tra- dition took them, they met with certain classes of indivi- duals who appeared to have been possessed of some strange and unusual power over their fellow beings. That power, however probable, had been somewhat exaggerated owing to ignorance and superstition. Still, throughout all ages, these men existed under the various names of magicians, wizards, sorcerers, mesmerists, spieitualists, and, more startling than all, thought readers. The question which had been asked for some time was "What is this power, and how is it experienced?" They spoke of man- kind in three divisions—as body, soul, and spirit—and it was perhaps a somewhat natural question to ask, in which of these divisions or combinations of them was it that this power was exercised in the spiritual side of their nature, ' while others told them it was exercised through a sort of exudation or atmosphere which each of them was supposed to possess, and that the will of one mue was exer- cised over the will of another. A later explanation was that of animal magnetism, while a still later was that of muscular action. Mr. Sugden would, however, give them a proper expression of thought reading as a part of the phenomena they saw, and as a minister of religion he felt -sure he would not have overlooked the spiritual side of the qeestion, while his knowledge of the arts and sciences assured a careful ex- planation of the mental and physical aspects. Besides this he possessed some part of the power himself, which led him (Mr. Lake) to believe that they could not have a better ex- ponent than Mr. Sugden.—The LECTURER alluded to speech and writing as marvellous modes of thougnt reading, but they were such common place methods that people had ceased to regard them as extraordinary. Thoughts could be transferred, it was contceded, from one mind to another without direct contact or communication, but there was not sufficient accumulation of data to enable him to speak with any certainty upen this kind of thought reading. The kind to which he would address himself would be where there was contact between the thought reader and his subject. Mr. Sugden then com- menced to illustrate this phenomenan, and the Rev. George Hack volunteered to be the "subject." Mr. Hack was in- structed to fix his mind upan some person in the audience, then upon some article the person was wearing, and lastly upon another person to whom he would like the article to be given. Leaving Mr. Hack thus mentally employed, Mr. Sugden retired, and on returning blind-folded; took Mr. Hack's left hand in his. For a few moments he held it against his forehead, then without the slightest hesitation he quickly walked to Mr. S. C. Beckett, almost dragging Mr. Hack after him. Placing his hand upon Mr. Beckett's head, he exclaimed "This is the man." A reply in the affirmative was greeted with loud applause, Which was repeated, when Mr. Sugden drew from Mr. Beckett's neckerchief a gold pin, which was declared by Mr. Hack to be the article he thought of. With Mr. Hack's hand still in his, Mr. Sugden thought a few moments, then rapidly walking to another part of the hall, stopped before Mr. T. Handley, saying he was the gentleman to whom the pin was to be given. Mr. Hack said that was so, and Mr. Sugden returned to the platform amidst the hearty plaudits of the audience. -The more difficult feat of discovering the number of a cheqae, which consisted of six figures was attempted. On the first trial, Mr. Sudgen wrote on the blackboard, three wrong figures, but in the second attempt be succeeded in writing the correct number. In a different manner he told the number of a £5 note or. the first trial, the successful experiment being loudly cheered. Mr. Sug- den dealt with the various explanations of these phenomena, an:4 effectively ridiculed that put forward by the Spiri- tualists. To disprove the theory of magnetic currents being the connecting media, he performed the delicate experiment of finding a person in the audience, his only means ot com- munication with the subject being a short wood rod. Mr. Sugden next endeavoured to discover the exect locality of a pain, which Mr. F. Fairhurst imagined he had in his little finger, but he was unsuccessful. His next patient was Mr. Watson who had an actual pain in his right leg, and with- out the least difficulty Mr. Sugden pointed out the spot. A winding chalk line was then made on the hall floor; and Mr. Sugden, besides having a bandage over his eyes, had a bag tied over his head, so that it was impos- sible for him to see any object; but standing about six yards from the commencement of the line, holding the band of his subject in his own, he walked Kraight to it, and with remarkable fidelity followed out the convolutions of the line. This successful accomplishment of a most difficult
experiment waa greeted with loud. cheers from a delighted

audience. The eiperiment of finding a pin, which brought Mr. Bishop into notoriety, was then attempted. The Rev. S. Mees secreted a pin in the coat collar of Mr. Unsworth, but after a prolonged search Mr. Sugden, who walked straight to the place where tne pin was hidden, had to desist. It then transpired that the pin had been removed, and it having been hidden in another part of the Hall, he suc- ceeded in his quest. He concluded a most interesting evening's entertainment with an explanation of his theory . .

of thought reading, which was to the effect that the " reader " was guided by the muscular action of the "subject." The mind being under a certain degree of ten- sion, acted on the body, which gave such indications that no difficulty was experienced in reading them.—The usual votes of thanks was passed.
FRAUD BY A WIDNES BANKRUPT DRAPER.

At the Liverpool County Sessions, yesterday week, before Mr. Meekly and other justices, Patrick O'Connor, aged 38, who had carried on business as a draper at 69, Waterloo- road, Widnes, was charged rith having, on the 19th of January and on other dates, removed certain goods from his premises with intent to defraud his creditors.—Mr. R. T. Richardson and Mr. W. F. Taylor prosecuted on behalf of the trustee, Mr. Samuel Tilzey, secretary to the Manchester Guardian Society for the Protection of Trade; and Mr. M'Connell appeared for the prisoner.—The case for the prosecution was that within four months of his bankruptcy the prisoner removed from his shop a number of bales of goods, some of which he concealed at Widnes and others he sent to his brother, Martin O'Connor, in Ros- common, Ireland. Previous to last autumn he had stock in his shop amounting to £650, and in the autumn he was pressed for money by Messrs. Trenbath land Co., of Manchester, who issued a writ against him. On the 21st of December following he filed his petition for liquidation. At that time he wrote a letter to his brother Martin, informing him that he had despatched three bales of goods to him, and subsequently at the prisoner's request his brother came from Ireland to Widnes. Together they sent further goods to Ireland, and several bales were con- cealed in different houses at Widnes. Goods to the value of £124 were seized at the Clarence Dock, Liverpool, while in transit to Ireland. In addition thereto £ll6 worth of goods had been recovered at Widnes by the trustee.—Martin O'Connor was examined, and he deposed to receiving goods and removing bales under the direction of the prisoner. He stated that on the night of the 13th January he collected the various bales which he had deposited in houses at Widnes, and placing them on a cart took them to the Clarence Deck at Liverpool. There the police seized the goods, and he r?- turned the following day and reported the matter to his brother Patrick. Between that day and the day of the statutory meeting he packed up, by direction and with the assistance of his brother, several bales and took them to certain residents in Widnes. At this point the prisoner's counsel said he thought it would be futile to allow the case to proceed further, seeing that there was not from the evi- dence adduced any doubt whatever of the removal of the goods. He had accordingly advised the prisoner to plead geilty to the charge, but he wished to make a few remarks in extenuation of the prisoner's conduct. An arrangement was come to at the first meeting that the prisoner should be allowed the privilege of buying his estate from the trustee under section 28 of the Bankruptcy Act for a sum equal to a dividend of 13s. 41. in the pound, and it was in view of being able to do this that he had setabout removing the goods to Ireland and other places. The whole of the goods shown in the debtor's statement of affairs had now been recovered by the trustee, and he (counsel) hoped that as the prisoner had been in custody since 26th February the magistrates would see their wav to deal leniently with the C,ISC. It was explained on behalf of the prosecution, in reply to this, that the whole of the goods bad been removed prior to such an arrangement for the sale of the estate of the debtor being suggested, and that such terms were enter- tained in ignorance of the fact of the goods being removed.' On the question of the goods being returned, Mr. Richard- son stated that Mr. Price (accountant to the Manchester Guardian Seciety) was prepared to show from the prisoner's own statements and figures at different times that there still remaieed about £250 worth of stonk unaccounted for. The magistrates. taking into account the fact that the prisoner had already suffered two months' imprison- ment, sentenced him to be imprisoned with hard labour for nine months.

BILLIARD MATCH AT ST. HELENS. On Wednesday evening, a billiard match was played at the Royal Raven lintel, St. Helens, between Mr. A. W. Morgan, of Manches- ter, and Messrs. J. Cook and W. Smith, of St. Helens com- bined, 750 points being up. Mr. Morgan, who is a well- known cueist, showed a superiority over his antagonist from the commencement, and ultimately von with compara- ti vo ease. His score of 750 included several large breaks, amongst which was one of 81, another of 69, and a third of 117 points, the latter including 38 spot strokes. Both Mr. Cook and Mr. Smith, as amateurs, showed some very good olay, and their score of 492 included a few coneVerable breaks.
THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
DR. GORNALL'S ANNUAL REPORT,

Dr. J. H. Gornall, the Medical Officer of Health for the borough, has just issued his annual report on the health and sanitary condition of the borough for the twelve months ending 31st December last. By order of the Sanitary Committee, to whom it was presented, it has been printed in pamphlet form, and it will well repay perusal by all in- terested in the preservation of the health of the inhabitants. The report is very exhaustive, and great care has been be- stowed upon its compilation. We append a few extracts :

THE BIRTHS AND DEATHS. During the year 1882 the number of deaths registered in .he entire borough was 1,057:— Registration di triet: Males. Females. Total. Warrington ... ... 522 459 ... 931 Latelatord ... 43 ... 33 ... 76

565 492 1057 From this total, however, must be deducted the following : Two deaths from scarlet fever at the Fever Hospital belong- ing to the rural district; 18 deaths at the Workhouse Hos- pital, amongst persons belonging to the adjoining townships of Newton and Haydock, to the rural sanitary district, and to the towns of Prgston, Bury, and Manchester. This will leave 1,037 due to the borough, and calculated on a popula- tion of 42,600 estimated to the 30th June, will give a death rate of 24.3 per 1,000 for the year. 253 deaths (exclusive of immigrants) were recorded from the seven principal zymotic diseases, which, calculated on the same population, gives a zymotic death rate for the past year of 58, the highest re- corded since 1875. This is chiefly due to a very fatal epi- demic of measles, and a continuance of scarlet fever. The births numbered 1,775, giving a birth rate of 41.6 per 1,000, against 42 4 in 1881, and an average on the last 5 years (1877 to 1881) of 44 6. The Medical Officer adds that the attention of the committee should be called to the very high death rate of young children. "Considerably more than half the deaths were children under 5 years, and 170 per 1,000 of the registered number of births were in- fants under 1 year old. The rate is not higher than that of other towns, and it was increased in Warrington last year by the prevalence of measles, but it does seem as if in our state of civilization some steps should be taken to lessen such a high rate of infant mortality."
INFECTIOUS DISEASES AND THE WORKING OF THE ACT OF 1879.

The following are the diseases reported to the Medical Officer of Health, under sections 23-25 of the Improve- ment Act of 1879 :—Smalipos, cholera, scarlatina, diph- theria, typhus fever, enteric or typhoid fever, relapsing fever or puerperal fever. Smallpox.—Three cases were reported during the year. The first case, a young man, a lodger, had been on a visit to Bolton, where the disease was prevalent. The case was notified on the afternoon of the 23rd July, and promptly removed to the Fever Hospital. The house was disinfected, all bedding and clothing being removed for disinfection in Ransome's stove, but sufficient time had elapsed for the disease to be communicated to the mistress of the house, whose case was notified and removed on the 6th%Bf August. Both persons had been vaccinated in infancy. They had the disease in its mildest form, and were discharged well. The other case was of a more decided character. The sufferer was a child, aged 8 years. Here again, immediate isolation at the hospital was effected on the 13th Septem- ber. The father of the child had, a few weeks previously, buried a brother from smallpox, at Wednesbury, and there had been recent communications between the two families. As the hygienic condition was favourable to the propagation of zymotic disease, it is a matter for congratulation that the infection was limited to these three cases, and it is only reasonable to assume that the prompt notification and isol- ation had some slight influence in preventing its furthur spread. Measles.—This disease at the time of my last report was ' assuming an epidemic character, and continued its fatal course during the first six months of the year. No less than lli deaths were recorded, 114 being children under five years, the average number of deaths for the last ten years being only 23. Though a great number of the cases were of a malignant character, lam sorry to say that the death- rate from this disease was materially increased by the igno- rance, and in some cases by the negligence, of parents, in exposing the children to cold during convalescence, pro- ducing fatal inflammatory affections of the lungs. Diphtheria was the cause of three deaths, the promoting cause in each case being sewer emanations from defective drains, associated with general insanitary surroundings. Whooping Cough : This serious disease caused 27 deaths It has been generally prevalent during the latter part of the year, and is still so. The public, through ignorance, are iü many instances directly responsible for its extension. At the vaccination station, hardly a week passes by in which I have not to compel mothers to take their children home who thoughtlessly bring them to be vaccinated whilst suffering from this disease, but they tritely observe, "it is only the chin-cough,"—" only ?" a very fatal disease -amongst the young, and, what is of great importanee, it frequently produces lasting injury to the constitution, and therefore ought to be avoided, if possible. Fevers (Typhus).—This dire disease has, on several occa- sions, made its appearance in the town. Two cases were introduced from other towns, which came under the notice of the parochial authorities, and were removed to the Work- house Fever Hospital, where they died. The third case was a resident of the town, who had slept at a lodging-house in the bedroom previonsly occupied by one of the above cases. He was removed to the Fever Hospital, and recovered. The other two cases (both fatal) occurred in dwellings where personal filth and overcrowding abounded. Enteric or Typhoid Fever.-Beventeen cases in all were reported, four of whom died. Six cases occurred where there was no apparent sanitary defect, in five cases there were drainage defects, and in the remainder there was general ilthtness and overcrowding. _ _

Scarlet Fever.—This disease, which was extensively prevalent in 1881 in a mild form and with a low death- rate, gradually assumed during the year 1832 a malignant character. THE NOTIFICATION AND ISOLATION OF INFECTIOUS CASES.

In my last report I referred at some length to the connec- tion of scarlet fever with the working of notification and isolation. As I strenuously advocated the removal of all such cases, wherever practicable, to the fever hospital, I feel called upon briefly to justify the position I took up, especially as a neighbouring city, notorious for its high death-rate and prevalent zymotic disease, has paid us the compliment of sending a deputation to enquire into the working of the Act. I am quite aware that the opponents of notification attribute the lowering of the death-rate in past years to the general sanitary improvements which have been carried out in Warrington during the last few years rather than to the working of the Act. Let me point out, Ido not imagine notification and removal of infectious diseased to be the "be all and the end all " of sanitary science. It is an adjunct, and a valuable one, to other measures for the pre- th scarlet fever has, in my opinion, been beneficial, and though our ultimate object, the immediate stamping out of all outbreaks, as not been reached, the nearer we approach the goal the better for the community. Without going into the question as to whether this disease can begin de novo, or always results from germs distributed, it is generally allowed that, where there are potent disease germs afloat, and a soil fitted for their reception, the fever develops into startling virulence and fatal activity. Now, in the year 1863, the germs of scarlet fever permea- ted the whole town, no less than 383 deaths being regis- tered, and the zymotic death rate being 19.0 per 1,000. It is the opinion of a leading medical practitioner that the influence of this epidemic has continued to the present day, and it is a fact that scarlet fever has seldom been absent from the town. Here. then, We have the infective germs, the first factor of the disease, always with us. How important it is to lessen the second factor, the proneness to receive the germs, arising generally from in- sanitary surroundings! Unfortunately, in Warrington there are still dread forces it is our duty steadily to combat ; there still exists unhealthy dwellings, overcrowding, defective ventilation and sewerage, impure air, sewer emanations, per- sonal filth, associated with improvidence, &c ,&c. Can any- one, in face of these too common disease factors, doubt the experience, nay, the necessity of notification and isolation, or any other method which makes for the prevention of zymo- tic disease ? Against the working of the Act it is asserted that " deep discontent is felt, not only by the medical pro- fession, but by the public, at the powers conferred on the Sanitary Authority." As regards the public, it is, of course, to be expected that at the first there should be some little irritation. They naturally resent any infringement of their liberty to do as they like for their neighbours' good or evil. But I am glad to shy a feeling of con- fidence is gradually coming over the public mind, and I contend that our precautionary measures, stringent and drastic as they at first appeared, new corn-mend themselves to the majority of sensible men. rhe change of feeling is exemplified in the appended letter from a shopkeeper: "I am very glad to be able to say that my dangt.ter, when under your charge, received the kindest treatment. I had a very decided objection to my child being removed until you put the mate so clearly before me. I really believe it was the means of stopping the spread of infection, as the rest of my family (10) remained in their usual good health. The hospitai is a great boon to the town. I should be willing to send any of my family if you. thought it necessary." I have abundant testimony of the same character. It is, then, an outrageous misstatement that there is deep dis- content. I venture to assert, that of the 600 families who have benefited by our hospital, there is not 1 per cent, but would acknowledge that it had been a blessing. As regards the fancied heart-burnings and hostility of the medical pro- fession, I can only say I have experienced very little of it here, my medical brethren being always ready to work in common with me. We should be taking too flattering a view of human nature, or treating the medical body as angels rather than men, if we imagined there were mot some sordid natures which viewed with deep distrust, ii not with open antagonism, any measures that deprived them of the fees they grasped at. 1 am happy to say . there has been none of this feeling shown in Warrington, and it is incorrect to say there is deep discontent among the medical profession. Opponents of notification assert that it leads to extensive wilful concealment, thereby producing an increased spread of the disease. This atatement is wholly unwarranted by the facts; concealment does not prevail to any great extent, and where it does occur, it is often from ignorance rather than wilful oppoaltion. . There has always been a certaiu claw of people who are thew OWII doctors, lad

when the epideD-1;s li7se that of 181 is of so mRd a type as to produce little or mo constitutional disturbance, it is not ta be wondered at that crs.;es occasionally escape notice. Take the experience of the pnblic elementary schools, which are frequently the cause of the dissemination of disease. In the height of the epidemic last year (1881) the examinations were held; and the masters thus write to me : Finney, Heath-side (600 scholars) :—" As a school- master I feel greatly relieved, and I think other teachers must feel the same. To have had our schools closed would have been a most serious thing, but now I hope that danger is averted. Cases as they fall out are duly reported, promptly attended to, and removed to the Fever Hospital for isolation. Speaking generally, I don't hesitate to say that I think the Sanitary Authorities of Warrington are taking a wise, a liberal, and a comprehensive view of their duties in this matter."

M. Spensley, Silver-steed School (200 scholars) :---" Out of over twenty families afflicted in 1881, I believe only three or four children were absent on the day of H.M. In- spector's visit (being actually in the hospital at the time, but all afterwards recovered), and it is my firm belief that had the hospital not been available, or vigilant oversight not constantly maintained, we should have been compelled to close school at least for three months." 44,F, Twiss, People's College (1,000 scholars), says : " During the epidemic, four years ago, there were 86 cases of fever amongst children attending the Infant School, Bank Quay, and last year (1381) it escaped almost entirely. In main school the attendance suffered but little. Mr. Demhztrst, Yatioaal School ,(600 scholars)." Though many cases occurred in connection with my school, isola- tion and disinfection were so promptly carried out that we worked the school as usual, and presented 600 children for examination" Could these satisfactory results have been obtained if there had been extensive concealment ? I think I not.

CAUSES INJURIOUSLY AFFECTING THE PUBLIC HEALTFI. These were fully commented on in the last annual report. I have only to reiterate my former appeal to wipe out the foul blots that are still in our midst, that endanger the lives of our townsmen, and are in most cases remov- able.

Might I again express the hope that the committee will carry out the suggestion I made 18 months ago, that a house-to-house visitation should be made for the examina- tion of the drainage, and their connection with the main sewers and ether sanitary conditions. * * * * " This would be an immense boon to your officers—indeed, I would go so far as to say that it should be the first step in your sanitary efforts, the foundation on which your further attempts should rest." INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. The annual report of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, a table of meteorological observations, and a record of the work done in the department of the inspector of nuisances, accompanies the report. With respect to the hospital, it appearsthat the total number of patients admitted since the hospital was opened on 28th May, 1877, was 736; that the number admitted since the Improvement Act received the Royal Assent was 659; and that the number admitted during the year 1882 was 228. The general management has been most satisfactory, strict attention having been paid to economy and cleanliness in every department. Of the 229 patients admitted during the year, 51 have been attended by private practitioners, and 178 by Dr. Gornall. During the year 6,042 articles have been disinfected in Rausome's stove, including beds, mattresses, blankets, rugs, sheets, carpets, &c., &c., and various articles of clothing. The actual cost of maintenance of all inmates of the hos- pital, including matron, nurses, servants, and patients is 15s. Sid. per week. Food alone averaged ss. Bd. Last year the figures were—Maintenance, 15s. 2d; food, ss. 6/d. per week.

THE INSPECTOR'S WORK. The annual statement of Mr. Ralph Norman, inspector of nuisances, shows in table No. 1 the amount of bad meat and other unwholesome commodities seized and destroyed during the year. To seizures comprised five of beef and one each of liver, sausages, pork, and fruit, nine in all. The total weight of the articles seized was 1,0241b5. The number of persons summoned was four, the number of orders obtained eight, and the number of convictions three. The amount of penalties imposed realised £l5. Table No. 2 shows the sanitary work for the year as follows: Nuisances reported by In- spector, 264; notices served to abate nuisances, 367; nuisances removed or abated, 272; houses disinfected, 192; and old privies converted to pail system, 254. Table No. 3 shows the number of houses visited by the in- spector, reported, and dealt with for infringement of lodg- ing bye-laws, during the year, as follows —Houses visited by inspector, 149; cases reported for infringement of bye- laws, 28; cases dismissed by Sanitary Committe, 15; cases heard and decided by magistrates, 12; penalties imposed by magistrates, 9; and cases dismissed by magistrates, 3. , Amount of penalties imposed by magistrates, £3 2s ad. The following is a table of general information :—Slaughter- houses within the borough, 14; bakehouses, 73 ; public urinals, 10; public mortuary, 1 ; public baths, 1; privies on pall system, 7,211; privies on midden system, 140; and water closets (about), 400.

div.head: WELSH WESLEYANISM AT WIDNES.
div.p: WELSH WESLEYANISM AT WIDNES.
SALE OF WORK.

The Welsh Wesleyans of Widnes are zealously striving to raise funds for the erection of a new chapel. At present they worship, and have done for the past 25 years, in a somewhat dilapidated edifice in Cromwell-street, a locality not regarded as suitable for the site of a place of worship. About twelve months ago, therefore, it was decided to build a new chapel in a more central part of the town. By various means, including the balding of a bazaar and a concert, about £3OO has been obtained for this object. There is still required a further sum of £BOO. The 'Sale of the old chapel whl doubtless realise a good sum, and when the fund has reached a certain limit, the North Wales Building Fund Committee will make a grant of several hundred pounds. The members are lending their energies to the attainment of this limit, and on Tues- day a sale of work was held irr Lacey-street Wesleyan school-room. There were two stalls containing a variety of articles, and a refreshment stall, with a tempting array of edibles. No. I stall was under the superintenden of Mrs. Roberts (Alexandra-terrace), who was assisted by Mrs. Crawford and Mrs. Rowland Roberts (Cholmondeley- street). Miss Evans was in charge of No. 2 stall, being as- sisted by Miss Kenrick, Mrs. John Roberts, and Miss Tilley. The refreshment stall was in care Mrs. Rowland Roberts, Mrs. Lord, and Mrs. Jones (Irwell-street). There was only a moderate attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Mr. John Houghton, who was supported by the Rev. D. A. Richards, the Rev. D. Davis. and Mr. Roberts.—Mr. HouGferosr said he was exceedingly sorry there were so few persons present, but had he been aware of the fact before, it would not have prevented him from coming amongst them that day. He was exceedingly glad under the circumstances to help them in any way he could. He dare- say it would be about 36 years since he first knew Methodism in Widnes, and during the period that had elapsed he had enjoyed many precious privileges. Abcut 28 years ago be first made the acquaintance of their old friends Mr. and Mrs. Roberts, but he was not then aware that there was such a body as the Welsh Wesleyans. For two years the Welsh and the English Wesleyans worshipped together in a room over the "Iron Bridge," and afterwards i they entered together a chapel in Sutton-lane. Then the Welsh Wesleyane who could not understand the English language became so numerous that for three or four years they worked anxiously, zealously, and unitedly to procure a chapel for themselves, and they were not satisfied until they had reared a church wherein to worship Cred, in Crem- well-street. He remembered very well taking part in the opening services, and he might remind those present that the services were conducted in English, by the Rev. John Walton, of Liverpool For years and years the Welsh Wesleyans were i-structed by ministers who came from Liverpool weekly, but the time arrived when they were able to support a "travelling preacher" of their own, similar to Mr. Richards. (Applause.) Now they not only found the place in Cromwell-street too small, but so dilapidated that it was not fit for worship, and they were putting forth their best efforts and energies, so that they might be enabled to build another House of God wherein to worship him in spirit and in truth. That was the one great reason why they had assembled that day. It had been asked why did not the Welsh and the English Wesleyans worship together. They might as well ask why the English Wesleyans and the Roman Catholics did not worship together. It was necessary that the Welsh people who could not understand the English language, should have a place where they could worship God in their own familiar tongue. (Applause.) He hoped they might be enabled, through the untiring labours and energy they were putting forth, to build a chapel for the honour and glory of God, a chapel wherein precious souls might be reclaimed, and made happy in God's redeeming love, until they reached their heavenly home, where there would be no divisions of language, but all would be able to worship God in love and ia faith. He had great pleasure in declaring the sale open. —lt was announced by Mr. Roberts that Mr. Houghton had presented the trustees with a cheque for £5 ss. (Applause.) The sale was continued on Wednesday, the receipts at the conclusion reaching the sum of £5O.

div.head: CATHOLIC MISSION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CATHOLIC MISSION AT RUNCORN.

ISt. Edward's Catholic Chapel, Runcorn, was the scene of A most Successful religious revival during the fortnight which concluded oti Monday evening last. During that petiod the Passionist Fathers Robert atid NarCellus, of St. Ann's Retreat, Sutton, near St. Helens, have conducted mission services, and, there can be little doubt, done a great amount of good amongst a numerous population in Run- corn. Each morning three masses, followed by a meditation, have been held, while each evening a service, which in- cluded a special devotional hymn, has taken place. On every occasion the sacred edifice has been crowded to its utmost capacity. Hundreds of "believers in the faith" who , bad not seen the interior of the church for months, perhaps years, have been regular in their attendance and devout in their demeanour; and considerable numbers of Protestants have also been present, and shown great interest in the ser- vices. The labours of the mission have been equally divided lyatween the fathers, who, we ought to state, received the assistance of the Rev. Father Fennelly, the parish priest. Father Marcellns delivered each evening a lecture explana- tory of the devotional exercises the Catholic Church re- quired from its members, and his lucid expositions seemed Ito be much appreciated. Father Robert fulfilled the task I of preaching, and his evening sermons were eloquently de- livered. He has a clear, powerful voice, and a rather grace- ful and impressive manner' which had an unmistakable 1 effect upon his audiences. His discourses abounded with 1 beautiful similes and picturesque phrases, but, nevertheless, ; were well adapted to his audiences, who could feel no doubt !of their real purport. He attacked the sin of drenkenness 1 with vigorous denunciations, and never failed to make known that misery was the lot of the drunkard here and hereafter. About 20 converts have been received into the ; church, and many indifferent members brought to a sense of I their duty. The concluding service of the mission took I place, as we have intimated, on Sunday evening. Fully I an hour before the time the service was announced to cotn- Imence every available seat was occupied, and when Father ; Marcellus ascended the temporary platform to speak a few j words of farewell, the sacred edifice was full to overflowing. : The Rev. Father thanked the congregation for their kind- ness during the fortnight, and expressed the hope that the I work which had begun at the chapel would not end with 1 the mission but continue for years, and even to the end of 'their lives. Considering the small congregation, it was surprising what a great number had attended the morning meditations, and he wished them to promise him that un- less they had some legitimate reason they would attend the Holy Communion once a month. He sincerely asked to be remembered by them in their prayers, and he in his turn would not forget them and their kindness. The Rosary was then said by the whole congregation, and previous to the performance of the ceremony of the renewal of the bap- tismal vows, Father Robert delivered a sermon, taking for his text the 21st verse of the 7th chapter of Mark. He said t the life of Christian in this world might be compared to the I journey of one who passed at midnight between two lofty I mountains, and who amid the darkness had jto find his path and to watch lest his eye failed, or his foot slipped, or his judgment misguided him. In passing through this world we passed through the valley of the chadow of death, for in this life we were in a valley, and over that valley there ever hung the dark shadow of death. Death was before all—before the . youth in his bloom, the man in his golden prime, the old man in the evening of his existence, over every joy, over every pain, over success and over failure—over all things there fell that envious shadow of death. We had all to go through this valley of death which we called life, but at baptism the church placed in our hands the lamp of faith, which cast its radiance clearly before us. It showed us the pathway by which we must walk. It opened out before our minds infinite and eternal truths—the infinity of sorrow for the lost, of joy for the blessed. By that light of faith the mysteries of the world to come were unfolded, and made clear to us, and everyone into whose hands the light of faith had been put at baptism, cauld not say they knew not the path, and went astray because they could not see it. The light of faith showed us the outlines of the enemies which lined our pathway—the enemies, the world, the devil, and the flesh. Who was it that with flattering voice and lying accents whispered poison into our ears? Was it not that powerful spirit of evil that denied all things, that denied that there was a maker for this vast, this beautiful, and well arranged world. "The spirit of iniquity worketh still," and that evil spirit that lifteth himself against God in the beginning, still worked with the same end, but in a different way, to make men forget that there was One to whom they were responsible, One from whom their soul came, and to whom that soul must return. The world at9out us was another enemy. The world was indeed a pleasant and easy one. It condoned every offence, and passed its word of absolution over every sinner. It told us not to trouble about the things of the future, but to look upon our- selves merely as the creatures of time. With death, according to the world, came the end of all things. But the world was a liar and a deceiver, and was based upon iniquity and un- truth, and into its mighty streams was drawn all the empires of the earth, and all that was lovely in art, even as the cur- rent of the river sucked in every small stream that flowed in its coarse. By the light of faith we had to fight against even that almost irresistible curreet of the world, so stem- ming it that we might reach the harbour of everlasting hap- piness. Then there was within us another world, for the world without was as nothing to the world within. Men knew not themselves. With study they could trace the course of every visible star, tell to a moment when the sun would rise, and understand the movements of the heavenly bodies, but when they came to study them- selves men were lost. Man was a mystery to himself. But ! man's worst enemy was his own flesh. We might master the spirit of evil that sought to domineer in the world, but could we resht ourselves ? There was that love of pleasure which made us trample on the hopes of the future in our insane pursuit of the gratification of the flesh. There were, no doubt, many present in that congregation who had within the last fortnight resolved to overcome the sins that had led them astray up to the present. Let him warn them agaiest that last enemy, that fatal love of drink, which drew them, for the sake of a moment's pleasure, for the sake of an hour's conversation, for the sake of spending an evening in thc company of one who spoke pleasant things to sin and folly.

div.head: LONGFORD DEPOT. ANOTHER REPORT.
div.p: THE LONGFORD DEPOT. ANOTHER REPORT.

The Sanitary Committee have :Pa's-9;d a recommenda- tion that an agreement be made with Mr. John White, agent for Mr. Beamont, for the use of a field adjoining the Depot at Longford, as a tip for ashes upon the terms con- tained in the following letter :—" Warrington, April 7th, 1883.—Dear Sir,—Mr. Beamont has shewn me your letter, and is willing to accede to your request if you or the Town Clerk will write a letter agreeing to the following condi- tions. 1. That you arrange with the tenant of the land so that he claims no abatement of rent whilst the filling up goes on. 2. That the soil is properly removed and replaced. 3. That the drainage is not interfered with. 4. That the filling up is done in such a manner as shall be agreed upon between you and me. 5. That the land be left fit for agri- cultural purposes, and to the satisfaction of Mr. Beamont, or his agent—Yours truly, John White. Thomas Longdin, Esq." _

Vie following report of the Borough Surveyor and Man- ager of Longford Depot was, at a recent meeting of the Sanitary Committee, read, adopted, and ordered to be entered on the minutes :—" Town Hall, Warrington, April 11th. 1883.—T0 the Chairman and Members of the Sanitary Cammittee.—Gentlemen,—ln accordance with the resolu- tion passed by your committee, on March 28th, That the IBorough Surveyor and Mr. Dinwiddie be empowered to visit the Manure Works at Birmingham, and to report to this committee the result of their visit.' The Borough Surveyor and Manager of Longford DepOt beg to report they visited the Birmingham Cor-poration Depot, and found that several additions and alterations had been made in the depot since the visit of your deputation on July 31st last. The particu- lar matters which engaged the attention of your officials were the working of the large machines, erected by Mr. Farmer, of Salford, and the condensing of the vapours passing from the evaporating process. We noticed that, since July last, the tanks which were then erected and from which the excreta passed into the large machine, and in which the excreta was partially warmed by the ex- haust vapour from the machine; had been altered by the addition of six rows of 14in. cast-iron pipes, which conduc- ted hot air through the tank, generated by ashes in a fur- nace constructed for the purpose. This addition, we were in- formed, did a large amount of work in reducing the excreta before passing into the machine. Hot air is also passed into dryer by a Gin, pipe, and drawn along with the vapours accruing from the evaporation in tanks by a blower to the condenser. Alterations had also been made in the shaft bearings of the dryer with a beneficial result. The figures given in July last, as regards the work of this machine, is borne out by the continued working, viz.—a charge of 16 tons reduced in 18 hours to manure, containing 18 13. per cent, of moisture. We were informed that the Committee are so satisfied with the result of the working, that they have erected two more machines, and have ordered two more of a similar type. Difficulties had arisen since the visit in July last, in condensation and destruction of the vapours arising from the evaporation of the excreta, and new condensers have been erected, consisting of large cast-iron tanks, containing three sets of 2in. tubes, with 48 tubes in each set. Cold water is constantly kept over these pipes, and after passing through the tubes, the vapour is carried through the fire of a special-built furnace before passing into chimney. At the visit in July, the vapour from condenser was passed into the fire under boilers, but the effect upon the plates and rivets was such that it had to be discontinued, hence the erection of the special furnace. Many matters of detail in the working and conducting of the depOt were examined, and will be of value in the de- velopment of your own depOt.—Yours obedientlyr, THOMAS LONGDIN, THOMAS DINWIDDIE."

EARLFSTOWN BLUE EIMSON GOSPEL 71447ERANCE MOVEMENT:A meeting in connection with this movement was held on Wednesday evening in the Mission Tent, Legh- street, Earlestown. There was a good attendance, and Mr. Weaver presided. After singing, prayer, (ic., Mr. Weaver gave a short address, in which he spoke of the exicouraging aspect of the movement, and encouraged alt to stand to- gether, and help forward the Gospel Temparance cause. He urged each individual member to do what they could to reclaim others in, their various spherea. of labour. Mr. Weaver then threw the meeting open for impromptu speeches and recitations, when there was a liberal response. At the close eight persons signed the pledge and donned the blue ribbon, making a total of 787 ribbons and 649 new pledges. -

HELENS and RAIN- FORD PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY by the Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Lancaster, was, on the 24th day of April, 1883, presented to the Chan- cellor of the Duchy and County Pa,atine of Lancaster, by MICHAEL McGREE, of Liverpool-street, St. Helens, in the County of Lancaster, Provision Dealer, a creditor of the said Society, and that the said Petition is directed to be heard before the Vice-Chancellor at the sittings of the court to be holden at St. George's Hall, in the city of Liverpool, on the 7th day of May. 1883, and any Creditor or Contributory of the said society desirous to oppose the making of an order for the winding-up of the said Society under the above Acts should appear at the time of hearing by himself, or his counsel, for that purpose; and a copy of the petition will be furnished to any Creditor or Contributory of the said Society requiring the same by the undersigned, on payment of the regulated charge for the same. LEWIS'S IN LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVIDING OF THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE' INSTITUTIONS THROUGH- OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM, Who are Lewis',? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known in London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago. and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always soil Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of prccuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints, and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved t s buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's cou'd hardly believe there could be such a change fix the 12etter in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would sarely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make the sale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20,000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite Price with Lewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not tilt after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and 3s 6d for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every householder to the great advantage there is in busing Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength FO very great, that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea; they are sure to be satisfied and astonished with the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's In Liverpool ' for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; It is only to send 2s in stamps to Lewis's in Liverpool, and In return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a bent carriage paid, to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewis's in Liverpool.
